Myths: - Tag: Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr Title: The Seven Who Brought the Head Home Text:

Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life.

At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move. At Gwales in Penfro they find a royal hall with two doors open and one shut — toward Cornwall — and there they pass eighty years in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head, forgetting every sorrow, until Heilyn fab Gwyn says 'shame on my beard if I do not open the door' — and opens it, and all their losses come back at once like a tide. Then they do as the head had commanded: they carry it to London and bury it in the White Mount, facing France, and the triads count that burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain. Manawydan, who had counseled the wedding, survives its end — the pattern of his whole life in one branch.

- Tag: Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr Title: The Counsel and the Marriage Text:

While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan the fairest compensation the tale can imagine: his mother's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed. Manawydan and Rhiannon wed, and the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship.

- Tag: Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr Title: The Thunder and the Mist Text:

They go up Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where, in the First Branch, wonders came to Pwyll — and wonder comes. As they sit, a peal of thunder falls, and with it a mist so thick they cannot see one another. When it lifts, Dyfed is gone: no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman — only the four of them and the empty land, house and court and courtiers vanished together. For a year they live by hunting and the kindness of the emptied land; for a second year they bear it; in the third they grow weary of it, and the tale turns from endurance to answer.

- Tag: Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr Title: The White Boar and the Golden Bowl Text:

Hunting, Pryderi and Manawydan rouse a boar shining white, which leads their dogs to a fortress neither has ever seen — and no one ever sees twice. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in after the dogs and finds a fountain with a marble slab, and on the slab a golden bowl fastened by chains, wrought with a craftsmanship he cannot fathom. He reaches for it: his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon, hearing her son lost, reproaches Manawydan for returning without him, goes in, lays hold of the bowl, and is taken the same way — and with thunder and a fall of mist the fortress vanishes with them both. Manawydan is left with Cigfa, and the branch's second act belongs to them alone.

- Tag: Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr Title: The Three Crafts of Hereford Text:

Manawydan will not beg his bread in an emptied kingdom: 'Let us go into Lloegr,' he tells Cigfa, 'and take up a craft.' At Hereford he becomes a saddler, and his saddles are so fine that Hereford's saddlers, losing every customer, conspire to kill the strangers; Pryderi's heir would fight, Manawydan counts the odds, and they move on. He becomes a shield-maker — the same beauty, the same conspiracy, the same dignified retreat. He becomes a shoemaker, gilding the shoes, and the cordwainers drive them out like the rest. Three trades, each mastered at first attempt, each surrendered rather than repaid in blood: the triads never forgot it, ranking Manawydan among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain.

- Tag: Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr Title: The Trial of the Mouse Text:

Back in empty Dyfed, Manawydan sows three crofts of wheat, and they come up the finest in the land. The first croft, ripe for reaping, is found in the morning stripped to the bare straw; the second goes the same way. On the third night Manawydan keeps watch, and sees a host of mice descend on the ears, each mouse stripping an ear and carrying it off. He runs them down and catches one — the fattest, and slow, and heavy with young. He sets a miniature gallows on the gorsedd and condemns her as a thief.

Then the ransomers come: a scholar, then a priest, then a bishop, each more richly robed than the last, each offering money for the felon's life, and to each Manawydan answers that he will not sell a convicted thief — until the bishop, pressed to name his terms, hears them whole: Pryderi and Rhiannon freed, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, no vengeance taken on the mice, and no spell ever laid on the seven cantrefs again. The bishop is Llwyd fab Cil Coed, enchanter and friend of Gwawl fab Clud — Rhiannon's jilted suitor from the First Branch — and the whole desolation was his long revenge; the mice were his own household and warband under shape, and the fat one his wife. Pryderi comes back with the gate-hammers he had been made to carry, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about her neck, the mist lifts from Dyfed, and Manawydan keeps his word to the letter: not one mouse is harmed. It is the Mabinogi's most complete victory, and no sword is drawn in it.

Syncretism:

Manawydan's one great comparison is also the deepest fact about him: he is the Welsh form of the figure Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], the sea god and guardian of the Otherworld. The names are cognates — Ifor Williams derived both from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, so that 'Manawydan' and 'Manannán' each mean, in effect, the Manxman — and the fathers match exactly, Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each a personification of the sea. What the Welsh tradition did with the inheritance is the interesting part: where Manannán strides through Irish myth as a god of mist, ships, and wonder-working treasure, the Mabinogi keeps only the sea-kinship and the uncanny craft, and makes its Manawydan mortal, patient, and wise — a euhemerized sea god filed down to a counselor. Whether the Welsh figure is descended from the Irish, or both from a lost common sea god, is debated (Mac Cana; Koch); the handbooks register the kinship and leave the direction open. In Manx folklore the same figure survived as Mannan beg mac y Leir, first man of the island, and gave the Isle of Man its name. No Gaulish counterpart has ever been convincingly proposed; the comparison is an insular affair, Irish Sea water on both sides of it.

Cultural Legacy:

Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Manawydan into English, and the Third Branch has held a special place ever since: critics from Ifor Williams onward have called it the most perfectly constructed of the Four Branches, and the trial of the mouse — the courtly ransomers, the miniature gallows, the terms exacted one by one — is the anthology piece of Welsh prose comedy and wisdom in one. Scholarship gave the name its modern standing: Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text and the Manaw etymology, and Mac Cana's The Mabinogi made the branch's architecture a set text of Celtic studies. Modern Druid and pagan practice honors Manawydan as a patron of craft, patience, and the sea-kinship; in Wales the name survives as a rare literary given name, carried less by folk memory than by the sheer durability of the Third Branch, which has never gone out of print since Guest.

Extended Meditation:

Manawydan is the Mabinogi's argument that wisdom is a kind of patience. Every test the tale sets him, he passes by declining the heroic option: when Caswallawn usurps the crown, he counts the cost of war and stays his hand; when Dyfed is emptied, he hunts, endures, and waits; when his companions are taken, he does not storm the fortress — he learns three trades and practices them beautifully in exile. Even his victory is procedural: a watch kept, a mouse caught, a gallows built, three ransoms refused, and terms — release, restoration, amnesty, guarantee — exacted one by one before the noose is loosened. He is the only hero in the Four Branches who wins everything he wants and kills nothing to get it. The sea-named son of Llŷr spends his great story on land, but the sea is in the method: he outlasts what he cannot fight, and the tide turns. The question the branch leaves is uncomfortable and exact — how much of what we call courage is only impatience wearing armor?

Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: manawydan.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. Manawydan Archaeology: Manawydan is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the Third Branch is real and visitable: Dyfed is the historic kingdom of southwest Wales; Arberth is Narberth in Pembrokeshire, and the gorsedd is traditionally located on the hill above it; the seven cantrefs of Dyfed were still an administrative reality when the tales were written. The nearest linguistic trace of the sea-kinship is onomastic rather than archaeological: Manaw survives in the Welsh name of the Isle of Man and in Manaw Gododdin, the district of the old North remembered in place-names such as Clackmannan and Slamannan. Cult:

No cult of Manawydan is attested, and honesty requires saying so plainly: no inscription, votive, or sanctuary names him anywhere in Wales. The evidence is manuscript evidence — the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, composed around 1060–1120 and preserved complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410). What the texts preserve is the memory of a cult, not the cult itself: a sea-god's son euhemerized into a patient counselor, his divinity surviving only in his name and parentage — Manawydan fab Llŷr, brother of Brân. His worship in the present is modern: Druid and pagan practice since the twentieth century honors him as patron of craft and patience, a veneration offered in the full knowledge that the medieval tale, not any temple, is his only scripture.

Iconography:

No image of Manawydan survives from the Middle Ages, and none was likely ever made: early Welsh tradition, unlike the Irish, left no figural cycle of its gods, and the manuscripts that carry his tale are decorated with calligraphy, not narrative illustration. His iconography is entirely textual, assembled from the Third Branch's own props: the sea-kinship implied by his name and father, the three golden crafts mastered at Hereford — saddlery, shield-making, gilded shoemaking — and the miniature gallows of the mouse-trial at Gorsedd Arberth. Every picture of him is modern, in book illustration and contemporary Celtic art that depicts the grey, patient craftsman of the emptied Dyfed; the pre-modern art-historical record is simply blank. Artists who attempt him keep choosing the same scene — a man sitting still on a silent land, outwaiting the enchantment — which is perhaps the truest portrait the texts allow.

Reception:

Manawydan reached the modern world by the narrowest of roads: two medieval manuscripts. The Third Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6 — a transmission chain in which professional storytellers' art became the literature of Welsh identity. The antiquaries met it late: Edward Lhuyd's Archaeologia Britannica (1707) first signaled the tales' value to outsiders, and Iolo Morganwg's Romantic forgeries muddied the record around them for a century. Philology then carried the name home: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed text and etymology, Proinsias Mac Cana read the branch's architecture, and the Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru tracks the word from medieval manuscript to modern dictionary. The triads, riding the same manuscript tradition, kept a second Manawydan alive — one of the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain. His is the record of a tale that never left the language it was written in, and never had to.

Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers.

Myths: - Tag: Math fab Mathonwy Title: The Geas of the Footholder Text:

Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead.

The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war.

- Tag: Math fab Mathonwy Title: The War for the Swine Text:

Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required.

At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock.

- Tag: Math fab Mathonwy Title: The Queen and the Three Skins Text:

Goewin would not hide what had been done to her, and Math's first act was redress: he took her as his wife and made her queen, so that the disgrace should not fall on her. Then came judgment. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third.

Each year's offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — the king took in beast-shape, restored to human form, baptized, and raised. After the third year he struck the brothers back into men: they had had punishment enough, he said, and been greatly shamed, and he received them back into honour. It is the most exact justice in the Mabinogi — transformation as sentence, a year for each skin of the debt, and restoration without residue.

- Tag: Math fab Mathonwy Title: The Stepping over the Wand Text:

A new footholder was needed, and Gwydion named his own sister, Arianrhod daughter of Dôn. Math put the question plainly — was she a virgin? — and set the test: step over my wand. As she stepped, she dropped a sturdy yellow-haired boy. Math had him baptized at once and named him Dylan, and the boy made straight for the sea and took its nature, Dylan son of Wave.

And as Arianrhod turned to go, she dropped 'something small', which Gwydion swept up and hid in a chest at the foot of his bed — the boy who would be Lleu Llaw Gyffes. The wand that punishes is also the wand that proves: in one gesture the age of footholders ended and the age of the Children of Dôn began.

- Tag: Math fab Mathonwy Title: The Bride Made of Flowers Text:

Arianrhod, shamed before the court, laid her tynghedau on the boy: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion's craft undid the first two; for the third there was no earthly answer, and it was Math who joined him in making one. The two enchanters took their wands and, from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet, fashioned the fairest and most beautiful maiden anyone had seen, baptized her, and named her Blodeuwedd — and gave her to Lleu.

The tale records no death for Math. The branch ends with Lleu restored and avenged, ruling Gwynedd after, and the old king simply withdraws from the record — the stillness at the centre to the last.
Continue.

Syncretism:

Math is the Welsh reflex of a pan-Celtic institution: the sacral king whose rule is bound by taboo. Irish tradition gives the condition its clearest grammar — the gessi of kings, the network of prohibitions whose slow breaking dooms Conaire Mór in Togail Bruidne Da Derga — and Math's footholder geas is the same machinery in Welsh dress, a kingship valid only while its condition holds. Mac Cana reads the Children of Dôn as the Welsh counterpart of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the name itself crosses the water on its own root: Cath Maige Tuired names Mathgen as the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish epigraphy attests Matugenos — both 'bear-born', from the *matu- that names the king and his father. Within the Mabinogi the root echoes across the branches: [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the Irish king of the Second Branch, carries the same Math- element. His closest kin are the members of his own house — his sister [[don|Dôn]]'s children, above all [[gwydion|Gwydion]], whose plots the geas licences and whose punishments the king's wand performs — and the co-made bride [[blodeuwedd|Blodeuwedd]], his one act of creation.

Cultural Legacy:

Math's afterlife is quieter than his nephews', but the Fourth Branch carried him far. In the twentieth century the branch was remade twice over: Evangeline Walton's The Virgin and the Swine (1936) retells his story as a tragedy of old religion and new, with the geas and the three animal years as its moral engine, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain made Math son of Mathonwy the aged High King of Prydain for a generation of young readers — the geas laid aside, the grave authority kept. Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) drew its haunting from the Blodeuwedd strand that Math's wand set in motion, the branch repeating itself down the generations of a Welsh valley. In scholarship he stands at the centre of the Mabinogi industry: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi fixed the text, Sioned Davies's Oxford translation carries it to the world's readers, and Mac Cana's and Koch's handbooks treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose, with the footholder geas among the most-discussed cruxes in Celtic studies.

Extended Meditation:

Math is the proof that a story's most powerful figure can be its stillest. He does not trick, march, or seduce; he sits, and the sitting is the kingship — feet in a maiden's lap, the realm held by nephews, the whole arrangement waiting for someone to notice that war is the one door out of the geas. What makes him great is what he does after the door is used against him: redress before revenge, a wronged girl made queen, a sentence fitted exactly to the crime and limited exactly to it, and then — the rarest thing in any mythology of punishment — restoration without residue. His wand does everything the tale needs: it tests, it transforms, it creates. But its deepest work is juridical. Math is the king whose magic is law and whose law has a measure — three years, three skins, and the account closed — and whose stillness is not weakness but the condition of rule itself.

Cult:

No cult of Math is attested anywhere: no inscription, no votive, no Welsh feast-day, no holy place bears his name, and the medieval church calendar ignores him. What survives is not a cult but a fossil of kingship — the geas binding the king's life to a virgin's lap, which Celticists read as a literary memory of sacral kingship, the office made valid by taboo. In that reading Math is the institution's portrait rather than its object: a lord of the Children of Dôn — the Welsh counterparts of the Túatha Dé Danann, as Mac Cana showed — wearing the costume of a medieval Welsh prince. Even modern revival currents have not made him a figure of rite. His true afterlife runs through manuscripts and scholarly argument, not worship.

Iconography:

Math was never imaged. The two great codices that carry his branch — the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest — are text without illustration, and no medieval artist, Welsh or continental, is known to have drawn the king whose wand made brides of flowers and brothers into beasts. His attributes are verbal: the hutlath, the wand of testing and transformation; the virgin's lap that serves as his throne; the stillness itself, which is his portrait. Modern artists have only occasionally taken him up — Alan Lee's illustrations for a 1982 edition of the Mabinogion give the Four Branches their most familiar painted face — but for most readers Math has no image at all. That may suit him: a king whose power is a condition, not a posture.

Reception:

Math's afterlife is the afterlife of his branch, for the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi carries his name — Math fab Mathonwy — and has done since the Middle Ages. The text rests on two pillars, the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), and it first saw print in the antiquarian wave of the Myvyrian Archaiology of Wales (1807), then crossed into English with the first complete translation of the Mabinogion (Guest, 1838–49). Scholarship made him a problem worth solving: William John Gruffydd devoted a monograph to the branch (Math vab Mathonwy, 1928), and Proinsias Mac Cana's The Mabinogi (1975) set the geas and the flower-bride within the comparative study of Celtic kingship and myth. The standing debates — the branches' date, their unity, the meaning of the footholder taboo — have kept Math at the centre of Celtic studies for a century, and the name itself has quietly returned to Welsh use as a given name. A king with no temple and no statue owns the rarer afterlife: a text scholars cannot stop reading.

Matholwch has essentially one story — but it is the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, the tale medieval Welsh literature remembers as its national tragedy: a marriage between the two islands that ends with the hosts of both destroyed.

Myths: - Tag: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch) Title: The Thirteen Ships at Harlech Text:

Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed, crowned king of Britain — was seated on the rock of Harlech above the sea, with his brother Manawydan and his half-brothers Nisien and Efnisien, when they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland, fair and swift, their shields above their gunwales. It was Matholwch, king of Ireland, come to ask for Branwen, Brân's sister, fairest maiden in the world, so that Ireland and the Island of the Mighty might be joined by marriage and grow stronger together. Brân consented, and the wedding was held at Aberffraw — and because no house had ever been built that could contain Brân, they slept in tents.

- Tag: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch) Title: The Maiming of the Horses Text:

Efnisien, the half-brother whose gift was quarreling, had not been consulted, and he took the omission as an insult to his honor. Coming on Matholwch's horses stabled apart, he asked whose they were, and hearing, he fell on them in a rage: he cut their lips back to the teeth, their ears back to their heads, their tails to the skin, and their eyelids back to the bone. Matholwch's men could make no sense of it — a king given a bride and mutilated horses in the same week. They armed for home in silence, which Brân read rightly as the beginning of a war.

Brân sent an embassy led by Manawydan to ask what recompense would content him. Matholwch was offered the full replacement of the horses, a silver staff as tall as himself, a golden platter as broad as his face — and, beyond all price, the Cauldron of Rebirth. The tale is exact about the transaction: the honor-price was paid, the peace was sworn, and neither was ever real again.

- Tag: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch) Title: The Cauldron of Rebirth Text:

Matholwch asked where such a cauldron had come from, and Brân told him: it had come to him out of Ireland itself. A man named Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and his wife Cymidei Cymeinfoll — a woman who gave birth to a fully armed warrior every six weeks — had fled the Irish king's plot to burn them alive in a white-hot iron house, and had brought the cauldron with them to Wales. Its property was this: cast a slain warrior into it at evening, and by morning he rises as fighting-fit as before, except that he never again has the power of speech.

So the cauldron returned to Ireland as a wedding-gift of reconciliation — a thing that cancels death but keeps its silence, given to heal an insult that would not stay healed. The irony is the tale's own: the Irish fought their last battle with it, feeding their slain back into the war, until it was destroyed from within.

- Tag: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch) Title: The Starling and the Crossing of the Sea Text:

Matholwch sailed home with his bride, and Ireland welcomed her; gifts were given, and in due time she bore a son, Gwern. But the insult of the horses would not lie down. Matholwch's nobles nursed the grudge until they drove their king to atone for it: Branwen was put out of the chamber and into the kitchen, and the butcher came every day and struck her a blow on the ear. All passage to Wales was stopped, so that no word could reach her brother.

Branwen reared a starling at the edge of the kneading-trough, taught it speech, tied her letter beneath its wing, and sent it across the sea. The bird found Brân at Caer Seint in Arfon and settled on his shoulder. What followed is the great set-piece of the branch: the crowned king of Britain crossed the sea at the head of his host — wading, for no ship could hold him — and when the Irish destroyed the bridges and his men asked his counsel, he answered with the sentence Welsh has never let go: 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and lay down across the river so the host could pass over him.

- Tag: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch) Title: The Hundred Pillars and the End of the Cauldron Text:

The Irish sued for peace on their knees: they would give the kingship of Ireland to Gwern, Matholwch's son by Branwen, and build Brân a house — the first ever made that could hold him. The house was raised with a hundred pillars, and on every pillar a bag, and in every bag an armed man. Efnisien came in first to inspect the peace, asked what was in the bags — 'Flour,' they said — and crushed each head between his fingers, one by one, until he felt the bone give.

At the feast the boy Gwern was passed lovingly from lap to lap until he came to Efnisien's, and Efnisien rose and cast him into the fire. Branwen would have leapt after her son; Brân held her with one hand and took up his shield with the other. Then came the battle the whole tale had been marching toward. The Irish threw their slain into the Cauldron of Rebirth and sent them back each morning, mute and fighting — until Efnisien, in the act that pays for all the rest, lay down among the Irish dead as if slain, was cast into the cauldron with the corpses, and stretched himself out inside it until the cauldron burst in pieces and his own heart burst with it. Of the Irish there escaped only five pregnant women, from whom the five provinces of Ireland were repeopled; of the Welsh host, seven men — Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu, Taliesin, Ynawg, Grudyeu, and Heilyn — and Brân, dying of a poisoned spear in the foot, who bade them cut off his head and carry it home. Branwen died of a broken heart on the bank of the Alaw, crying that two good islands had been laid waste because of her. Of Matholwch himself the tale says nothing more: he is not given a death-scene, only swallowed in the general ruin of his kingdom.

Syncretism:

Matholwch is a Welsh invention wearing an Irish crown, and the tradition knows it: no Irish-language tale names him, and his kingship of Ireland exists only inside Branwen ferch Llŷr. The honest comparisons are structural, and Proinsias Mac Cana's monograph Branwen Daughter of Llŷr mapped them: Brân's sea-crossing against the Voyage of Bran mac Febail (Immram Brain), the children of Llŷr against the Irish family of Lir, and above all the Cauldron of Rebirth against the cauldron-lore of Ireland — the Dagda's cauldron from Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standard parallel for the Celtic vessel of inexhaustible power. The Welsh and Irish cauldrons divide the two ends of the motif between them: Ireland's feeds the living, Wales's revives the dead — and takes their speech as payment. Arthurian scholarship, from Loomis onward, has long set the cauldron and the carried head beside the Grail procession of Peredur; the comparison is illuminating and unprovable, and this temple registers it as such.

Cultural Legacy:

Matholwch entered the world's reading with Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49), which carried the Second Branch into English and made the maimed horses and the Cauldron of Rebirth part of the general inheritance of fantasy literature. Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text for scholarship, and Sioned Davies's translation (2007) is the modern English standard. The branch's sentences have never left Welsh letters — 'a fo ben, bid bont' is quoted wherever leadership is discussed — and Evangeline Walton's The Children of Llyr (1971) retells the whole catastrophe as a novel. The cauldron motif, transmitting through the Welsh tradition, stands behind every modern cauldron that raises armies of the dead; Lloyd Alexander's Prydain chronicles drew freely on the Mabinogion's world. On Anglesey, the Bronze Age cairn beside the river Alaw still answers to the name Bedd Branwen, Branwen's grave — the tale's one fixed point in the landscape of two islands.

Extended Meditation:

Matholwch is the king who accepted the compensation and could not accept it. Nothing in the tale is more carefully drawn than the failure of the settlement: the horses replaced, the silver staff, the golden platter, the cauldron itself — a full honor-price, formally paid, formally received. And still the insult kept working, not in him alone but in his nobles, until it expelled the queen to the kitchen and the butcher's daily blow. The Second Branch is the Mabinogion's treatise on the difference between settling a wrong and healing one.

His cauldron is the perfect emblem of the settlement's logic: it undoes the death and keeps the silence. The men who climb out of it fight as well as ever and cannot speak — cannot say what the war cost, cannot forgive, cannot testify. Matholwch ends as he began, a king whose kingdom is decided by what others do around him: Efnisien maims his horses, his nobles disgrace his wife, his guests massacre his peace, his bridegroom's gift arms his own destruction. The tale does not even grant him a death. It grants him something more instructive — a marriage made in good faith between two islands, and the proof that good faith is not enough when honor has been taught to count higher.

Matholwch was never worshipped, and Ireland — whose crown the Welsh tale sets on him — never heard of him. The honest sentence is the whole one: no Irish text names him, no ogham stone or place-name records his kingship, and his existence is confined to a single Welsh tale, Branwen ferch Llŷr. Nothing attaches to him even inside the story: he comes to a wedding-feast and leaves at the head of a war, and the branch grants him no rite, no oath-cult, no grave-visit of his own. The nearest thing his branch owns to a holy place is Bedd Branwen, the Bronze Age cairn on Anglesey that belongs to his bride. What is known of him is purely narrative: a wronged king, a maimed stable, a cauldron, and the most catastrophic hospitality in Welsh literature.

Iconography:

No image of Matholwch survives from any period, medieval or modern, and the tale itself gives him no personal attribute beyond the marks of his station — a king among kings at a wedding-feast — and the cropped ears and docked tails of his horses. The iconography of his branch belongs to things: the maimed steeds, the Cauldron of Rebirth that yields living warriors dumb as the dead, the starling that carries his queen's message across the sea. Later illustrators of the Second Branch reach for those objects and for Branwen; Matholwch remains a function in a crown, the guest whose grievance sets the machine turning and who is forgotten the moment the war begins. The reader who wants his likeness must build it from the tale's strongest note — the dignity of a man whose justice was handled like a debt, and priced in silver, gold, and a cauldron.

Reception:

Matholwch's reception runs entirely through the fortunes of his branch. Branwen ferch Llŷr survived complete in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, entered print in the Myvyrian Archaiology (1807), and became world literature in the nineteenth century, when the first complete English Mabinogion (Guest, 1838–49) carried his catastrophe abroad. Scholarship then gave him what Ireland never did: a study. Proinsias Mac Cana's Branwen Daughter of Llŷr (1958) remains the standard monograph on the branch, weighing its Irish affinities, and the tale's cauldron has been set beside real metal since 1891, when the Gundestrup cauldron was lifted from a Jutland bog — silver-gilt, its figured panels of death and rebirth an irresistible, if debated, analogue for the vessel that raised the dead to fight. His name, meanwhile, stays a Welsh curiosity, built on the same Math- 'bear' element as the Fourth Branch's king — a Welsh ear wearing an Irish crown, as Mac Cana first mapped him.

Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which.
Continue.

Myths: - Tag: Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I Title: The Pillow-Talk Text:

One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht.

That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war.

- Tag: Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I Title: The Bride-Gift Speech Text:

The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight.

Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan.

- Tag: Táin Bó Cúailnge Title: The Debility and the Boy at the Ford Text:

Medb timed the raid for the cess noínden, the pangs of the Ulstermen — the debility laid on the warriors of Ulster by [[macha|Macha]], whom they had forced to race the king's horses when she was great with child. With Ulster's fighting-men abed, Medb marched the hosting of four provinces north — Connacht's own, the Leinster Galeóin, and the exiles of Ulster under Fergus mac Róich, who knew every road and ford of the way and, the tale says plainly, shared the queen's bed with Ailill's leave, for the road could not be found without him.

One boy stood against the whole hosting: [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], untouched by the debility, who held the fords in single combat and took the heads of the best of Connacht one by one. Medb spent everything on him — terms, ambushes, satirists, her daughter Findabair promised to a dozen champions at once — and the hardest price fell on Ferdia, Cú Chulainn's own foster-brother, whom she plied with drink and the promise of Findabair until he took the ford. Four days they fought; the gae bolga ended it; and the march went on over the body of the one man Medb could not buy twice.

- Tag: Táin Bó Cúailnge Title: The Battle of the Bulls Text:

The hosts met at Gáirech and Irgáirech when the pangs lifted and Ulster rose; Medb's army broke, but the prize was already driven south — she had the Donn of Cúailnge, and she covered the retreat herself, in the tale's most unsparing passage, when her gush of blood came on her and she asked Cú Chulainn's protection for her army's rear. He granted it: 'no coward's weapon is the weapon of a woman.' Fergus mac Róich, looking back over the ruin of the hosting, gave the raid its verdict: 'This is what usually happens to a herd of horses led by a mare — their substance is taken and carried off and destroyed as they follow a woman who has misled them.'

The bulls settled the account themselves. Finnbennach saw the Donn and bellowed; they fought through the night across Ireland, and in the morning the men of Connacht found the Brown Bull standing over the White-Horned trampled to pieces. The Donn carried Finnbennach's carcass on his horns through Connacht — scattering the loin at Áth Luain, the liver at Trim — then turned north for Cúailnge and died there of his wounds and his victory. Medb had her bull, and her equality, and the Táin's dry arithmetic: the two most valuable beasts in Ireland, both dead, and nothing left to count.

- Tag: Aided Meidbe Title: The Cheese of Inis Cloithrinn Text:

Medb outlived the raid, outlived Ailill — slain at Conall Cernach's hand — and kept her sovereignty into age, spending her last years at Inis Cloithrinn, her island on Lough Ree, where she bathed in the pool every morning at sunrise. She had killed her sister Clothru, and Clothru's son Furbaide had been cut from his mother's womb — whence his name, Ferbend, 'of the cutting' — and he grew up with the debt of it.

Furbaide found the queen's bathing place and measured it the patient way: morning after morning he stood on the shore opposite and practiced his cast against the distance, until the stone flew true by habit. Then one sunrise, as Medb came to her bath, his sling let fly — a ball of hard cheese, the tale insists, the humblest weapon in Ireland — and the queen of Connacht, who had moved four provinces against Ulster and asked no man's leave for anything in her life, died by her nephew's hand at the water's edge. Her grave, the local tradition says, is the great cairn on Knocknarea in Sligo, where she stands buried upright, facing Ulster.

Syncretism:

The Welsh corpus preserves no Medb — but it preserves her word: Welsh meddw, 'drunk', is the same adjective, and the Mabinogi gives the Brythonic side of the theme she embodies: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] arriving as a mounted marvel no rider can catch, and the footholder Goewin whose office is bound to Math's life, are the Welsh faces of the kingship-and-goddess complex that Mac Cana traced through Irish literature. Medb's deepest kin are lexical and ritual at once. Her name is the same word as the drink by which kings were made: the Irish inauguration knew the banais ríghe, the 'wedding-feast of kingship', in which the goddess of the territory offered the king the cup — or the bed — and scholars since Mac Cana's foundational study of king and goddess have read Medb of Crúachan as that figure euhemerized into a queen. The tradition kept a second Medb to prove the point: Medb Lethderg of Tara, of whom the Book of Leinster records that she slept with nine kings of Ireland and that no king ruled at Tara who had not slept with her. Her closest kin inside the lexicon are the pantheon's other keepers of the land's consent: [[macha|Macha]], whose curse opened Ulster to her army, and [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]], who rides the same war-paths from the Otherworld side.

Cultural Legacy:

The Táin's modern reception made Medb the most argued-over woman in Irish literature. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) carried the epic into English; Thomas Kinsella's translation (1969), with Louis le Brocquy's ink drawings, fixed the Táin as the Irish national epic for the modern reader — and Medb at its centre as its engine, not its ornament. Scholarship split over her nature: Mac Cana read her as the sovereignty goddess of Connacht demoted to a queen, the standing type-case of the king-and-goddess theme; more skeptical voices, notably J. P. Mallory's, have tested the Táin against the Iron Age record and found a tale shaped by its medieval tellers rather than a window on the pagan past. Popular culture settled the argument in its own way: the Anglicized Maeve has become one of the most fashionable Irish girls' names in the English-speaking world, and 'Queen Maeve' — the woman who wrote her own terms, chose her own husbands, and out-argued every man in the tale — stands as a feminist icon far beyond the universities. The cairn on Knocknarea that folklore calls her grave draws climbers every summer; the visitor centre at Rathcroghan interprets her rath; and in Irish itself Meadhbh never left: the living name has meant the same ungovernable queen for twelve hundred years of the written language.

Extended Meditation:

Medb is the only great figure in the Celtic corpus who insists, in her own voice, on being counted equal — and then proves the point by going to war over the one item on which she was not. Read her as a goddess and she is sovereignty itself, the land auditing its king; read her as a woman and she is something rarer in medieval literature: a ruler whose motives are entirely legible and entirely her own. The pillow-talk is not vanity. It is the whole doctrine of her queenship in one scene — that the account must balance, that consent is owed to her and not by her, that a husband is a choice with terms attached.

The tradition punishes her and cannot dismiss her. The raid ends in ruin, the bulls destroy each other, the covering of the retreat is hers to do in the tale's most humiliating passage — and afterward she goes home and keeps the throne, keeps her terms, keeps choosing, until a nephew's measured patience and a piece of cheese end her at her morning bath. Medb asks the question the audit poses: what would you move an army to keep equal — and what, when the counting is done, was ever actually at stake?

Original Script Note:

Old Irish writes the name Medb (genitive Medba) in the Insular Latin script of the great codices — Lebor na hUidre and the Book of Leinster preserve the Táin; normalized Old Irish spells it with plain Latin letters and no diacritic. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, carries the name-type exactly once, and in the most suggestive place in Ireland: on a stone in the Oweynagat cave at Rathcroghan, Medb's own royal complex, reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI — '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb'. Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: medb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

The textual witnesses are exact: the oldest substantially complete Táin (Recension I) is in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow, written at Clonmacnoise around 1106, and the fullest recension in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; O'Rahilly's editions are the modern bases. J. P. Mallory's In Search of the Irish Dreamtime (2016) is the standard archaeological cross-examination of the whole epic. Cult:

No festival, priesthood, or votive of Medb is recorded anywhere in the surviving medieval corpus — her worship, if worship is the word, was folded into kingship itself. What the texts dramatize is the sovereignty transaction at her seat: the offering of the cup and the night audit of wealth at Crúachan, the royal complex the tales treat as the ritual capital of Connacht. Around her person gathered a real ceremonial landscape that never needed her name carved on it — Rathcroghan's mound, Oweynagat's cave from which the Otherworld's herds and armies issue at Samain in the tales, and the great cairn on Knocknarea that folklore calls her grave. Later folk practice kept the sites rather than the goddess: seasonal climbs to Miosgán Meadhbha persisted within living memory, and the cave draws visitors still. The honest summary is that Medb's cult survives as landscape and story, not as liturgy.

Iconography:

No image of Medb survives from before the modern era — no carved stone, no manuscript figure, no Insular initial gives her a face. The medieval texts supply what attributes she has, and they are regalia rather than signs: the chariot at the ford, the counted wealth of the pillow-talk, the bride-gift weighed in red gold, the morning bath at Inis Cloithrinn. Irish art of the period simply did not illustrate the Ulster cycle, so the queen who dominates Ireland's greatest epic went unportrayed for a thousand years. Her visual tradition begins with the Celtic Revival, when translators and painters of the Irish twilight gave her a body at last — crowned, mounted, arguing — an image assembled from the words of the Táin rather than from any antique original.

Reception:

Medb's afterlife is the afterlife of the book that carries her. The Táin lived in the mouths of storytellers before it was written, and its two great medieval recensions — Lebor na hUidre (c. 1106) and the Book of Leinster (c. 1150) — fixed the text scholars still edit. The early modern tradition kept retelling her: Geoffrey Keating rehearsed the whole saga-history in Foras Feasa ar Éirinn (c. 1634). Her modern recovery ran through translation: Charlotte Brooke's Reliques of Irish Poetry (1789) first carried Irish epic verse into English; Standish O'Grady's bardic histories (1878–80) made the Táin a national epic; Winifred Faraday (1904) and Joseph Dunn (1914) gave English readers complete Táins for the first time. The scholarly tradition then took her measure — Thurneysen's structural study of the saga (1921), Kenneth Jackson's claim that the Táin preserves a genuine Iron Age window (1964), and the long debate those provoked. The epic's translation history is, in large part, her biography.

Midir — Old Irish Mídir, styled the Proud — is the lord of the síd of Brí Léith and the central figure of Tochmarc Étaíne. His power is the strangest of the síd-lords: not the spear but the board game, the wager, and the patience that spans two lifetimes of the same woman. He fostered [[aengus|Óengus]], won Étaín by her father's impossible labors, and took her back at a fidchell board in Tara.

Midir's mythology is a single long courtship told in two lifetimes — the fullest Otherworld dossier in the corpus (Tochmarc Étaíne). It begins with a sloe-thorn and a bride-price, passes through jealousy, transformation, and a rebirth eleven hundred years later, and ends at a fidchell board in Tara and a war of spades against the hollow hills. Around that spine stands the fosterage: the lord of Brí Léith reared [[aengus|Óengus]].

Myths: - Tag: The Bride-Price Title: The Sloe and the Bride-Price Text:

Midir of Brí Léith was the foster-father of Óengus, and he came to Brú na Bóinne to visit his fosterling. While the boys of the Brug were at their hurling, a sloe-thorn sprang from the play and put out Midir's eye; he stayed a year in the mound while Dían Cécht, the physician of the Túatha Dé Danann, made him whole. For his reward and his heart's desire he named Étaín Echraide, daughter of Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland — and it was Óengus who went to win her.

Her father Ailill mac Máta, king of the Ulaid, set a bride-price no mortal could pay: twelve plains cleared of their stones and wood, and twelve rivers led out of the land to the sea. Óengus performed the labors with the Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir brought Étaín home to Brí Léith as his wife. The tale's arithmetic is exact: the god's first possession of Étaín was bought by service, the price of a wounded eye — and it was the one part of the story that ended peaceably.

- Tag: The Fly Title: The Fly in the Crystal Bower Text:

Midir already had a wife: Fuamnach, foster-daughter of Bresal the druid, and versed in her foster-father's arts. When Étaín came home to Brí Léith, Fuamnach's jealousy found its instrument — a rod of scarlet quicken-tree — and one stroke made her rival a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly of wondrous size and sweetness. For seven years the fly that was Étaín went with Midir wherever he went, and he knew her in her shape; but Fuamnach's malice outlasted his keeping.

The fly came at last to Brú na Bóinne, where Óengus knew her and built her a grianán, a crystal sun-bower filled with healing herbs — until Fuamnach raised a magic wind that swept her across Ireland for seven years more, to fall into the cup of the wife of Étar, an Ulster warrior, at the Bay of Cíú. She was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth: Étaín, daughter of Étar. Midir's house is the still center of the storm — the husband whose hall became the battlefield of two women's powers, and who waited out the centuries the tale demanded of him.

- Tag: The Game Title: The Long Game at Tara Text:

In her second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, high king of Ireland at Tara, and Midir came for her as the tale had promised. First he came in the shape of Ailill Anglonnach, the king's brother, who was wasting with love of her — three nights he lay beside her in that likeness and did not touch her, and so saved both her honor and Ailill's life. Then he revealed himself and asked her to come away with him; she answered that she would not go without her husband's leave. So Midir took the leave the hard way. He came to Tara and challenged Eochaid to fidchell, and game after game Midir lost, paying the stakes without stint — horses and treasures in such plenty that the king's greed was schooled by the god's purse.

Then the board was set once more, and the stake named was an embrace and a kiss from Étaín; Midir won. Eochaid deferred the payment for a month, and when the month was out Tara stood ringed with warriors. Midir appeared all the same in the midst of the hall, sang to Étaín the invitation to the wondrous land, took her in his arms, and the two rose through the smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, and the host of Ireland could do nothing.

- Tag: The Choice Title: The Fifty Women in One Likeness Text:

Eochaid's answer was the spade: he set the men of Ireland to digging up the síd-mounds one by one, a war of delving against the hollow hills, until the host stood over Brí Léith itself. Then Midir came to the parley, and the bargain struck was surrender of a kind: on the morrow fifty women came out of the mound, every one of them in Étaín's exact likeness, and the king was told to choose his wife.

He chose — and chose his own daughter, born to Étaín in the síd and hidden in the likeness of her mother. By that unwitting union a daughter was conceived who was exposed and spared, reared as Mess Búachalla, the cowherd's fosterling, and through her the line ran down to Conaire Mór, the doomed king of the Bruiden Da Derga. When Midir revealed the deception he gave back the true Étaín as well; the tale lets the god keep the last word and the king keep his shame. It is the Otherworld's coldest jest: the wager was never about the game, and the digging was never going to win.

- Tag: The Fosterage Title: The Foster-Father of the Young God Text:

Behind the wooing stands the fosterage. When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, his son Óengus was away with Midir of Brí Léith, being fostered, and received nothing — the absence that led to the famous quibble of the day and the night, and to Brú na Bóinne passing to the son. The tradition thus ties the two mounds together from the beginning: the young god reared at Brí Léith, the proud god's eye healed at the Brug.

The foster-bond runs both ways through the dossier. It was for Midir that Óengus won Étaín Echraide and performed her father's labors; it was in Óengus's bower that Étaín the purple fly found her one refuge. Irish fosterage was no light tie — it stood beside blood, and the tales honor it. Midir's proudest title is not lord of Brí Léith but the one the stories keep proving: the man who raised the son of the young.

Syncretism:

Midir has no cross-border witness of his own, and the honest comparison is typological rather than genetic. No Gaulish altar names him and no scholar has proposed one; where the Dagda can be set beside Sucellos on the strength of club and cauldron, Midir's dossier — the wager, the hunted bride, the mound that is a court — belongs to the Otherworld-king figure-type that Mac Cana and Sjoestedt trace through the Celtic materials without anchoring it to any single epigraphic god. Within Ireland his structural kin are the síd-lords of the neighboring tales: Bodb Derg of the Munster síde, who answers the Dagda's search in the Aislinge, and [[manannan|Manannán]], the sea-going master of the Otherworld's glamour. The Welsh corpus offers only a functional parallel — [[arawn|Arawn]], the lord of Annwn who likewise binds a mortal king by a bargain with a hidden edge — and the parallel is a pattern, not a pedigree. The comparisons instruct; none of them identifies him.

Cultural Legacy:

Midir's afterlife is the afterlife of Tochmarc Étaíne itself, the tale that never let him go. P. W. Joyce carried 'The Wooing of Etain' into modern English in Old Celtic Romances (1879), and Lady Gregory made the fidchell game and the swans part of the Celtic revival's furniture in Gods and Fighting Men (1904). James Stephens gave the story its strangest modern retelling in In the Land of Youth (1924), where Midir's arrival at Tara is staged as high comedy turning to awe. Bergin and Best's edition in Ériu (1938) fixed the text for scholarship, and Jeffrey Gantz's Penguin translation (1981) put the whole dossier on the general reader's shelf, where it has stayed: the fidchell game is now the standard citation whenever Irish literature wants to prove that its gods play a longer game than its kings. The name itself took no second path — no Angus, no Brigit: Midir never became a given name, a place, or a pub, and remains what the manuscripts made him, a proper noun with a single bearer.

Extended Meditation:

Midir is the god of the long game, and the tradition tells you so in his name before it tells you in his story: the handbooks gloss it, cautiously, as judge — and a judge is exactly what a wager needs. Watch how he plays Eochaid. He loses, and loses, and pays without stint, because the losses are the lesson: the king is being taught that the man across the board can afford anything, that the stakes are a language, and that the only sentence being written is the last one. When the final stake is named — an embrace, a kiss — the game has already been won for a month. The fidchell board is a court, and the house always already holds the verdict.

That patience is the Otherworld's whole tempo. A mortal wooing is measured in seasons; Midir's spans a thousand and twelve years, two births of the same woman, and a war of spades against his own roof — and he never hurries, because time is the one currency his kind does not spend. His foster-son [[aengus|Óengus]] parses time into a loophole and holds a mound on a day without a term; the foster-father plays time into a stake and holds a woman across two lifetimes. Between them the síd of Ireland teaches the same doctrine: the hollow hills do not take what they want. They wait until the wanting itself concedes.

Original Script Note:

The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Insular Latin script as Midir — the spelling Bergin and Best print from Lebor na hUidre; many modern editors add the fada and write Mídir to mark the long vowel, an editorial convention rather than the manuscript norm. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: midir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

Brí Léith is a hill by Ardagh in County Longford, the mound the Dindsenchas names as his síd, and the surrounding Longford bogland preserves one of the showpiece monuments of the Irish Iron Age: the Corlea Trackway, a massive oak togher across the bog a few miles south of Ardagh, excavated under Barry Raftery and fixed by dendrochronology to 148–147 BCE — a road of the very centuries in which the síd-lord's landscape was being imagined. The tale's other stage is Tara in County Meath, where the earthworks of Ráith na Rí, the Forrad, and the long banquet-hall trench called Tech Midchúarta still ridge the hill on which Eochaid Airem kept his court and lost his wager. The manuscript witnesses are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved, incompletely, in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre (RIA MS 23 E 25) and completed in the fifteenth-century Yellow Book of Lecan, the twin bases of Bergin and Best's edition; the companion Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's. Cult:

Midir's cult, such as it was, is the cult of the síd itself. No inscription invokes him and no temple stood to him — Irish gods generally left literature, not dedications — but his mythic residence is a real, named sanctuary: Brí Léith, the hill by Ardagh in County Longford, which the Dindsenchas tradition glosses as his dwelling, the mound that opens as a court of crystal and silver. Within the mythological frame the síd-mounds are the Otherworld's halls, and Midir rules one of the greatest: the Wooing of Étaíne and the Taking of the Síd make him host at Brí Léith, and the young god Óengus is fostered in his house. If anything like devotion attached to him in the medieval imagination, it attached there — to the mound and its wonders — not to any rite we can recover.

Iconography:

No image of Midir survives — no cross-slab, manuscript miniature, or bronze — and the texts dress him only in the standard beauty of the síd-lords. His one true attribute is the fidchell board: the splendid board and men the tale equips him with, which he stakes game after game against the high king at Tara until the stake is Étaín herself. Every other image the tradition offers belongs to his world rather than his person: the crystal bower, the silver thatch, the fly whose music betrays the reborn bride. Later illustration, sparse as it is, has seized on exactly one object — the board with its pieces, the longest game in Irish literature — and ignored the rest. The lord of Brí Léith otherwise arrives at Tara in every retelling as a man of unremarkable splendour whose single marvel is patience.

Reception:

Midir's reception is the reception of his tale, and the tale's modern life began in the great age of Irish manuscript scholarship. Preserved chiefly in the Yellow Book of Lecan (c. 1400), the Wooing of Étaíne surfaced for Victorian readers in the lecture-rooms of the Royal Irish Academy, where Standish O'Curry's pioneering lectures set the mythological romances before an audience that had hardly suspected their existence; the tale has rarely left print since. Comparative scholarship then made Midir a case-study of the Celtic Otherworld: Alwyn and Brinley Rees's Celtic Heritage (1961) read his games and wagers as part of the grammar of the síd itself, and H. J. R. Murray's History of Board-Games Other Than Chess (1952) gave his fidchell its permanent footnote in the history of the tafl family of games. Each generation's editors have since repeated the old verdict — that the Wooing is the finest of the Irish Otherworld tales — and Midir, the patient player, survives wherever Irish literature wants to prove that its gods play a longer game than its kings.

Myrddin is the original Welsh form of the name the world knows as Merlin: the prophet who went mad at the battle of Arfderydd in 573, fled into the Caledonian forest, and lived there as a wild man — lamenting his dead lord Gwenddolau, sheltering beneath an apple tree, and uttering the prophecies that made him the canonical voice of Welsh vaticination before Geoffrey of Monmouth made him the wizard of the Arthurian world.

Myrddin's dossier divides in two, and the tradition itself knew it: the northern prophet who went mad at Arfderydd and fled to Coed Celyddon, preserved in the Welsh Triads, the Annales Cambriae, and the Black Book poems; and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Merlinus, who carried the wild man into Latin and grafted him onto the Arthurian world. Gerald of Wales already separated them in the twelfth century: Merlinus Ambrosius, the boy prophet of Vortigern's tower, and Merlinus Celidonius — Sylvester — the wild man of the Caledonian forest.

Myths: - Tag: Annales Cambriae / Trioedd Ynys Prydein Title: The Battle of Arfderydd Text:

The Annales Cambriae enter under the year 573 the battle of Arfderydd, fought in the north between the sons of Eliffer and Gwenddolau son of Ceidio — a historical-seeming conflict of the British Old North. The Welsh Triads count it among the futile battles of the Island of Britain, brought about, in the triad's famous understatement, for a lark's nest; and the triad records the consequence that matters here: Gwenddolau fell, and Myrddin became mad.

From that seed the whole legend grows. Myrddin son of Morfryn, his lord dead and his side defeated, flees the world of the mead-hall into Coed Celyddon, the Caledonian forest, and becomes Myrddin Wyllt — the Wild — living from the forest's gifts and speaking only in verse and prophecy.

- Tag: Black Book of Carmarthen Title: The Apple Trees and the Oianau Text:

The earliest Welsh manuscript, the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), preserves the poems that give the wild man his own voice. In Yr Afallennau, 'The Apple Trees', Myrddin addresses the sweet apple tree that shelters him: he laments Gwenddolau, slain in the bloodshed of Arfderydd; he grieves that he endures want while once he rode at the head of warriors; he hides from Rhydderch's men; and the refrain returns to the tree, his one companion and hiding-place.

The companion poem, Yr Oianau, keeps the same voice — the outcast prophet calling his mournful 'oian' through the forest, mourning his dead, marked out by madness as the gods' or fate's chosen sufferer. These are not narrative poems but laments with prophecy threaded through them; together they made Myrddin the patron and mouthpiece of the whole Welsh prophetic genre.

- Tag: Red Book of Hergest Title: The Conversation of Myrddin and Gwenddydd Text:

The Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei chwaer — 'The Conversation of Myrddin and His Sister Gwenddydd' — is the tradition's most human document. Gwenddydd, wife of Rhydderch and sister of the wild prophet, questions her brother across the gulf his madness has opened: she mourns the warrior he was, the mead-feasts he no longer honours, the lord they both have lost. Myrddin answers her with prophecy — the fate of Wales, the coming of its deliverers — but the prophecy keeps breaking against grief.

The dialogue fixes what the poems imply: the wild man is not forsaken but watched from the world he left. Gwenddydd survives in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin as Ganieda — Rhydderch's queen, Myrddin's sister, and, at the end of the Vita Merlini, his successor in prophecy itself.

- Tag: Vita Merlini Title: The Threefold Death and the Life of the Forest Text:

Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini (c. 1150) is the wild man's fullest biography. Merlinus — poet, prophet, and king in Geoffrey's telling — loses his reason at a battle among the northern princes and flees to the Caledonian wood, where he lives as a silvester homo, a man of the forest, feeding on roots and fruit, snow on his shoulders, unknown to his own court. Rhydderch's men find him and drag him back; at court he laughs at things no one understands, and his laughter is always a prophecy. To a boy he foretells a threefold death: from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — and the boy, falling from a cliff, is caught by a tree with his head in the stream, dying all three deaths at once, as no human prudence could have guarded against.

The poem lets him go home to the forest at last. He appears riding a stag, driving the woodland herds before him like a shepherd of the wild; [[taliesin|Taliesin]] — Telgesinus in the Latin — comes to him, and the two seers discourse at length on the winds, the waters, the fishes, and the making of the world. In the end Merlin gives his observatory to his sister Ganieda, who takes up the prophetic gift, and retires to the forest for good — the mad king become the wise wild man, the only sovereignty he can still keep.

- Tag: Historia Regum Britanniae / Historia Brittonum Title: The Boy at Vortigern's Tower Text:

Geoffrey's other Merlin came from another book. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum of Nennius tells of the boy Ambrosius — a child without a father — brought to King Vortigern to be sacrificed so that his collapsing tower at Dinas Emrys might stand; the boy instead reveals the pool beneath the foundations and the two dragons, red and white, whose battle is the prophecy of Britain: the red dragon of the Britons, the white of the Saxons.

Geoffrey took Nennius's boy and gave him Myrddin's name: Merlinus Ambrosius. The graft made one figure of two traditions — the royal prophet of the tower and the mad prophet of the forest — and Gerald of Wales, a generation later, was already insisting they were two. The composite Merlin who results is the one the world inherited: prophet to Vortigern, architect of kings, and, in the romances that followed, counsellor of Arthur himself.

Syncretism:

Myrddin's comparisons run north, not east. The twelfth-century Life of St Kentigern by Jocelyn of Furness knows a mad prophet at the court of Rhydderch Hael named Lailoken, who foretold his own threefold death; a fragmentary Latin life of 'Merlin the Wild' preserved in the Cotton collection tells the same penitence, conversion by Kentigern, and triple end — stoned, fallen on a stake, drowned in the Tweed. Nikolai Tolstoy's Quest for Merlin argued that Lailoken and Myrddin Wyllt are two records of one north-British wild-man figure, and the modern handbooks treat the kinship as real, its exact shape unproven. The Irish tradition offers no namesake — the wild men of the Irish tales, Suibhne Geilt above all, share the type rather than the name: the king driven mad by battle who lives in trees, speaks in verse, and is watched by the court he left. Within the Welsh corpus his truest kin is [[taliesin|Taliesin]], the other great prophetic poet, with whom the Vita Merlini pairs him in discourse; and his own tradition split him in two, as Gerald of Wales records — Merlinus Ambrosius of Dinas Emrys and Merlinus Celidonius of the Caledonian forest, the tower-boy and the wild man the romances later fused.

Cultural Legacy:

No Celtic figure has had a stranger second life. Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini — the seventh book of the Historia — circulated separately for centuries and became the most copied political prophecy of the Latin Middle Ages, mined for omens by kings and rebels alike; the romances then turned the prophet into the enchanter, and by the thirteenth-century Vulgate cycle Merlin is Arthur's maker: arranger of Uther's night at Tintagel, keeper of the Round Table's founding, and prisoner of the Lady of the Lake. Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49) and the nineteenth-century Arthurian revival carried the Welsh roots back into English view, and modern scholarship — Jarman above all — rebuilt the northern prophet behind the wizard. In Welsh memory the original never disappeared: Caerfyrddin, 'Myrddin's fortress', still bears the folk etymology Geoffrey loved, and the Myrddin of the Black Book remains the patron of Welsh prophecy — the figure every later brud quietly pretended to be. The name now means the wizard worldwide; the temple's task is to hand the name back to the wild man it began with.

Extended Meditation:

Myrddin is the figure who paid for knowledge with the ordinary world. Every version of him loses something before he sees: a lord, a battle, his reason, his hall. The tradition is strikingly honest about the transaction — the prophecy is real, and so is the madness, and the same event, the slaughter at Arfderydd, gives him both. He is the answer Celtic literature gives to the question of what a seer is: not a priest with a technique but a survivor whom grief has put outside the human settlement, close enough to the trees that the future can get a word in. His sister comes to the edge of the forest to ask what will happen; he tells her, and stays. That is the shape of the gift — the future, at the price of the present.

And his name tells the same story in miniature. It is not a theonym but a place-name: Caerfyrddin, the sea-fort, Moridunum, given to a man. The wild prophet carries a fortress in his name — the ordered world he was driven out of, remembered every time anyone calls him.

Original Script Note:

The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Myrddin — attested in the Black Book of Carmarthen (NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250, the earliest Welsh manuscript) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), and in the Welsh Triads. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the restoration to recover — the digraph dd for the soft 'th' is orthography, not a lost character — which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: myrddin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

Merlin, Myrddin Archaeology: Myrddin is a textual figure, and his witnesses are among the most precisely identified in Welsh letters. The Afallennau and Oianau stand in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250), the earliest surviving manuscript in Welsh; the Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd stands in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410); Geoffrey's Vita Merlini survives complete in a single manuscript (British Library, Cotton Vespasian E.iv, thirteenth century). The landscape behind the texts is real and partly recoverable: Arfderydd is traditionally identified with Arthuret near Longtown in Cumbria, in the Old North the poems remember; Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) overlays the Roman fort of Moridunum, 'sea-fort', attested in the Antonine Itinerary and confirmed by excavation — the place-name from which, on the scholarly account, the prophet's name derives; and Dinas Emrys, the hillfort in Gwynedd where Nennius sets the fatherless boy and the dragons, yielded post-Roman occupation material in Savory's excavations of 1954–56. No inscription names Myrddin, and none would be expected: the early stones of Wales record the dead, not prophets. Cult:

Myrddin was never a cult figure. No Welsh church kept his feast, no shrine received votaries in his name, and the map of Welsh holy wells and saint-cults has no entry for him; the border country that remembered his madness remembered it in prophecy, not prayer. Later folk tradition did raise him toward the rank of Carmarthen's tutelary seer — the town's very name was heard as 'Myrddin's fortress' — but that is civic mythology, and antiquarian myth at that: philology long ago showed Caerfyrddin descends from Roman Moridunum. His true cult was one of manuscripts and political prophecy — for centuries Welsh poets issued darogan under his name, and a nation read its destiny in the madman of the Caledonian wood. That is the commemoration of a text, not the worship of a power.

Iconography:

The medieval Myrddin is text without portrait: the Black Book of Carmarthen gives him poems and no picture, and no Welsh illuminator ever drew the wild man of Arfderydd. But his other self was drawn constantly. From the twelfth century the Merlin of Geoffrey of Monmouth became one of the most-imaged seers of the European Middle Ages — the boy before Vortigern's tower, discoursing between the two dragons, in the illustrated manuscripts of the Historia and of Wace's Roman de Brut, and in the woodcut gallery of the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493), which sets him among the prophets. The iconography settled early and barely changed: long beard, hood or astrologer's robe, the bearing of a man reading the future as others read weather. Early-modern prints and Victorian stage romanticism added the pointed hat and starry mantle of the storybook wizard — an outfit the Welsh prophet never wore, though it has largely swallowed him.

Reception:

Myrddin's afterlife is the strangest transmission in Celtic letters: a northern madman became the Western archetype of the wizard. The Welsh dossier — the Arfderydd poems of the Black Book of Carmarthen, the dialogue with his sister Gwenddydd in the Red Book of Hergest, the notices gathered in Rachel Bromwich's Trioedd Ynys Prydein (1961) — kept the wild prophet in continuous Welsh memory from the thirteenth century onward. Geoffrey of Monmouth performed the alchemy, first in the Historia (c. 1136) and then the Vita Merlini: welding the northern madman to the boy Ambrosius of the Historia Brittonum, renaming him Merlinus — most scholars think, to spare Latin readers a name too close to a French obscenity — and sending him, mad again, back to his Caledonian forest. Thereafter the Prophetiae ran the medieval prophecy industry for five centuries, and the romances made him Arthur's maker, while Welsh letters, from Thomas Stephens's Literature of the Kymry (1849) through the modern editions of the Black Book poems, kept separating the native prophet from his Latin mask. The boldest modern attempt to put him back in a recoverable landscape is Nikolai Tolstoy's Quest for Merlin (1985) — speculative, and a fair measure of how far the journey has run from the Black Book's grey figure.

Nanna, daughter of Nepr, is the wife of Baldr the Good and the mother of Forseti — and the only figure in the Norse corpus who dies of a broken heart. When she saw her husband laid on his pyre aboard Hringhorni, her heart burst with grief, and the Æsir laid her on the fire beside him. In Hel she keeps her place at his side, and when Hermóðr comes to ransom the dead god, it is Nanna who sends gifts back up the road: a linen robe for Frigg, a gold ring for Fulla — love's tokens out of the land of the dead.
