The bꜣ enters literature as a fully formed theological concept in the Pyramid Texts and remains central through the Coffin Texts and the Book of the Dead. Its mythology is not a single story but a set of possibilities: the ba may ascend, return, lament, or be transformed, depending on the rites performed for it.

### The Components of the Egyptian Person (The Fivefold Self)

Egyptian anthropology is relational and composite. The most widely cited 'five components' are the **ka** (vital double, life-force sustained by offerings), the **ba** (mobile personality), the **akh** (transfigured effective spirit achieved after judgment), the **ren** (name, the marker of identity), and the **sheut** (shadow, the protective silhouette). To these some sources add the **ib** (heart), the seat of thought and moral record. None of these map neatly onto a single Western 'soul'; together they form a networked self sustained by ritual, memory, and ma'at.

### A Man with His Ba (The Dialogue)

The Middle Kingdom text known as the *Dialogue of a Man with His Ba* is one of the most intimate documents in Egyptian literature. A man, despairing of life, argues with his ba, which urges him to accept death and the continuity of the name. The ba speaks as a separate, wiser self — proof that the Egyptians experienced personality not as a unity but as a conversation. The text ends with the man reconciled, preparing for the rites that will let his ba prosper.

### Flying with Re (The Solar Journey)

Book of the Dead spells assure the deceased that their ba will leave the tomb at will, 'go forth by day', and join the sun-god Re in his bark. Pyramid Texts describe the king's ba ascending to the circumpolar stars. This mobility is the ba's defining privilege: unlike the ka, which is tied to the corpse and the offering table, the ba is free to travel the cosmos.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Bꜣ concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Human-headed bird** — The union of human identity with avian mobility; the ba in its standard iconographic form
- **Ba-bird** — A small falcon or sparrowhawk body bearing the face of the deceased
- **Heart scarab** — The heart (ib) is weighed; the ba depends on the heart's truth for its continued freedom
- **Sun-bark** — The vessel on which the ba journeys with Re across the day and night skies
- **Cartouche** — The ren (name) must survive for the ba to be remembered and effective

## Archaeology & Evidence

The human-headed ba-bird enters the archaeological record massively in the New Kingdom. The papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470) illustrates Spell 89 with the corpus's defining image — the ba-bird hovering over the mummy it rejoins — and the tombs of the royal workmen at Deir el-Medina, among them Sennedjem's chapel (TT1), show the ba drinking at the tomb pool and flying out by day. In the Third Intermediate Period the motif becomes three-dimensional: wooden ba-bird figures with painted or gilded faces were set upon or beside Theban coffins, and sheet-gold ba amulets were laid upon the mummy's chest. Stelae and coffin panels in the British Museum and the Egyptian Museum Cairo keep the image alive into the Late Period, and the bird's human face remains its constant rule: the ba must stay recognisable, because it is the person.

## Realm & Domain
Continue.

The **bꜣ** is not the Egyptian word for 'soul' in the modern, singular sense. It is the mobile, recognisable aspect of a person — the part that leaves the body at death, flies above the marshes, boards the sun-bark, and returns to the tomb. In life it is personality; in death it becomes the self that moves between worlds. Where the *ka* stays with the corpse and eats the offerings, the *ba* is the one who goes abroad.

### Personality

The distinct presence that makes a person recognisable — 'what shows forth' of the self.

### Manifestation

The ba appears — to gods, to the dead, and even to the living in dreams — as a visible sign of the person.

### Mobility

Depicted as a human-headed bird, the ba can leave the tomb, fly through the sky, and travel the Duat.

### Reunion

If the ba and ka reunite after judgment, the deceased becomes an akh — an effective, transfigured spirit.

## Across Cultures

Later Egyptian texts sometimes speak of the *ba* of gods — Re travels the underworld as a ram-headed ba, and Banebdjedet of Mendes is identified with the *ba* of Osiris. In Greco-Roman Egypt, the ba was partially mapped onto the Greek *psyche*, though the Greek concept lacks the ba's specifically mobile, bird-shaped iconography. Coptic Christianity inherited the word as *bē*, now meaning 'soul' in a more unitary sense, smoothing away the older plurality. Through Theosophy and modern Kemetic revival, the ba has returned as a term for the traversable, dream-capable aspect of the self.

Within the Egyptian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[ab|Ꜣb]], [[akh|Ꜣḫ]], [[amun|Ꜣmun]], [[ankh|ꜥnḫ]], [[apep|Ꜥpp]], and [[bastet|Bꜣstt]].

## Cultural Legacy

The idea that the self has more than one component — that part of us stays with the body while another part flies free — is one of Egypt's most enduring gifts to the imagination. Medieval alchemy, Renaissance hermeticism, and modern psychology all found in the ba a precedent for divided or layered personhood. Today the ba appears in fantasy fiction, in role-playing games, and in contemporary pagan practice as the 'astral body' or 'travelling soul'. The human-headed bird remains one of the most recognisable images of the afterlife, a visual shorthand for the conviction that we are not finished when the body stops breathing.

## A Meditation

To think about the ba is to think about what in us is portable. The Egyptians did not believe that a person simply survived death; they believed that a person survived in several different modes at once. The corpse stayed in the tomb, the life-force fed at the offering table, the name waited to be spoken, and the ba — the ba went out into the light. This is not confusion. It is a more honest anthropology than the single, disembodied soul that later traditions inherited.

The ba asks us to recognise that identity is not a substance but a relationship: between body and image, memory and presence, the one who stays and the one who goes. When we say of someone that they 'live on in memory', we are speaking the language of the ba. When we feel our own personality leave a room and travel elsewhere in a dream, we are touching what the Egyptians named. The ba is the part of us that is visible to others even when the body is absent — the manifest self, still in motion.

# The hidden history behind Baꜥal

Behind the modern ASCII form *baal* hides a much longer story. **Baꜥal** reaches back through manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral tradition long before it ever touched a keyboard, and every mark in the restored spelling is a receipt from that journey. In what follows we trace the name from its Ugaritic attestations through its mythology, its cult, its symbols, and its afterlife in other cultures — and we show how the PuniCodex project turned that philological record into a Unicode domain that resolves today. The history was never lost. It was only waiting for the infrastructure to catch up.

## Overview

**Baꜥal** (*baal*) — Rider of the Clouds · Lord of the Storm — is the storm and fertility god of the Canaanite pantheon, catalogued in this edition under the domain "Storm God, Lord of the Heavens." The name began as a title — *baʿlu*, "lord," a word applied to many local deities — and became at Ugarit the proper name of one god above all others.

Baꜥal is the **storm made king**. In a land where rain is life and drought is death, he is the deity who rides the clouds, shatters the sea-monster, and opens his palace windows so that the rains may fall. He is young, vigorous, and hungry for a throne — yet even his kingship depends on the older god Ēl. The Baꜥal Cycle is the great myth of his rise, death, and return.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Baꜥal** and serves its temple at [baꜥal.com](https://xn--baal-re8o.com). The restoration preserves the voiced pharyngeal *ʿayin* — the signature consonant of the name — through the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ, U+A724), the only DNS-registrable stand-in for a sound the Latin alphabet never had; this single distinctive phoneme, which the ASCII form erases, places the name in Tier 1. The ASCII *baal* doubles the vowel and loses the throat entirely.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Ugaritic as **𐎁𐎓𐎍** — Northwest Semitic cuneiform alphabet, attested Late Bronze Age, c. 1400–1200 BCE, in Ugarit (modern Ras Shamra, Syria). The script is written left-to-right.

The scholarly transliteration is *Baꜥal* (Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform), giving the normalized reading /ˈbaʕlu/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is written 𐎁𐎓𐎍 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet.
- Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability.
- Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons.
- The Unicode restoration Baꜥal is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

Ugaritic writes the name 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (b-ʿ-l), literally 'lord.' The middle sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative. Because Semitic ʿayin is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX renders it with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724). In many contexts the name is an appellative rather than a personal name; at Ugarit the storm god is often called Baꜥlu-Haddu.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/baʕ.al/** — Ugaritic/Phoenician Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **ba-** — Plain voiced bilabial [b] plus open [a]; the word means 'lord, owner, husband' across Semitic languages.
- **-ʕal** — Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] plus [a] and [l]. The pharyngeal is the signature consonant; we render it with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for registrability.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Ugaritic** — 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl), 'lord'; as divine name often paired with Hadad/Haddu, the storm/thunder god
- **Hebrew** — בַּעַל (Baʿal), 'lord, husband'; later a polemical name for Canaanite gods
- **Akkadian** — Adad/Hadad (dIM), the storm god with whom Baꜥal was equated

Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. The ideal form includes Semitic ʿayin, which is blocked at the DNS root; the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is the registrable compromise. The name is Tier 1 because it preserves the ʿayin as a distinctive phoneme — a feature the ASCII form loses. In texts he is often 'Baꜥlu-Haddu' or simply the 'Rider on the Clouds.'

## Mythology

The Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is the central myth of Canaanite religion. It tells how Baꜥal wins kingship from the chaotic Sea, builds his palace, confronts Death, and returns to bring back the rains. The cycle is a seasonal drama of drought and renewal, but also a political statement about divine legitimacy.

### Baꜥal and Yamm (The Baal Cycle)

Ēl grants kingship to Yamm, the Sea, who sends messengers demanding that Baꜥal be delivered as a slave. Baꜥal refuses. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs forges two clubs, Yagrush ('Chaser') and Ayamur ('Driver'). With them Baꜥal strikes Yamm on the skull and scatters the chaotic waters, claiming the throne for himself (KTU 1.2 iv).

### The Palace on Zaphon (The Baal Cycle)

Victorious, Baꜥal still has no palace. He sends ꜥAnat to petition Ēl, but it is Asherah who finally secures permission. Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs builds a cedar palace on Mount Zaphon. Baꜥal hesitates over a window — it will let his voice out, but it may also let Death in. He opens it, and his thunder resounds across the earth (KTU 1.3–1.4).

### Descent into Mot (The Baal Cycle)

Death, personified as Mot, invites Baꜥal to the underworld. Baꜥal descends with his clouds, winds, and rains; the earth dries up. His sisters ꜥAnat and Aštart mourn him, and ꜥAnat destroys Mot, scattering his body like seed. Baꜥal returns, the rains resume, and fertility is restored (KTU 1.5–1.6).

### Protector of Ugarit (Cult)

A ritual prayer from Ugarit (KTU 1.119) invokes Baꜥal to drive the enemy from the city gates and walls. Votive anchors from his temple show his importance to seafarers; having conquered Yamm, he protects those who sail the waters he once defeated.

## Symbols & Iconography

Baꜥal's attributes are those of a storm king, stable from the Ugaritic tablets to the stelae:

- **Bull** — He wears his father Ēl's animal as a sign of fertility and storm power; seals and figurines show the smiting god standing upon a bull.
- **Lightning club** — Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs forges the magic clubs Yagruš ("Chaser") and Ayāmar ("Driver") that fell [[yam|Yām]] (KTU 1.2 iv); the raised weapon becomes his fixed pose.
- **Thunder through the window** — When the palace window opens on Mount Ṣaphon, his holy voice shakes the earth (KTU 1.4 vii): the aperture is the conduit of rain and sound.
- **Cloud chariot** — His title *rkb ʿrpt*, "Rider of the Clouds," names the storm cloud itself as his vehicle — an epithet the Bible later transfers to YHWH (Psalm 68:4).
- **Smiting-god stance** — The Baꜥal au foudre stela from his Ugarit temple (Louvre AO 15775) shows him striding forward, mace raised, a spear planted like a thunderbolt above stylized waves.

## Archaeology & Evidence

Baꜥal has the richest material dossier of any Ugaritic god. His temple on the acropolis of Ugarit — excavated by Claude Schaeffer from 1929 onward, one of the city's two great sanctuaries beside that of Dagan — yielded stelae including the Baꜥal au foudre and dozens of votive stone anchors, the thank-offerings of sailors to the god who mastered the sea; the Baꜥal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6) themselves come from the nearby library of the high priest.

Beyond Ugarit, the Karatepe bilingual (KAI 26, 8th century BCE) equates Phoenician Baꜥal with the Luwian storm god Tarhunza, and the Yehimilk inscription from Byblos (KAI 4, 10th century BCE) names Baꜥal-shamem, "Lord of the Heavens." In the first millennium the cult travels: the Temple of Bel dominated Palmyra until its destruction in 2015, and the tophet of Carthage preserves thousands of votive stelae dedicated "to the lord, to Baꜥal-Ḥammon."

## Across Cultures

Baꜥal is inseparable from the older West Semitic storm god Hadad/Haddu; in texts and inscriptions the two names are often combined as Baꜥal-Haddu. In Mesopotamia he was equated with Adad (dIM), and in Egypt he influenced the Levantine storm god imported during the New Kingdom. The Greeks saw in him a Near Eastern Zeus, a sky-storm king, though they did not directly worship him. In the Hebrew Bible, Baꜥal became the archetype of apostasy, the 'false god' opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel. Later Jewish and Christian tradition demonized the name, turning 'Baal' into a byword for idolatry and, in medieval occultism, for a class of demons.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[enlil|Enlīl]], [[oya|Ọya]], [[perkunas|Perkūnas]], [[shango|Ṣàngó]], [[thor|Þórr]], and [[trengtreng|Trengtreng]], each linked through thunder / storm sovereignty.

## Cultural Legacy

No Canaanite name was more reviled or more enduring than Baꜥal. The prophets of Israel spent generations attacking his cult, yet his imagery — the storm god who rides the clouds, defeats the sea, and sends rain — was quietly absorbed into the figure of Yahweh. In the New Testament, Beelzebub ('Lord of the Flies,' probably a distortion of Baꜥal-Zebul, 'Prince Baꜥal') becomes a name for Satan. In modern fantasy and occult literature, Baal persists as a demon-king. But beneath the polemic remains the old Levantine truth: a god of storm and fertility whose absence means drought and whose return means life.

## The Original Script

The Yoruba language had no phonetic writing system before the nineteenth century; the names of its powers, including **Ọbalúayé** and his older, more dangerous praise names, were transmitted orally in the Ifá corpus, in oríkì praise poetry, and in the liturgy of the smallpox cult. The first printed records of the language are mission vocabularies: John Raban's *A Vocabulary of the Eyo or Aku* (1830–1832), then Samuel Ajayi Crowther's *A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language* (1843) and his *Grammar and Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language* (1852).

Modern standard Yoruba orthography, codified from Ayo Bamgbose's 1965 study and the 1966 Yoruba Orthography Committee, writes the Latin alphabet with sub-dots (**ẹ, ọ, ṣ**) and tone marks; the mid tone goes unmarked. **Ọbalúayé** follows this convention — ọ marks the open vowel [ɔ], ú and é carry high tones — while diaspora spellings (Obaluaiê, Babalú Ayé, Omolu) record the same spoken name through Portuguese and Spanish orthographies.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɔ̀.bà.lú.à.jé/** — Yoruba Reconstruction.

- **Ọ-** — Open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] with low tone, written with a dot below.
- **-bà-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b] followed by open [a] with low tone.
- **-lú-** — Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l] followed by close back rounded vowel [u] with high tone.
- **-à-** — Open central vowel [a] with low tone.
- **-yé** — Palatal approximant [j] followed by close-mid front vowel [e] with high tone; the name means 'father whose scourge is the world'.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: aw-bah-loo-ah-YEH — low on the first three syllables, then high on 'YEH'.

- **Cuban Santería** — Babalú Ayé, the old man on crutches who both inflicts and removes sickness.

Ọbalúayé is Tier 1: the acute accents on ú and é preserve high tones — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — while grave accents would mark low tones. The dot below ọ distinguishes open [ɔ] from close [o].

## Mythology

Ọbalúayé's mythology is less a set of heroic adventures than a meditation on illness, marginality, and the earth's power to break and remake the body.

### The Scourge of the World (Origin)

Ọbalúayé is called 'Father of the World' not because he nurtures it but because his diseases touch everyone, high and low. In some accounts he was once a proud king who was brought low by sickness and learned compassion only after he himself had suffered. His myth teaches that the healer must know the body from the inside of affliction.

### The Dog and the Herb (Healing)

Stories of Ọbalúayé often involve a dog who leads a sufferer to a healing herb or a stream. The dog is his messenger, moving between the realm of disease and the realm of cure. The myth encodes the practical work of finding medicine: one must follow signs that do not speak in human language.

### Babalú Ayé at the Crossroads (Diaspora)

In Cuban Santería, Babalú Ayé is depicted as an old beggar at the crossroads, leaning on crutches, accompanied by dogs. He receives offerings of roasted corn, tobacco, and dry wine. The image preserves the Yoruba sense that illness can reduce anyone to dependence — and that dependence, rightly borne, becomes a form of holiness.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Ọbalúayé concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Crutches** — His diaspora attribute, marking lameness and the limit of the human body.
- **Burlap or sackcloth** — Poverty, humility, and the rough texture of illness and recovery; in ritual it also veils the marked body from view.
- **Two dogs** — His messengers and guardians at the boundary of sickness and health.
- **Earth-coloured beads** — Brown, black, and purple beads that link him to soil and burial.

In Candomblé his ritual whisk, the xaxará, is woven from palm ribs and swept over the body and the temple to lift illness away, and his ceremonies are conducted in lowered light, his power kept partially veiled. The attributes converge on a single lesson: affliction concealed is affliction ungoverned, and the cult makes the marks of disease visible in order to master them.

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monumental cult of Ọbalúayé is attested, and the explanation is partly historical: smallpox cults in Yorubaland were feared institutions, and in the colonial period the Ṣọ̀pọ̀nná cult was suppressed in several districts on the charge that its priests spread the very infection they claimed to control. What survives is ethnographic rather than archaeological — shrine vessels, earth-toned bead strands, and the brooms and staffs of the healing cult preserved in ethnographic collections.

The fuller material record lies in the diaspora: Candomblé houses preserve the xaxará whisk, the burlap garment, and the sequestered shrine of Obaluaiê, while Cuban devotion centres on the pilgrimage shrine of San Lázaro at El Rincón outside Havana, where crutches, candles, and ex-votos accumulate each December.

## Realm & Domain

**Ọbalúayé** is the orixá who both strikes and heals. He governs infectious disease — especially smallpox — and the earth that receives the body after death. His name means 'king whose scourge is the world,' and his presence is feared because illness arrives without warning and leaves without explanation. Yet he is also the one who can lift what he has sent, and his devotees often become the most skilled healers.

In the diaspora he appears as an old man on crutches, wrapped in burlap, accompanied by dogs. He is poverty, affliction, and survival at once.

### Disease and Pestilence

Smallpox, leprosy, and epidemic illness walk in his shadow.

### Healing

### Earth and the Grave

## Across Cultures
Continue.

In Brazilian Candomblé, Ọbalúayé became Obaluaiê, syncretised with Saint Lazarus (the beggar covered in sores) and Saint Roch (who shows the plague sore on his thigh). In Cuban Santería he is Babalú Ayé, often identified with Saint Lazarus. ## Cultural Legacy

Ọbalúayé's legacy is the theology of illness. In Yoruba and Afro-Atlantic thought, sickness is not mere biological accident; it is a message, a punishment, or a calling. When the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, his oldest enemy vanished from the earth, yet the cult did not vanish with it: devotion in Cuba and Brazil turned toward the epidemics that remained, and during the AIDS crisis the orisha of epidemic and cure gathered a new generation of devotees.

His name also travelled far beyond the temple. Margarita Lecuona's Afro-Cuban song 'Babalú' (1939), popularised internationally by Desi Arnaz, carried the orisha's name into global popular culture — a secular afterlife detached from the theology but proof of the diaspora's reach. In an age of global pandemics his mythology retains its force: the earth can still send plagues, and the boundary between health and sickness remains thinner than modern medicine likes to admit.

## A Meditation

Ọbalúayé is the god nobody wants until they need him. He is smallpox scars, crutches, the cough that will not stop, the fever that empties the world. And yet he is also the one who knows the herb, the cool stream, the moment when the crisis turns.

To approach him is to accept the fragility of the body. He does not promise that illness is meaningful, only that it is real and that survival is possible. In a culture that often hides disability and death, Ọbalúayé stands at the crossroads in sackcloth, leaning on crutches, accompanied by dogs. He makes poverty and sickness visible — and in making them visible, he begins to heal them.

# Pronouncing Badb: a guide for the curious

Saying **Badb** aloud is harder than reading it on a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Celtic transcription writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode domain. ## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Badb
- **ASCII form:** badb
- **Meaning:** "Crow, scald-crow"
- **Domain of influence:** Battle, Death, Crow

## Overview

**Badb** (*badb*) — Battle, Death, Crow · Crow, scald-crow — is the Irish war-goddess whose name is her shape: Old Irish *badb*, the scald-crow, is the common noun for the hooded crow (*Corvus cornix*) and the theonym in a single word, and the medieval writers never felt the need to choose between them. Her standing title in the texts is *badb catha*, 'crow of battle' — the bird that haunts the field and the goddess who owns it, named in one breath.

She belongs to the war-goddess complex the Lebor Gabála Érenn calls the daughters of Ernmas — Badb, Macha, and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair — a genealogy the verse recension gives as Badb, Macha, and the Morrígu, so that the tradition itself is of two minds as to whether the Morrígan is the third sister or the single name for all three. The same book marries her to the war-god: Neit son of Indui had two wives, Badb and Nemain. Her dossier is voice and omen rather than adventure: the shriek over the hosts in the Táin that kills a hundred warriors with fright, the war-goddess washing at the ford of the Unius before Mag Tuired, and the scald-crows settling on the dying Cú Chulainn's pillar-stone.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Badb** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Irish writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the goddess. No domain is claimed: the plain-ASCII **badb.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

## The Name

The theonym is attested in Old and Middle Irish as **badb** (later *badhbh*), a feminine noun whose first and never-abandoned sense is zoological: the scald-crow, the grey-and-black hooded crow of the Irish countryside. The Dictionary of the Irish Language records both registers — the bird and the supernatural battle-being — and the texts exploit the identity deliberately: when the war-goddess is named, the hearer already knows her shape. Her standing phrase is *badb catha*, 'the crow of battle', used of the battlefield terror itself as readily as of the goddess.

The etymology is old Celtic, not Irish alone. Vendryes' LEIA and Matasović's Proto-Celtic dictionary trace the word to Proto-Celtic *bodwā*, 'battle, fighting' — a root the continental languages kept in war-names — and the Gaulish altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to **Cathubodua**, *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow': the precise reverse compound of the Irish phrase. The crow of battle is therefore not an Irish literary conceit but an inherited Celtic formation, attested in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland.

Within the Irish tradition the name shades into her sisters': the Táin couples her with Bé Néit, 'woman of battle', and Némain, and the Lebor Gabála's two recensions of the daughters of Ernmas make the Morrígan now the third sister, now the collective name. The honest verdict of the handbooks is fluidity, not error: Badb, Macha, Némain, and the Morrígan behave as one complex with several voices.

The ASCII form *badb* loses nothing, because the normalized Old Irish spelling is already plain Latin letters; the restoration is therefore a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **b** → **B** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **b** → **b** — Same

The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **badb** — Old Irish / Middle Irish in Insular script, attested Old Irish, c. 7th–10th c. CE, in the glossaries and in the great codices that preserve the Táin and the Lebor Gabála. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, predates the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on an ogham stone; the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Old Irish was written in the Latin alphabet using Insular minuscule from the early medieval period; the spelling badb requires no diacritic.
- The word is a common noun — the scald-crow, the hooded crow — and the theonym is the same word; the Dictionary of the Irish Language records both registers.
- The medial d and final b are lenited in pronunciation — [ð] and [β] — but the orthography writes plain d and b; nothing distinctive is lost in ASCII.
- The Unicode restoration Badb is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

## Mythology

Badb's mythology is genealogy, sound, and omen rather than adventure: she is the sister in the list, the voice over the army, the bird on the pillar-stone. Four texts carry her dossier, and the commentators have spent a century and a half working out where she ends and her sisters begin.

### The Daughters of Ernmas (Lebor Gabála Érenn)

The Lebor Gabála Érenn gives the war-goddesses their pedigree: 'Badb and Macha and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair, were the three daughters of Ernmas the she-farmer.' The verse recension sings the family in another key — 'Badb and Macha, greatness of wealth, Morrígu, springs of craftiness, sources of bitter fighting, were the three daughters of Ernmas' — so the tradition itself is of two minds about the third sister. The same book marries her into the war-god's house: Neit son of Indui, god of battle, had two wives, Badb and Nemain, and the pedigree records their slaying at Ailech by the Fomorians. Cormac's Glossary had already fixed the marriage in the record: Neith, the god of battle among the pagan Gael, and Nemon his wife.

### The Shriek over the Hosts (Táin Bó Cúailnge)

When the men of Ireland march under [[medb|Medb]] for the brown bull of Cooley, the Táin marks the nights of the hosting with the sound of the war-goddesses: 'Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above them that night in Gáirech and Irgáirech, so that a hundred of their warriors fell dead of fright.' She does not wound; she announces. The shriek is prophecy delivered as noise — and the Irish phrase for battlefield terror, *badb catha*, is simply her name at work as a common noun.

### The War-Goddess at Mag Tuired (Cath Maige Tuired)

On Samain night before the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, [[dagda|the Dagda]] met the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius in Connacht, where she stood washing with one foot on either bank; she pledged herself to the Túatha Dé Danann's cause, promising the hearts of the Fomorian host and the blood of their king Indech. After [[lugh|Lugh]]'s sling-stone felled [[balor|Balor]], it was the Morrígan who proclaimed the rout to the heights of Ireland and uttered the prophecy — 'Peace up to heaven, heaven down to earth, earth beneath heaven' — and then its darker twin, the vision of the world's ending. The texts keep the sisters' voices interchangeable; what the manuscript gives to the Morrígan, the tradition hears also in Badb's register.

### The Crow on the Pillar-Stone (Aided Con Culainn)
Continue.

Cú Chulainn's death-tale, Brislech Mór Maige Muirthemni, gives the crow-goddesses the last word. Mortally wounded, [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] lashed himself to a pillar-stone to die on his feet, and for three days his enemies would not close in — until the battle-goddess Morrígu came with her sisters in the form of scald-crows and settled on his shoulder. 'That pillar is not wont to be under birds,' said Erc, and only then did the host dare take the hero's head. The living man keeps her off; the dead man is her perch.

### The Washer at the Ford (Gaelic tradition)

The medieval texts give the war-goddess her washing-place at the ford of the Unius; the later Gaelic tradition gives the figure her full shape — the washer at the ford, rinsing the blood-stained garments of those about to die in battle. In Scottish Gaelic folklore she is the bean nighe, and the commentators, Mac Cana among them, treat her as the folk continuation of the Badb's own figure. The washing is prophecy, not threat: the doom is already written, and she merely launders the evidence.

## Symbols & Iconography

Badb's attributes are a species, a sound, a place, a number, and a chore — the sparest regalia in the Irish corpus, and the most exact:

- **The scald-crow** — The hooded crow, grey and black: her name, her shape, and her retinue on every field
- **The shriek** — Panic as a weapon: the sound over the hosts that kills men with fear before the spear is thrown
- **The ford** — The boundary between bank and bank, living and dead: the water where the war-goddess stands washing
- **The triad** — Badb, Macha, Némain: the three of war, one terror in three voices
- **The washing of spoils** — The harness and garments of the soon-dead, rinsed in the ford before the battle that will bloody them

## Archaeology & Evidence

Badb is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Táin Bó Cúailnge survives in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (Royal Irish Academy, c. 1100), and in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; Lebor Gabála Érenn likewise rests on the Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition.

The nearest epigraphic witness is continental: the altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicating to **Cathubodua**, 'battle-crow', is the standing proof that the crow-of-battle compound is old Celtic and not an Irish literary invention — comparative evidence across the water, never an identification.

## Realm & Domain

**Badb** is catalogued under the domain 'Battle, Death, Crow' — three words that map exactly onto her dossier: the field she haunts, the knowledge she carries, and the shape she wears.

### Battle

She never fights, and the texts are exact about it: her weapon is the voice. In the Táin, Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shriek above the marching hosts at Gáirech and Irgáirech until a hundred warriors fall dead of fright — the battle's true opening, fought and won before a spear is cast.

### Death

She is the reader of the doomed: the war-goddess washing at the ford of the Unius on the eve of Mag Tuired, the scald-crows settling on [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]]'s pillar-stone to tell his enemies he is gone — 'that pillar is not wont to be under birds'. Death is not her doing; it is her knowledge.

### Crow

Her name is the animal: *badb*, the scald-crow, the grey-and-black hooded crow that comes down to the field when the field is finished. The theonym refuses metaphor — the goddess has a species.

### The Moment Before

The connective tissue of all three domains is foreknowledge: shriek, washing, and settling are the same act in three scenes — the end of the day, seen at its beginning. The later Gaelic washer at the ford, the Scottish bean nighe, keeps exactly this brief.

## Across Cultures

Badb's clearest cross-border witness is Gaulish, and it is exact. An altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to **Cathubodua** — *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow' — the precise reverse compound of Irish *badb catha*. Delamarre and Koch treat the two names as one formation across the Celtic languages: the crow of battle named in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland. The Welsh corpus, by contrast, is silent on her — no figure of the *Mabinogi* continues the name, and the Brythonic silence is recorded rather than repaired. Typological comparison has set her beside the Norse valkyries, the raven-feeding choosers of the slain; the handbooks note the parallel without claiming descent.

Within the Irish tradition her closest kin are her own sisters, [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]] and [[macha|Macha]] — one complex with several voices — and the war she prophesied binds her to [[dagda|the Dagda]], [[lugh|Lugh]], and [[nuada|Nuadu]]. The Christian scribes who preserved her did not euhemerize her into a queen or a druid, as they did the great gods; they left her what she was, a bird and a voice, which may be why the name needed no rehabilitation.

## Cultural Legacy

The crow of battle rode the Celtic revival in English dress. W. M. Hennessy's 'The Ancient Irish Goddess of War' (Revue Celtique, 1870) had already gathered the Morrígan material for scholars, and Lady Gregory's *Gods and Fighting Men* (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired and its war-goddesses to a wide reading public, crow-form and prophecy complete. Modern fantasy and games have made the war-goddess's crow-shape one of the stock images of the genre, and contemporary pagan practice honors Badb among the three of the Morrígan.

In the Irish language the word never needed reviving: *badhbh* has meant the hooded crow all along, and the grey bird on the battlefield needed no gloss for any Irish hearer. Across the water, the Scottish bean nighe kept her folk shape washing at the ford deep into the era of the great folklore collections — the longest-lived of all her forms, and the one that never had to be reconstructed.

## A Meditation

Badb is the rare theonym that refuses to be a metaphor: the word for the bird and the name of the goddess are one, and the medieval writers never felt the need to choose between them. To name her is already to say what she does. Other gods have attributes; she has a species — the grey scald-crow that comes down to the field when the field is finished, and the texts simply ask us to understand that the bird knew all along.

Her power is the moment before. In no surviving text does she strike a blow: she shrieks over the marching column, washes at the boundary water, settles on the pillar-stone — the goddess of foreknowledge and of aftermath, of everything in a battle except the fighting. That is not a small dossier but a strange and exact one: she is what war feels like to those who already know its end. The name keeps the question open in every grey bird on a fence-post: if you could see the end of the day at its beginning, what would you do with the hours between?

The name is preserved in Hangul + Hanja as **백두산 (白頭山)** — Korean alphabet + Chinese characters, attested Modern Korean, in Korea. The script is written left-to-right.

## Mythology

The mythology of Baekdusan is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

### The Descent Place of Hwanung (Foundation myth)

Some Korean traditions identify Baekdusan as the mountain where Hwanung descended from heaven beneath a sandalwood tree. From this sacred volcano the Korean people trace their origin and their connection to heaven.

### Baekdusan as Sansin (Mountain spirit)

Like other great mountains, Baekdusan is inhabited by a mountain spirit (sansin) who protects the land, grants visions to seekers, and serves as an intermediary between humans and heaven.

### The Ancestral Mountain (Manchu-Korean cult)

Both Korean and Manchu shamanic traditions regard Baekdusan as an ancestral mountain and a source of spiritual power. Rituals and pilgrimages to the mountain sought blessings, healing, and contact with ancestral spirits.

The iconography associated with Baekdusan concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Snow-capped peak** — The white head that gives the mountain its name and signifies purity and height.
- **Lake Chonji** — The crater lake at the summit, a mirror of heaven and a symbol of origin.
- **Tiger and bear** — Animals of the mountain forests, echoing the Dangun myth of bear and tiger.

# The many faces of Bāguà

No important name has only one face. **Bāguà** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Chinese characters original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *bagua* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

- **ASCII form:** bagua

**Bāguà** (*bagua*) — Cosmology, Divination · Eight trigrams — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cosmology, Divination". The name means "Eight trigrams".

**Bāguà** is the Chinese universe reduced to eight three-line figures. Each trigram — 乾 Qián, 坤 Kūn, 震 Zhèn, 巽 Xùn, 坎 Kǎn, 離 Lí, 艮 Gèn, 兌 Duì — stacks yin and yang lines in every possible combination of three, producing a complete symbolic alphabet for describing situations, forces, and transformations. From the trigrams come the sixty-four hexagrams of the *Yijing*, the oldest continuously used divination manual in the world.

Bāguà is not only a fortune-telling tool. It is a map of reality: directions, seasons, family roles, body parts, and moral qualities all attach to the eight figures.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Bāguà** and serves its temple at [bāguà.com](https://xn--bgu-cla6n.com). ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Chinese characters as **八卦** — Hanzi (Sino-Tibetan), attested Oracle-bone – present, c. 1200 BCE –, in China. The script is written left-to-right; traditional top-to-bottom.

The scholarly transliteration is *Bāguà* (Hanyu Pinyin with tone mark), giving the normalized reading /pa˥ ku̯a˥˩/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is written with the Chinese characters 八卦.
- Each character is a logogram that encodes meaning and historical pronunciation.
- Hanyu Pinyin with tone marks preserves Mandarin pronunciation; the ASCII form loses tone.
- The Unicode restoration Bāguà is the registrable form because hanzi are outside the .com IDN table.

The original script is 八卦; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is *Bāguà* (Tone 1 + Tone 4). *Bā* means 'eight' and *guà* means 'trigram' or 'hexagram' in divinatory usage. The registrable form uses tone-marked Pinyin so the domain remains readable across scripts; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. The two graphs are treated in the standard reconstructions: Karlgren's GSR series 0281 (八) and 0879 (卦), with the Middle and Old Chinese values tabulated by Pulleyblank and Schuessler; Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 八 as *pret and 卦 as *[k]ʷre-s.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/pa˥ kwa˥˩/** — Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **bā** — Syllable with unaspirated bilabial stop [p], open front vowel [a], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥). Pinyin 'b' is unaspirated, unlike English 'b' in word-initial position.
- **guà** — Syllable with unaspirated velar stop [k], labio-velar glide [w], open vowel [a], and Tone 4 (falling, ˥˩). The 'u' after 'g' indicates labialization [kʷ].

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: BAH-GWAH — first syllable high and level, second syllable falling (high to low) like a command.

- **Simplified** — 八卦
- **Wade-Giles** — pa¹-kua⁴

八卦 (Bāguà) refers to the eight trigrams of the Yijing: 乾 qián, 坤 kūn, 震 zhèn, 巽 xùn, 坎 kǎn, 離 lí, 艮 gèn, and 兌 duì. ## Mythology

The Bāguà are surrounded by origin stories that credit culture heroes, sages, and even river creatures with their discovery. Whether these are history, legend, or mythic shorthand, they reveal how seriously the Chinese tradition took the trigrams as a key to cosmic order.

### Trigrams from the River (Legend of Fuxi)

Tradition says that the culture hero Fuxi observed the patterns on a dragon-horse that emerged from the Yellow River — the *Hétú* — and derived the eight trigrams. The *Luoshu*, a numeric diagram borne by a turtle from the Luo River, later supplied the magic-square arrangement used in feng shui.

### King Wen and the Sixty-Four Hexagrams (Yijing Tradition)

King Wen of Zhou, imprisoned by the Shang king, stacked the eight trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams and composed the hexagram statements. His son, the Duke of Zhou, added line statements. Confucius or his school later wrote the Ten Wings, transforming a divination manual into a philosophical classic.

### The Sage Who Invented the Yijing (Xici)

The *Xici* appendix claims that in antiquity the sages invented knotted cords, writing, agriculture, and the Yijing in response to human need. The trigrams were not abstract speculation but practical tools devised by wise rulers to help people navigate change.

### Bagua Mirrors and Protective Charms (Daoist Usage)

In popular religion the eight trigrams are arranged around a central taijitu and mounted as a mirror to deflect harmful *qi*. The bagua mirror is still hung above doors across the Chinese diaspora, a compact cosmogram that claims the whole of space and time in a single octagon.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Bāguà concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Qián ☰ (Heaven)** — Creativity, strength, the father, the creative impulse
- **Kūn ☷ (Earth)** — Receptivity, devotion, the mother, the power of bearing
- **Zhèn ☳ (Thunder)** — Arousal, movement, the eldest son, sudden change
- **Xùn ☴ (Wind/Wood)** — Gentle penetration, the eldest daughter, influence
- **Kǎn ☵ (Water)** — The abyss, danger, the middle son, the testing flow
- **Lí ☲ (Fire)** — Clarity, attachment, the middle daughter, brightness
- **Gèn ☶ (Mountain)** — Stillness, keeping still, the youngest son, boundary
- **Duì ☱ (Lake)** — Joy, openness, the youngest daughter, completion

## Archaeology & Evidence

The Bāguà are rooted in the Shang dynasty practice of pyromancy on oracle bones and turtle plastrons, though the trigram system itself reaches written maturity in the Zhou period. The oldest extant *Yijing* manuscripts are the Shanghai Museum bamboo slips (c. 300 BCE) and the Fuyang Han slips, excavated in 1977 from the tomb of Xiahou Zao (d. 165 BCE), both already organizing the hexagrams from the eight trigrams; the Mawangdui silk *Zhouyi* (tomb sealed 168 BCE) transmits the text with a markedly different hexagram order. Han commentaries, including the *Xici*, fixed the philosophical interpretation of the trigrams, while Song and Ming editions transmitted the diagrams that remain standard today.

## Realm & Domain

**Bāguà** is the Chinese universe reduced to eight three-line figures. Each trigram — 乾 Qián, 坤 Kūn, 震 Zhèn, 巽 Xùn, 坎 Kǎn, 離 Lí, 艮 Gèn, 兌 Duì — stacks yin and yang lines in every possible combination of three, producing a complete symbolic alphabet for describing situations, forces, and transformations. From the trigrams come the sixty-four hexagrams of the *Yijing*, the oldest continuously used divination manual in the world.

Bāguà is not only a fortune-telling tool. It is a map of reality: directions, seasons, family roles, body parts, and moral qualities all attach to the eight figures.

### The Three Lines

A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Three lines yield 2³ = 8 trigrams, the elementary vocabulary of change.

### Heaven and Earth

Qián ☰, three solid lines, is heaven and creative power; Kūn ☷, three broken lines, is earth and receptive yielding.

### Cosmic Directions

The Later Heaven arrangement assigns each trigram to a direction, a season, and a domain of human life.

### Divination Method

Yarrow stalks, coins, and milfoil turn trigrams into hexagrams, turning a question into a reading of timing and transformation.

## Across Cultures
Continue.

Bāguà is shared by Confucian, Daoist, and folk-religious traditions, each giving the trigrams a different emphasis. Confucians read them as moral archetypes; Daoists use them in talismans and internal alchemy; feng shui masters arrange buildings by their directions. The arrangement called the Early Heaven sequence is associated with Fuxi and cosmogony, while the Later Heaven sequence is associated with King Wen and the flow of time. In Korea, the trigrams appear on the national flag; in Japan, they influenced Onmyōdō cosmology. Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation, rendered into English by Cary Baynes, introduced the *I Ching* to modern Europe and America, where it became a countercultural classic.

## Cultural Legacy

The Bāguà are everywhere once you know how to look. The Korean flag places four of the trigrams at its corners; martial artists practice *Baguazhang*, the Eight Trigram Palm, walking in circles that map the directions; computer scientists and designers use the Unicode trigram block (U+2630–U+2637) as glyphs for menus and progress indicators. Feng shui consultants still lay the octagonal bagua over floor plans to diagnose relationships, wealth, career, and health. The trigrams have proved durable because they are not answers; they are a grammar for asking better questions about change.

## A Meditation

Bāguà is the intuition that reality can be modeled without being exhausted. Eight figures, each only three lines long, are enough to describe marriages, wars, harvests, illnesses, and revolutions because the trigrams do not describe events; they describe tendencies. A trigram is a weather pattern, not a weather report.

To consult the *Yijing* is to accept that you already know the answer but cannot yet see its shape. The trigram does not predict the future like a calendar; it clarifies the present like a mirror. In this sense Bāguà is less occult than psychological: it forces the questioner to recognize which forces are active, which are latent, and which direction the situation is turning. The eight figures are not magic. They are a discipline of attention.

# How Baiame got its name back

The ASCII form *baiame* is missing something. **Baiame** restores the conventional scholarly spelling of one of the most important creator figures in Aboriginal Australian mythology — and that spelling carries a responsibility. This post explains, with the full scholarly record behind it, what the name means, how it has been written, the mythology it carries, and why the restoration matters even when no diacritic is added.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Baiame
- **ASCII form:** baiame
- **Meaning:** "The maker" or "father"
- **Domain of influence:** Sky Father, Creator, Law-Giver
- **Pantheon:** Aboriginal Australian
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** oral tradition; scholarly romanization

## Overview

**Baiame** (*baiame*) — Sky Father, Creator — belongs to the Aboriginal Australian tradition, especially the Wiradjuri and Gamilaraay/Euahlayi nations of south-eastern Australia. The name means "the maker" or "father".

Baiame is the great ancestor who made the land, the animals, and the first people, and then gave them the laws, kinship systems, and initiation ceremonies by which they still live. After creation he withdrew to the sky, where his presence is felt in the Milky Way and in the dark shape of the Emu in the Sky.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Baiame**. The plain ASCII form *baiame* is the modern romanization; the restoration capitalizes the conventional scholarly spelling. Because the Aboriginal source traditions were oral and did not use an alphabet with diacritics, and because no diacritic or special letter is added in this restoration, the name is placed in Tier 2. The Unicode form remains the philologically complete reference, while the ASCII spelling is a practical convenience for the domain-name system.

## The Name

The name is attested in colonial-era ethnographies as **Baiame**, **Baayami**, and **Byamee**. Etymologically it is usually understood as "the maker" or "father" in the languages of the Wiradjuri and Gamilaraay/Euahlayi peoples.

Because the source traditions were oral, there is no single original script in the alphabetic sense. The name was first written down by European ethnographers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The standard scholarly form today is **Baiame**, with **Baayami** preferred in Gamilaraay language-revival contexts.

The ASCII form *baiame* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry Aboriginal-language phonetics or special characters; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Baiame** gives the conventional capitalized romanization, the standard scholarly way to cite a proper name in Australian Indigenous studies.

## Mythology and Symbols

Baiame's mythology is preserved in the oral traditions of the Wiradjuri, Gamilaraay, and neighbouring nations. The stories are title deeds to country, instruction manuals for law, and maps of the sky.

- **Creator of land and life.** Baiame shaped the hills, rivers, and plains, made the animals, and then made the first people.
- **Sky dwelling.** After creation he withdrew to the sky, where his camp is identified with the dark patches of the Milky Way.
- **Law and initiation.** He gave the first laws and ceremonies. His son Daramulum taught the people initiation and the songs that must be sung at each stage of life.
- **The Emu in the Sky.** The dark constellation in the Milky Way is both a celestial marker of Baiame's camp and a seasonal calendar for the people below.

## Why Tier 2 is the right classification

A Tier 2 classification does not mean a name is less important. It means that the ASCII form already encodes the same phonemic sequence and that the restoration's value is scholarly and cultural rather than diacritical. For Baiame, the work of preservation is to keep the conventional citation form alive against the flattening effect of plain ASCII domains. The mythology, the law, and the responsibility to country remain intact in either spelling — but the capitalized, scholarly form is the one that belongs in citation and public memory.

## The Meaning Behind the Name

The name **Baiame** encodes more than a simple label. In the Aboriginal tradition that holds it, the name carries the history of the country, the authority of ancestral law, and the obligations of the living custodians. The plain ASCII form *baiame* is a modern technological convenience: it allows the name to travel through the domain-name system and other digital infrastructure, but it cannot represent the full cultural weight that the name carries in ceremony and song.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Baiame** because the capitalized scholarly form is the standard way to cite a proper noun from an oral tradition. This restoration is not a cosmetic change. It marks the name as belonging to a living culture and asserts that digital infrastructure should be able to honor such names rather than flatten them into lowercase ASCII strings.

## Mythology and Worldview

The stories of Baiame are not entertainment or simple explanations of natural phenomena. They are title deeds to country, instructions for ceremony, and maps of moral responsibility. In the accounts recorded by anthropologists and preserved by custodians, Baiame appears as a figure whose actions shaped the land and established the patterns that human beings must follow.

These stories are held under traditional protocols. Some details are appropriate for public discussion, while others are restricted to initiated members of the community or to specific kin groups. The public scholarly record therefore gives only the outer layer of a much deeper body of knowledge. Even so, it is enough to show that Baiame is not a static mythological curiosity but a living presence in Aboriginal law and identity.

## Cultural Significance Today

In contemporary Australia, Baiame continues to appear in Aboriginal art, dance, environmental management, and public ceremony. Indigenous artists depict the figure in bark paintings, rock-art renewals, and digital media, always in ways that respect the custodial protocols of the communities that hold the name. Welcome-to-country ceremonies, language-revival programs, and land-care initiatives all draw on the authority of ancestral figures such as Baiame.

At the same time, the name reminds us that the digital world was built on assumptions that privilege ASCII text. Domain names, file systems, search engines, and social-media handles all tend to treat lowercase English letters as the default. Restoring **Baiame** as a flagship temple is a small but concrete step toward challenging that default and making space for Indigenous names in the digital realm.

## Why This Restoration Matters

PuniCodex classifies Baiame as a Tier 2 restoration. This means that the ASCII form *baiame* already represents the same phonemic and orthographic sequence as the restored form; no diacritic or special letter is required to recover the scholarly spelling. The restoration therefore focuses on the proper-noun convention: the capitalized form **Baiame** is the respectful citation form, while *baiame* remains a practical compromise for digital systems that cannot yet honor Indigenous typographic conventions.

Even without a registered Unicode domain, Baiame deserves a flagship temple. The domain-name market may make the exact string unavailable, but the name itself remains a vital part of human heritage. By building a temple around it, PuniCodex preserves the scholarly form, explains its significance, and keeps watch for the day when the digital infrastructure of names can fully include the world's oral traditions.

## A Note on Sources and Respect

The scholarly record on Baiame draws on nineteenth- and twentieth-century ethnography, more recent anthropological fieldwork, and the guidance of Aboriginal custodians and institutions such as AIATSIS. Contemporary presentations of Baiame therefore prioritize Indigenous authorship and custodial authority.

The Aboriginal traditions of Australia hold many figures whose stories overlap or contrast with **Baiame**. Sky beings, ancestral creators, and totemic ancestors appear in different regional forms, and the same figure may be known by more than one name or spelling across language groups. **Baiame** belongs to a network of names that includes **Baiame**, the Kamilaroi sky father; **Bunjil**, the Kulin eaglehawk creator; **Ngalyod**, the rainbow serpent of the north; and **Yurlungur**, the great copper python of Yolŋu country. Each name encodes a specific relationship to country, law, and custodial responsibility, and none is interchangeable with another.

For researchers and readers, the important distinction is between the capitalized scholarly citation form **Baiame** and the lowercase ASCII form *baiame*. The capitalized form marks the name as a proper noun and situates it within the scholarly and custodial discourse of Aboriginal studies. The lowercase form is a technological artifact, useful for domain names and search queries but carrying none of the cultural weight of the citation form.

# From Younger Futhark to Unicode: the journey of Baldr

Long before it was a domain, this name traveled through scripts. **Baldr** begins in Younger Futhark, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that journey preserves some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its spelling.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Baldr
- **ASCII form:** baldr
- **Meaning:** "Lord, prince (from *balþraz)"
- **Domain of influence:** Light, Beauty, Purity
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛒᛅᛚᛏᚱ (Younger Futhark)

## Overview

**Baldr** (*baldr*) — Light, Beauty, Purity · The Best and Fairest of the Æsir — is the shining son of Óðinn and Frigg whose death by the mistletoe shaft is the first grief of the gods and the certain herald of Ragnarǫk. Snorri introduces him with the formula the whole tradition repeats: he is the best, and all praise him — so fair and bright that light streams from him, wisest and most gracious of the Æsir, and yet shadowed by one flaw, that none of his judgments can stand.

His attestation is thin but pivotal. The Poetic Edda knows him through prophecy rather than deed: Völuspá's seeress sees his doom, and the whole of *Baldrs draumar* is Óðinn's ride to wring that doom from a dead völva. The Prose Edda gives the narrative — Frigg's oath, the gods' game, Loki's hand guiding blind Höðr's throw, the burning of Hringhorni with Nanna dead of grief beside him, Hermóðr's nine-night ride, and the giantess Þökk's one refusal. Saxo's euhemerized Balderus and the Second Merseburg Charm's enigmatic Phol are the only substantial witnesses outside the Icelandic corpus.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Baldr** — identical to the ASCII input, because the normalized Old Norse form is itself plain ASCII: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name is therefore Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — a property of its orthography, not of the god's standing. The plain-ASCII domain baldr.com is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release; the project claims no domain for this temple.

## The Name

The name is attested in Old Norse as **Baldr** (nominative; genitive *Balders*). Its etymology is genuinely disputed, and honesty requires both main lines. The stronger philological line derives it from Proto-Germanic *balþraz*, 'bold, lordly': Old Norse preserves *baldr* as a rare poetic common noun meaning 'lord, prince', and Old English *bealdor* 'prince, hero' is its exact cognate — the god's name would then simply be the title, 'the Lord'. The alternative, favored by scholars impressed by the god's shining character, connects the name with Baltic *baltas* 'white' (Lithuanian baltas), yielding 'the shining, the white one' — attractive to the myth, but philologically weaker, and Simek and Orchard both register the dispute rather than settle it.

The ASCII form is not a compromise here: normalized Old Norse *Baldr* is already written in plain ASCII letters. There is no diacritic, no thorn or eth, no vowel-length mark for the early domain-name system to have stripped. The name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — which is a statement about orthography, never about the god. The final *-r* is the Old Norse nominative masculine ending, borne by the plain letter itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **b** → **B** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Lord, prince (from *balþraz)

The reconstructed proto-form is **balþraz* (proto-indo-european), glossed as "Lord, prince".

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Baldr** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius and the codices of the Prose Edda, recording material centuries older. The manuscript form is itself plain ASCII: Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name, and the restoration changes nothing but the capital. In the Younger Futhark — the sixteen-rune Viking-Age row — the name would have been carved **ᛒᛅᛚᛏᛦ** (b-a-l-t-R); the runic row underspecifies what the manuscripts fix, with ᛏ writing both t and d and ᛦ the final nominative -r.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a single stem, *bald-* + the nominative masculine ending *-r*; no compound, no prefix.
- Old Norse orthography requires no accent: the a is short, and short vowels carry no mark.
- The etymology is disputed: Proto-Germanic *balþraz* 'bold, lordly' (with the poetic noun baldr 'lord, prince' and Old English bealdor as cognates) against the 'white, shining' line that would connect the name to the god's radiance; the handbooks register the dispute rather than settle it.
- The Unicode restoration Baldr is therefore identical to the ASCII form — a Tier 2 name by the mechanical rule, whose dignity comes from the god, not from rescued diacritics.

PuniCodex holds no domain for this name: the plain-ASCII **baldr.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈbɑl.dr̩/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **B-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b], fully voiced in initial position, as in English 'bald'
- **-a-** — Short open back unrounded [ɑ], held brief; Old Norse short a, not the long á
- **-ldr** — Lateral [l], voiced stop [d], and the syllabic trill [r̩] of the nominative ending, which carries its own beat

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BAHL-dur' — a short open 'ah', the l and d run together, and a light syllabic r at the end, as in modern Icelandic Baldur.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Baldr, son of Óðinn and Frigg; also a rare poetic noun, 'lord, prince'
- **Old High German** — Phol, paired with Wodan in the Second Merseburg Charm, widely read as Baldr
- **Old English** — Bældæg, son of Woden in the Anglo-Saxon royal genealogies
- **Latinized** — Balderus, the form Saxo Grammaticus writes
- **Modern Icelandic** — Baldur, the unbroken living form

Baldr is Tier 2 because the Old Norse form is already plain ASCII: nothing distinctive is lost in transit. The god's fame vastly outruns his name's orthography.

## Mythology

Baldr's mythology is a single arc — foreseen, enfolded, executed, mourned, and answered only after the end of the world — told across both Eddas with unusual agreement.

### The Dreams and the Prophecy (Baldrs draumar · Völuspá)

It begins with dreams: Baldr dreams balefully for his life, and the Æsir take counsel. In *Baldrs draumar*, Óðinn himself saddles Sleipnir, rides down to Niflhel, and raises a dead völva from her grave east of Hel's gate. She answers what she would not: the benches of Hel are strewn and the mead brewed for Baldr; [[hodr|Höðr]] will be the slayer; [[vali|Váli]], born to Óðinn, will avenge him one night old, neither washing his hands nor combing his hair until Baldr's foe burns; and Þökk will weep dry tears — let Hel hold what she has. Völuspá gives the same doom to its seeress: she saw the mistletoe, slim and very fair, and from that shoot the sorrow-dart, and Höðr shooting.

### The Oath and the Throw (Gylfaginning 49)

[[frigg|Frigg]] fights the prophecy with an oath, exacted from all things — fire, water, metals, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, serpents — that they will not harm Baldr. Only the mistletoe, growing west of Valhǫll, seemed too young to ask. The gods' pastime becomes shooting and hurling at Baldr, whom nothing can hurt, until [[loki|Loki]], in a woman's shape, learns the omission from Frigg, puts the mistletoe in blind Höðr's hand, and guides the throw. The shaft goes through Baldr and he falls — Snorri calls it the most ill-fated deed done among gods and men. The Æsir cannot even weep at first; and they cannot take vengeance, for the place is a sanctuary.

### The Burning of Hringhorni

The Æsir bear Baldr to the sea and bring out Hringhorni, greatest of all ships, which they cannot move; the giantess Hyrrokkin launches it with one shove, fire flying from the rollers. On the pyre they lay Baldr, and [[nanna|Nanna]], his wife, daughter of Nepr, dies of grief at the sight and is laid beside him. [[odinn|Óðinn]] lays the ring Draupnir on the fire; [[thor|Þórr]] hallows the pyre with Mjölnir and kicks the dwarf Litr into the flames.

### The Ransom and the Refusal

Hermóðr the Bold rides nine nights to Hel and begs for Baldr's release; Hel answers that all things, living and lifeless, must weep him out. Messengers go through the world and all things weep — men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and metals — save the giantess Þökk in her cave: 'Let Hel hold what she has.' The Æsir believed Þökk was Loki. The condition fails by one refusal, and Baldr remains with the dead.

### The Vengeance and the Return
Continue.

Váli, born to Óðinn for the purpose, kills Höðr when one night old, and Loki is bound until Ragnarǫk. Then comes the corpus's strangest consolation: after the fire and flood, Völuspá says, Baldr and Höðr come back together from Hel — slain and slayer reconciled — to the green earth, where the fields grow unsown.

### Saxo's Counter-Tradition

Saxo Grammaticus tells the death as heroic history: Balderus, a demigod son of Odin whom no ordinary steel can wound, and the human prince Høtherus contend for Nanna's hand; Høtherus wins the sword Mimming from the satyr Mimingus, wounds Balderus, and the demigod dies after three days; Bous — Saxo's Váli — is begotten to avenge him. The euhemerized skeleton keeps the myth's bones: the invulnerable man, the one weapon, the rival's hand, the begotten avenger.

## Symbols & Iconography

Baldr's iconography is the iconography of his death — the corpus gives him no regalia in life, but fixed around his pyre a set of objects no retelling can omit:

- **The mistletoe** — The one shoot Frigg judged too young to swear the oath: slender, fair, and fatal; Völuspá calls it high-grown and very beautiful, which is the myth's whole irony in a plant
- **Hringhorni** — His ship, 'greatest of all ships', which the Æsir could not launch until the giantess Hyrrokkin came riding a wolf with vipers for reins and shoved it to the sea
- **Draupnir** — The drip-gold ring Óðinn laid on the pyre; Baldr sent it back from Hel with [[hermod|Hermóðr]] as the token that the dead god had received the errand
- **Breiðablik** — The broad-gleaming hall, Grímnismál's seventh station of heaven, where the fewest evils lie
- **Baldrs brá (the daisy)** — The whitest of all plants, named for his eyelash: the only attribute Baldr carries in living botany
- **The ring of the fire** — The pyre itself, hallowed by Þórr's hammer Mjölnir, into which the dwarf Litr was kicked — the funeral as the gods' last ceremony in an unbroken world

## Archaeology & Evidence

Baldr is an almost entirely textual god: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and the place-name evidence sometimes claimed on his behalf is insecure. The material witnesses are indirect but real. Úlfr Uggason's *Húsdrápa*, composed about 983 and preserved in Skáldskaparmál, describes the funeral procession — Óðinn, Freyr, Heimdallr, the valkyries, and Hyrrokkin launching the ship — as carved on the panels of Óláfr pái's hall at Hjarðarholt in Iceland, proving that the Baldr myth was monumental art a generation before the conversion.

On the continent, the Second Merseburg Charm survives in a tenth-century theological manuscript from Fulda — the only Old High German text that may carry the god's name, whatever one makes of Phol. The poetic witnesses are likewise codicological: Völuspá and Grímnismál in the Codex Regius (c. 1270), while *Baldrs draumar* is found only in the fourteenth-century manuscript AM 748 I 4to — a reminder that the poem on which so much rests hangs by a single thread.

## Realm & Domain

**Baldr** is catalogued under Light, Beauty, Purity — and the sources earn every term of it: light streams from his face, his eyelash names the whitest plant in the world, and his hall admits nothing impure.

### Light

Snorri's portrait makes brightness a physical property: Baldr is so fair that a splendour radiates from him, and the daisy, whitest of all plants, is baldrs brá, 'Baldr's eyelash' — his brightness the standard by which whiteness itself is measured.

### Beauty

'He is the best, and all praise him': the formula is repeated across the corpus as the fixed epithet of the fairest of the Æsir, most beautifully spoken and most merciful.

### Purity

His dwelling is Breiðablik, the broad-gleaming, 'in the land where the fewest bale-runes lie' — Grímnismál's way of saying that nothing unclean has footing there.

### Peace and Judgment

He is the mildest of judges, and Snorri adds the haunting rider that none of his judgments can stand — as if the tradition already knew his goodness was not for this world. His son [[forseti|Forseti]] inherits the office of reconciliation in full.

## Across Cultures

The single continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, preserved in a tenth-century Fulda manuscript: 'Phol and Wodan rode to the wood; then Balder's foal wrenched its foot,' and Wodan charms the limb whole, bone to bone, blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Phol has widely been read as Baldr — which would make this the god's only Old High German attestation — but the identification is argued, not proven, and modern handbooks print it with a question mark. Old English offers a genealogical shadow rather than a myth: Bældæg, 'son of Woden', stands in the West Saxon royal genealogies, his name compounding the same word with 'day'.

The larger syncretic debate is the scholarship's own. Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century readers, struck by the innocent god who dies and returns, aligned Baldr with the Christ of the Gospels or with Frazer's dying-and-rising vegetation spirits — the 'Balder the Beautiful' volumes of The Golden Bough made him the type of the slain god. Current scholarship is cooler: Lindow and Orchard observe that Baldr's return is scheduled strictly after Ragnarǫk, that his death functions as the tragedy of the gods rather than as a fertility rite, and that the myth's true company is the northern complex of fratricide, failed ransom, and prophesied loss.

## Cultural Legacy

Baldr's afterlife is outsized precisely because his dossier is thin: the beautiful dead god became a vessel every age refills. Matthew Arnold's 'Balder Dead' (1855) made him the Victorian emblem of vanished perfection, and the nineteenth-century Norse revival cast him as the North's own god of light and innocence. Frazer's The Golden Bough built whole volumes — 'Balder the Beautiful' — on the mistletoe, and though the theory has faded, the phrase fixed Baldr in the English imagination as the slain god par excellence.

In the North itself the name never died: Icelandic Baldur and Danish-Norwegian Balder remain living given names, and the daisy still carries his eyelash in the Old Norse word baldrs brá. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep him at the centre of their rites of mourning and midsummer, reading his death and promised return as the tradition's theology of loss. In modern fiction, games, and comics he appears whenever a retelling needs the gods' innocence to break — his death is the standard first movement of any Ragnarǫk narrative.

## A Meditation

Baldr is the god the Edda built out of an absence. He is given no adventure, no trial, no weapon of his own — only perfection, prophecy, and the one overlooked thing. The myth's engineering is merciless: Frigg's oath is nearly complete, and nearly is the whole story; the gods' game is nearly harmless, and the mistletoe is nearly a plant; the world's weeping is nearly unanimous. Each near-victory is a door closing.

What remains is the strangest consolation in the northern corpus — not rescue, but return. After the fire and the flood of Ragnarǫk, Völuspá says, Baldr and Höðr come back together from Hel, the slain and the slayer reconciled, to a green earth. The Edda does not promise that loss can be prevented. It promises that what was best is not lost from the world for good — and asks, in the meantime, what a life is worth that is lived inside a prophecy it cannot escape.

## The Unicode Restoration

Baldr is classified as **Tier 2**: the restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The ASCII fallback *baldr* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Every stage of the journey from Younger Futhark to Unicode was an act of care: the scribe who first wrote the name, the lexicographer who glossed it, the engineer who taught the DNS to carry it. The PuniCodex restoration is the latest stage, not the last word — the Scholarly Edition is revised as the evidence improves. What does not change is the principle: a name deserves to be written the way its own tradition wrote it. **Baldr** in the address bar is that principle, made routable.

# The name Balor and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Balor** opens onto an entire world: the domain of destruction, evil eye, fomorians, a Celtic tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain that makes the whole structure addressable. *balor* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Balor
- **ASCII form:** balor
- **Meaning:** "Fomorian king whose destructive eye blasts armies when its lid is raised, slain by his grandson Lúg with a sling-stone at Cath Maige Tuired."
- **Domain of influence:** Destruction, Evil Eye, Fomorians
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Classification:** Tier 2

## Overview

**Balor** (*balor*) — Destruction, Evil Eye, Fomorians · the Fomorian king of the venomed eye — is the great antagonist of medieval Irish myth: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors who taxed Ireland from the outer islands until the second battle of Mag Tuired broke them. His weapon is the most feared in the corpus: a single eye, poisoned in his boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew, whose gaze made any army it looked upon worthless though it were many thousands strong — an eye never opened save on a battlefield, its lid raised by four men with a polished handle.

He is also, by the tradition's own reckoning, the grandfather of his destroyer. His daughter Ethniu bore [[lugh|Lugh]] to Cian, son of [[diancecht|Dian Cécht]]; and at Mag Tuired it was Lugh's sling-stone that drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that it was his own host that looked into it, and the Fomorian power over Ireland ended under his fall. The *Lebor Gabála Érenn* frames his lineage and records his wife Cethlenn's revenge — the wound she dealt [[dagda|the Dagda]] at Mag Tuired, of which the All-Father later died at the Brug.
