## The Name

The theonym is attested in Old and Middle Irish as **Balor**, and its etymology is one of the honest open questions of Irish onomastics: no derivation commands general assent, and the modern reference works register the proposals rather than endorse one. The tradition's own explanatory apparatus is the epithet — **Balor Béimnech** or **Bailcbéimnech**, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows', 'the Strong-Smiter' — which glosses not the name's origin but its owner's function: he is the one who strikes, and the whole corpus knows him by the blow. One scholarly line has connected the name with a root for 'blow, strike', which would make epithet and name say the same thing; this edition records the proposal without settling it, and the lexicon's meaning is given descriptively rather than etymologically.

His full manuscript style is genealogical: **Balor mac Doit meic Néit**, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét' — the ancestry the *Lebor Gabála* and *Cath Maige Tuired* agree on. The Donegal oral tradition keeps its own standing title, **Balor na Súile Nimhe**, 'Balor of the Evil Eye', the name under which the tower story and the stolen cow were still being told when the nineteenth-century collectors wrote them down.

The ASCII form *balor* loses nothing, because the normalized Old Irish spelling is already plain Latin letters; the restoration is therefore a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Balor** — Old Irish / Middle Irish in Insular script, attested in the codices that preserve Cath Maige Tuired and Lebor Gabála Érenn. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, predates the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this name has ever been read on an ogham stone; the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Old Irish was written in the Latin alphabet using Insular minuscule from the early medieval period; the spelling Balor requires no diacritic.
- The manuscripts give the name with its genealogy and epithets: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'son of Dot, grandson of Nét'; Balor Béimnech, 'of the Mighty Blows'.
- The consonants are broad — a velarized b, l, and r that Irish orthography marks by the surrounding vowels, not by any letter ASCII lacks; nothing distinctive is lost in transit.
- The Unicode restoration Balor is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

One caution attaches to the record: the name's etymology is unresolved, and this edition registers the proposals — including the connection with a root for 'blow, strike' that would match the epithet — without endorsing one.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈba.lor/** — Old Irish Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ba-** — Broad bilabial stop [b] and short open [a], stressed on the first syllable as in all Old Irish
- **-lor** — Broad (velarized) dental lateral [l̪ˠ], the dark Irish l; short [o]; a broad tapped or trilled final [rˠ], the second syllable unstressed

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped; the modern Irish *Balor* keeps essentially this shape.

## Mythology

Balor's mythology is a single arc — lineage, weapon, prophecy, and the stroke that answers all three — told between one great medieval text and the oral tradition that completes it.

### Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét (Lebor Gabála Érenn)

The book of invasions fixes his place before his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, king of the Fomorians, whose wife Cethlenn dealt [[dagda|the Dagda]] the wound at Mag Tuired of which the All-Father later died at the Brug — and whose daughter Ethniu bore [[lugh|Lugh]] to Cian, son of [[diancecht|Dian Cécht]], making the Fomorian king the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer.

### How the Eye Was Poisoned (Cath Maige Tuired)

The battle-text explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield; four men raised the lid with a polished handle passed through it, and any army the eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong. The poison had a childhood: as a boy he looked in on his father's druids brewing a charm, and the fumes of the brew struck the eye and venomed it for life.

### The Tower and the Prophecy (the Oral Tradition of Tory)

How Ethniu came to bear Lugh is told by the north-western oral tradition, collected in the nineteenth century around Tory Island, Balor's sea-girt fortress. A druid foretold that Balor would die by his own grandson's hand; the king prisoned his daughter in a tower on the rock with twelve matrons for guard. But Balor coveted and stole the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and Cian crossed to Tory for redress; with the druidess Biróg's help he won into the tower and to Eithne's side. When the child was born, Balor had him cast into the sea — and the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger came to [[nuada|Nuadu]]'s court and was asked what art he practiced.

### The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired (Cath Maige Tuired)

At the height of the second battle Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering, and commanded that the lid of his eye be raised to blast the enemy. As the four men set the handle to the lid, Lugh cast a sling-stone at him which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it; Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners, and the battle turned with the eye.

### The Price of the War (Lebor Gabála Érenn)

The tradition closes Balor's account slowly: the tribute was taken back from the defeated host, the Fomorian power over Ireland was broken for good — and years later, at the Brug on the Boyne, [[dagda|the Dagda]] died of the wound that Cethlenn, Balor's wife, had dealt him in the battle, the long-settled price of Balor's war.

## Symbols & Iconography

Balor's attributes are a weapon, the machinery that serves it, and the two objects of the oral tradition that explain his doom:

- **The venomed eye** — Poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of his father's druids' charm-brew; the gaze that made armies worthless — power taken in unguarded and carried incurably
- **The polished lid-lifter** — Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid: kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate
- **The tower of Tory** — The sea-girt prison built against the druid's prophecy, where Eithne was kept from every man's sight — the fortress that made the doom it feared
- **The Glas Gaibhnenn** — The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition: the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion
- **The sling-stone** — The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze, cast by [[lugh|Lugh]] at Mag Tuired — the grandson's hand the prophecy foretold

## Archaeology & Evidence

Balor is a textual and oral figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses, however, are exact: Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices.

His geographical anchor is one of the most dramatic pieces of coastline in Europe: Tory Island (Toraigh), nine miles off the Bloody Foreland of Donegal, whose cliffs and sea-stacks — above all the great rock called Tór Mór — the oral tradition names as Balor's fortress and the site of Eithne's tower. The nineteenth-century collectors who wrote the tower story down were recording a living Donegal tradition anchored to those rocks, and the island's medieval monastic remains and round tower have kept the name in continuous local memory.

## Realm & Domain

**Balor** is catalogued under the domain 'Destruction, Evil Eye, Fomorians' — three terms that are, in his case, one fact stated three ways.

### Destruction

His eye is the corpus's purest weapon of ruin: whatever army it looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong. He is given no craft, no counsel, no feast — nothing but the blow, whence his epithet Béimnech, 'of the Mighty Blows'.

### The Evil Eye

The boyhood accident at the druids' brew grounds the mythic weapon in the living Irish and Mediterranean folk-belief of the withering gaze — the look that blights cattle, milk, and men. Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat that folk complex as the ground on which Balor's eye was imagined.

### The Fomorians

He is king of the Fomorians, the sea-going adversaries of Irish myth who exacted Ireland's produce as tribute from the outer islands — under Balor and Indech the yoke that the second battle of Mag Tuired finally broke.

### Sovereignty That Poisons Its Possessor

Taken together, the three terms describe a single figure: kingship reduced to a weapon its owner cannot operate alone and cannot survive.

## Across Cultures

Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so much of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological.

First, the Greek **Acrisius**: the king who prisoned his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same. The Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the **Polyphemus** pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the **evil eye** itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze.

Within the Irish tradition his structural kin are the adversaries and the avengers his war sets in motion: [[nuada|Nuadu]], the king whose host he broke; [[lugh|Lugh]], the grandson the fortress was built to prevent; and [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]], whose war-counsel stood on the other side of Mag Tuired. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.

## Cultural Legacy

Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's *Gods and Fighting Men* (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's *Early Irish History and Mythology* (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king — a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short.

The second door was the folklore itself. The Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century by O'Donovan, Curtin, and Larminie, and never stopped being retold; 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address, and the Irish language never lost his name.

## A Meditation

Every part of Balor's story is about containment failing. The eye is contained — lidded, lifted only by machinery — and containment is the whole catastrophe: a gaze so dangerous it must be operated by four other men is no longer a weapon but an occupation, a king reduced to the caretaker of his own poison. The daughter is contained in a tower against a prophecy, and the tower is the prophecy's instrument: no tower, no Cian, no Lugh. Balor is the tradition's purest study of power that can only destroy — he is given no craft, no counsel, no feast, nothing but the eye and the tax it enforces.

And the answer the tradition gives him is exact. Not a bigger eye, not a stronger king, but a sling-stone: small, aimed, and thrown by the one hand the whole machinery existed to forestall. The venom that could wither an army is turned in a single instant into the Fomorians' own epitaph — it was his own host that looked into it. That is the Irish judgment on the evil eye, and on every power built to wither rather than to make: it ends by looking inward. The grandson does not defeat the weapon. He simply turns it around.

**Bꜣstt** begins as a lioness and ends as a cat. In the Old Kingdom she is a fierce daughter of Re, one of the raging eyes of the sun; by the Late Period she has become the benevolent lady of the home, her round face and upright ears copied by millions of household cats. The transformation is not a decline but an expansion: she learns to keep watch at the cradle as well as at the battlefield.

Her name may mean 'she of the ointment jar' (bꜣstt), linking her to perfumes, cosmetics, and the guarded substances of the bedroom. At her cult center, Per-Bastet — Greek Boubastis — pilgrims gathered for one of Egypt's most exuberant festivals: music, dance, wine, and the sacred procession of the goddess's barge.

The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓎯𓏏𓏏𓁐** — Egyptian hieroglyphic, attested Old Kingdom – Late Antiquity, c. 2600 BCE – 400 CE, in Egypt. The script is written right-to-left / top-to-bottom.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The Egyptian name is written 𓎯𓏏𓏏𓁐 in hieroglyphs.
- Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context.
- Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence.
- The Unicode restoration Bꜣstt uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com.

The name is written b-ꜣ-s-t-t, often with an ointment-jar determinative (V30) that gives rise to the gloss 'she of the ointment jar.' Allen reconstructs an early pronunciation close to buʔístit, with a glottal stop represented by the alef ꜣ (U+A723). The doubled t is orthographic; the final consonant is a feminine marker often silent in speech. Coptic writes ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste). The meaning of the root remains uncertain, and PuniCodex preserves the historic spelling Bꜣstt as a Tier 1 restoration that signals the alef and the feminine ending.

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/buˈʔistit/** — Egyptological Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **B-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bone'.
- **-u-** — Short rounded vowel in the first syllable.
- **-ʔ-** — Glottal stop [ʔ], the Egyptological alef (ꜣ, U+A723) that Allen reconstructs before the stressed syllable in the earliest form.
- **-i-** — Short close front vowel in the stressed syllable.
- **-s-** — Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'see'.
- **-t** — Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the second -t marks the feminine suffix and was usually not pronounced in speech.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'boo-ISS-tee' — say 'boo', then a tiny catch before 'iss', ending with 'tee' (the final t is often silent).

## Mythology

Bastet's myths are fewer than those of Isis or Horus, but her role in the solar cycle is vivid: she is the gentle dawn that follows the lioness's night.

### The Eye of Re Returns (Solar cycle)

In the mythology of the Distant Goddess, the solar eye — often in leonine form — leaves Egypt for Nubia in anger. Re sends Thoth or Shu to coax her back. When she returns, she is pacified as Bastet, the cat, and the festival of her homecoming is celebrated at Bubastis. The myth explains both the dangerous heat of the absent sun and the safety of its domesticated return.

### Bastet and Apep (Battle)

As a daughter of Re, Bastet takes part in the nightly battle against Apep, the serpent of chaos. In her lioness form she rips at the enemy; in her cat form she watches the prow of the sun barque, guarding Re with sharp eyes.

### The Pilgrimage to Bubastis (Festival)

Herodotus (Histories 2.60) describes the festival at Boubastis: boats of pilgrims, men and women together, sang, clapped, and exposed themselves in ribald jest as they traveled upriver. At the temple, great sacrifices of wine and animals were offered, and revelers honored the goddess with music and dance.

### The Gentle Healer (Healing)

Late Period and Greco-Roman amulets invoke Bastet against illness and the evil eye. Small bronze cats were deposited by the thousand in her temple precinct, votive bodies for a goddess who watched over the body's margins: birth, sleep, sexuality, and death.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The temple of Bastet at Tell Basta (Per-Bastet/Boubastis), excavated by Édouard Naville for the Egypt Exploration Fund in 1886–89, preserves the granite festival hall of Osorkon II with its sed-festival reliefs and has yielded statues, jewelry, and one of the largest animal cemeteries in Egypt: hundreds of thousands of mummified cats deposited as votives from the Late Period into Roman times. A second great center of her cult stood on the Saqqara escarpment: the Bubasteion, a Late Period to Ptolemaic temple raised above cat catacombs of its own. Bronze cat statuettes, often inlaid with gold earrings, are common in museum collections; examples come from Saqqara, Thebes, and Tanis. Reliefs in the Valley of the Kings show Bastet as a daughter of Re in the solar barque, keeping the older lioness alive beside the household cat.

**Bꜣstt** begins as a lioness and ends as a cat. In the Old Kingdom she is a fierce daughter of Re, one of the raging eyes of the sun; by the Late Period she has become the benevolent lady of the home, her round face and upright ears copied by millions of household cats. The transformation is not a decline but an expansion: she learns to keep watch at the cradle as well as at the battlefield.

Her name may mean 'she of the ointment jar' (bꜣstt), linking her to perfumes, cosmetics, and the guarded substances of the bedroom. At her cult center, Per-Bastet — Greek Boubastis — pilgrims gathered for one of Egypt's most exuberant festivals: music, dance, wine, and the sacred procession of the goddess's barge.

### The Cat

Bastet's later animal form; the cat protects the home from vermin and evil, and embodies solar warmth.

### The Lioness

Her older, fiercer aspect as a daughter of Re who fights the chaos serpent Apep.

### Music and Ecstasy

Her festivals featured sistrums, drums, and dancing; she is a goddess of controlled revelry.

### Guardian of the Home

Amulets of Bastet protected women in childbirth and children against malign forces.

## Across Cultures

Bastet overlaps with Sekhmet as the pacified form of the solar eye; one text's destroyer is another's house-cat. She was also identified with Hathor in her musical and erotic aspects, and with Isis as protector of the child Horus. Greeks equated her with Artemis, another virgin huntress with a fierce streak, and sometimes with Aphrodite because of her festivals' sexual license. In Roman Egypt her cult spread alongside that of Isis, and her cat iconography influenced medieval European images of the cat as both demonic and protective. The Coptic name Oubaste preserves her sound long after her temples closed.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], [[dagan|Dāgan]], [[demeter|Dēmētēr]], [[gaia|Gaîa]], and [[ishtar|Ištar]], each linked through earth / mother / fertility.

## Cultural Legacy

Bastet is the presiding genius of the internet cat: her image underlies every meme of a cat guarding a household, every statue of a seated feline, every association of cats with mystery and female power. In modern Witchcraft and Kemetic practice she is invoked for home protection, fertility, and pleasure. Her antiquity also has a sobering modern history: in 1890 some 180,000 mummified cats from the cat cemetery at Speos Artemidos near Beni Hasan were auctioned in Liverpool, most of them ground into fertilizer — an episode that appalled and galvanized the scholarship from which the modern study of Egyptian animal cults, and Jaromir Malek's standard work on the cat in ancient Egypt, descend. Egyptologists study the vast cat necropolis at Bubastis as evidence of animal cult and early pet-keeping. Bastet reminds us that the divine can sit on a windowsill, purring, and still be a daughter of the sun.

## A Meditation

Bastet is the goddess of thresholds. She lives where the wild presses against the wall of the house: the cat who sleeps on the bed but still dreams of the hunt. Her mythology is the domestication of solar power — not its weakening, but its decision to protect something small.

There is a wisdom in her later form that the earlier lioness could not teach. To guard a child, to keep watch through the night, to turn a corner of the home into a sanctuary — these are not lesser magics than tearing apart chaos. They are the magics that make chaos worth defeating. Bastet asks us to honor the fierce thing that has chosen to be gentle, and to remember that the claw and the purr belong to the same creature.

# The many faces of Baugi

No important name has only one face. **Baugi** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Younger Futhark original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *baugi* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Baugi
- **ASCII form:** baugi
- **Meaning:** "Ring-shaped"
- **Domain of influence:** Giant, Brother of Suttungr
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (Younger Futhark)

## Overview

**Baugi** (*baugi*) — Giant, Brother of Suttungr · the Keeper of the Door at Hnitbjǫrg — is the jötunn who makes the mead of poetry's theft possible: the brother of Suttungr, master of the nine thralls whose deaths open the labour bargain, and the wavering accomplice who bores the tunnel into the mountain where the mead is hoarded.

The name is usually connected with Old Norse *baugr* ‘ring, circlet’ — hence the traditional gloss ‘ring-shaped’ — though the derivation is not secure, and Simek registers the etymology as uncertain. Baugi's attestation is exactly as wide as his story: he appears in Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, in the mead-of-poetry narrative, and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door. In that one appearance he is the story's hinge: the labour-broker who contracts with the disguised [[odinn|Óðinn]], the man who honestly names his limits — ‘the mead is Suttungr's, not mine’ — and then sells access to it anyway, and the would-be betrayer whose auger-stroke misses the crawling snake by an inch.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Baugi** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name; the mechanical tier rule therefore places it in Tier 2, a statement about orthography and never about the figure. The temple is domain-less: the plain-ASCII baugi.com is held outside the collection and watched for release, and no form of the name is claimed as owned.

## The Name

The name is attested in Old Norse as **Baugi**, a masculine weak-form giant's name known from Skáldskaparmál's narrative and the þulur of jǫtna heiti. Its etymology is genuinely unsettled. The standard suggestion connects it with *baugr* ‘ring, circlet, coiled shape’ — the word that also stands in *baugeiðr* ‘ring-oath’ — yielding a gloss along the lines of ‘ring-shaped’ or ‘the coiled one’; Cleasby–Vigfusson and Zoëga document the underlying noun, while Simek treats the name's derivation as uncertain rather than solved. The resonance is worth registering without over-pressing: in Hávamál's own telling of the mead theft, the instrument Óðinn breaks is precisely a *baugeiðr*, a ring-oath — the god swears by the ring and leaves Suttungr defrauded.

The ASCII form is not a fallback but the original: the medieval manuscripts write five plain Latin letters, and no historically distinct Unicode spelling exists to restore. The mechanical rule therefore classifies the name Tier 2 — nothing distinctive is lost in transit.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **b** → **B** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

No domain is held. The plain-ASCII baugi.com is registered to a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; this temple claims no address it does not hold.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Baugi** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early 14th c.) and the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), recording material centuries older. Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the younger futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a giant's proper name of uncertain etymology, usually connected with *baugr* ‘ring, circlet’; Simek registers the derivation as unsettled.
- Old Norse orthography writes it in five plain letters: B-a-u-g-i, with no length mark and no special character.
- In the Younger Futhark it would run ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (b-au-k-i); the k-rune writes the g, and the medial fricative [ɣ] that the spelling g represents has no rune of its own.
- The Unicode form Baugi is therefore identical to the ASCII input — the restoration is a matter of canonical reference, not rescued letters, which is exactly what the Tier 2 classification records.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈbɑu.ɣi/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **B-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b], fully voiced initially, as in English ‘bow’
- **-au-** — The falling diphthong [ɑu], open back vowel gliding to rounded u; close to the ‘ow’ of English ‘cow’
- **-g-** — Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] between vowels, not a stop; before front i it palatalizes toward a glide close to English ‘y’
- **-i** — Short unstressed [i] in the final syllable

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘BOW-yee’ — first syllable rhyming with ‘cow’, the g softened to a glide so the second syllable lands almost like ‘yee’.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Baugi, brother of Suttungr, in Skáldskaparmál and the þulur
- **Younger Futhark** — ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (b-au-k-i), the normalized runic rendering; the k-rune ᚴ writes the g and no rune marks the medial fricative
- **Word-kin** — *baugr* ‘ring’ and *baugeiðr* ‘ring-oath’, the nouns to which the name is usually connected

Baugi is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII loses: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no vowel length. The five letters of the manuscripts are the five letters of the address bar.

## Mythology

Baugi's mythology is a single episode of the mead-of-poetry myth — but that episode is the hinge on which the whole theft turns.

### The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg (Skáldskaparmál)

Before Baugi enters, the mead has its own violent history: Kvasir, made from the peace of Æsir and Vanir, is killed by the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar, who brew his blood with honey into the mead that makes poets; the dwarfs drown the giant Gilling and kill his wife; Gilling's son [[suttungr|Suttungr]] takes the mead from them as blood-price, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it. Only then does Snorri write the genealogy the story needs: Suttungr had a brother named Baugi.

### The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls (Skáldskaparmál)

[[odinn|Óðinn]] comes to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, ‘Evil-doer’ — a name that announces rather than conceals. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay; Bǫlverkr sharpens their scythes with a whetstone so good that all nine want it, throws it up among them, and in the scramble the thralls cut each other's throats. That evening the stranger lodges with Baugi and hears him lament: nine thralls dead, the hay uncut. The vacancy the god is about to fill is one he made himself.

### Nine Men's Work for One Draught (Skáldskaparmál)

Bǫlverkr offers the work of nine men for the summer, his wage one drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi gives the story's one honest answer — the mead is not his to give, Suttungr alone controls it — and then commits himself anyway: he will go with Bǫlverkr and they will try together. The work is done; the pair go to Suttungr; the refusal is absolute. Baugi's brokerage has failed on its stated terms, and what remains is the half-promise of stratagems.

### Rati and the Two Blowings (Skáldskaparmál)

Bǫlverkr produces the auger Rati, and Baugi bores into the mountain. He declares the hole through; Bǫlverkr blows into it and the chips fly back into his face — the bore is blind, and Baugi meant to betray him. Baugi bores again; the chips fly inward. Bǫlverkr becomes a snake and crawls through, and Baugi strikes after him with the auger and misses. Inside, Óðinn lies three nights with Gunnlǫð, wins three draughts, empties all three vessels, and rises as an eagle with the mead in him, Suttungr hard behind in eagle-shape; the Æsir set out their vats, and what Óðinn cannot hold falls backward — the poetasters' share.

### Óðinn's Own Version (Hávamál 104–110)

Hávamál lets the god boast of the same theft in his own voice: Rati's mouth made room for him and gnawed the rock; Gunnlǫð gave him the drink from the golden seat; Óðrœrir came up among the Æsir; Suttungr was left defrauded and Gunnlǫð weeping, the ring-oath broken. But the poem never names Baugi. In the god's telling the doorkeeper has already vanished — contract, auger, and missed stroke absorbed into solitary cunning. Snorri's prose preserves what the boasting omits: the door had a keeper, the keeper had a price, and at the last moment he tried to close it on the snake.

## Symbols & Iconography

Baugi's iconography is narrative, not cultic — the corpus gives him no regalia, but the heist fixed a small set of objects around his one episode:
Continue.

- **Hnitbjǫrg** — The mountain of the mead, hoard and fortress in one; Baugi's auger makes the only door it ever had
- **Rati** — The auger, its name connected with the verb *rata* ‘to travel, find one's way’; tool of the breach and, for one stroke, almost the weapon that ends the story
- **The whetstone** — Óðinn's thrown bait: the thralls scramble for it and cut each other's throats, emptying Baugi's fields of nine workers at a throw
- **The nine scythes** — Harvest-tools honed too well; honest labour's edge turned to mutual death by a single act of sharpening
- **Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són** — The three vessels of the mead — ‘heart-stirrer’, ‘vessel’, and ‘reconciliation’ — that wait on the far side of Baugi's tunnel

## Archaeology & Evidence

Baugi is an entirely textual figure: no runestone invokes him, no picture stone has been convincingly read as the drilling of Hnitbjǫrg, and no place-name or votive deposit carries his name. His attestation is exactly as wide as his story — Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, preserved principally in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), with the Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis as the other main witnesses, plus his entry in the þulur of giant-names.

The mead myth he serves is materially older than its manuscripts. Kennings presupposing it — Kvasir's blood, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's booty — are already at work in ninth- and tenth-century skaldic verse, proving the story's currency centuries before Snorri wrote it down. Hávamál's telling survives in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), the same small codex that carries nearly all the mythological poems. The runic record is silent on the name, as it is on nearly all the jǫtnar.

## Realm & Domain

**Baugi** is catalogued under the domain Giant, Brother of Suttungr — a relational domain, because the tradition gives him no independent portfolio: he exists exactly where his brother's hoard needs a door and a doorkeeper.

### The Giant

He is of the jǫtnar, listed among them in the þulur, and his household — land, thralls, harvest — is the working farm on which Óðinn's deception is staged.

### The Brother of Suttungr

His one genealogical fact is his defining one: Suttungr's brother, and therefore the one man with a legitimate path toward the mead that Suttungr hoards in Hnitbjǫrg.

### The Labour-Broker

His nine thralls die by the whetstone trick, and his need for nine men's harvest-work becomes the contract that buys Bǫlverkr a summer's access.

### The Doorkeeper of Hnitbjǫrg

With the auger Rati in his hands he bores the only entrance the mountain ever has — and then strikes at what crawls through it, and misses.

## Across Cultures

Baugi himself has no cross-border reflex — no Old English or continental cognate figure, no cult, no charm; he is a person the Icelandic tradition made for one narrative. The myth he serves, however, sits in one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European study: the theft of the divine intoxicant. The standard parallel is Vedic — the śyena, the eagle or falcon that snatches the soma for the gods (Rigveda 4.26–27) — set beside Óðinn in eagle-shape carrying off the mead in his own body. The comparison was drawn in the nineteenth century and is still registered, with due caution, in the modern handbooks: Lindow treats the mead myth as the northern member of a genuine inheritance while warning against flattening its specifically Norse machinery — the labour contract, the auger, the broken oath.

Baugi's role belongs to that northern machinery: the intermediary who can be bought, the door that opens from the inside. Within the corpus his closest structural kin are the giants whose households Óðinn penetrates by guile — above all his brother [[suttungr|Suttungr]] and the deep giant-lore descending from [[ymir|Ymir]] — and the wisdom-figures the god elsewhere out-talls, [[mimir|Mimir]] among them. The mead he fails to keep becomes the drink of [[bragi|Bragi]]'s art.

## Cultural Legacy

Baugi's afterlife is mostly the afterlife of the drink he failed to keep. Skaldic poetry — the whole court-poetry tradition of the Viking and medieval North — named itself out of this myth: Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's theft, Óðrœrir's wave. Every character of the heist entered the poetic vocabulary except, so far as the corpus shows, its doorkeeper: no surviving kenning mints a ‘Baugi's mead’.

He survives instead as the specialists' hinge-figure. Every scholarly treatment of the mead myth, from Finnur Jónsson onward, must reckon with his two functions — the labour-broker who makes the theft logistically possible, and the wavering accomplice whose blind bore-hole and missed auger-stroke are the story's closest brush with failure. In the Norse-revival retellings and the modern handbooks he appears under his own name, always in the same posture: halfway through the mountain, one hand on the auger. The myth itself has become the North's great parable of inspiration as something hoarded and stolen rather than given — and [[bragi|Bragi]], god of poetry, pours out what Baugi could not guard.

## A Meditation

Baugi is the indispensable man nobody remembers. Strip him out and the myth stops cold: without the thralls' deaths there is no vacancy, without the contract there is no access, without the auger in his hand there is no door — and without the door there is no mead, and by the tradition's own accounting, no poetry at all.

Yet he is not the hero of his one story, nor even its villain. He is something rarer in the giant-world of the Eddas: a middleman. He names the limits of his power honestly — the mead is Suttungr's, not mine — and then sells access to what is not his anyway. He helps bore the hole and then tries to kill what crawls through it. The tradition leaves his motives exactly that tangled, and the tangle is the point: every hoard is opened from the inside, by someone whose loyalty is a price rather than a fact. The auger-stroke misses by the width of a snake — and because it misses, poems exist.

The ASCII fallback *baugi* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Baugi add up to a single argument — that a name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. The PuniCodex restoration keeps that record in working order: the temple presents it, the Scholarly Edition footnotes it, the lexicon catalogs it, and the domain makes it addressable. *baugi* will always exist as a fallback. # Pronouncing Bedwyr: a guide for the curious

Saying **Bedwyr** aloud is harder than reading it on a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Celtic transcription writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode domain. Whether you arrive as a linguist, a reader of myth, or a domainer, you will leave able to say the name the way the evidence suggests it was said — and able to type it the way it was written.

## Overview

**Bedwyr** (*bedwyr*) — Knight, One-handed · meaning unknown — is the great companion-hero of the oldest Welsh Arthurian tradition: Bedwyr fab Bedrawc, 'Bedwyr son of Bedrawc', the one-handed spearman who never shrank from any enterprise on which [[kai|Cei]] was bound, whose lance — *Culhwch ac Olwen* says — would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.

He belongs to the earliest stratum of Arthurian literature. The fragmentary poem *Pa gŵr yv y porthaur?* in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen — the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh — already names him in Arthur's roster; *Culhwch ac Olwen*, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives him its three finest paired episodes with Cei; and the Welsh triads crown him with a distinction no other companion receives: the triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan, Hueil, and Cei, then adds that one was battle-diademed above all three — Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. Geoffrey of Monmouth carried him into Latin as Beduerus, Arthur's cupbearer, slain in the Roman war and buried at Bayeux; from Geoffrey descends the Bedivere of romance and Malory — the last knight, who casts Excalibur back into the water.

## The Name

The name is attested in Middle Welsh as **Bedwyr**, patronymically Bedwyr fab Bedrawc (also spelled Bedravc, Bedrawd in the manuscripts) — 'Bedwyr son of Bedrawc'. Its meaning is unknown, and honest lexicography says so. The standard proposal, recorded in Koch's Celtic Culture encyclopedia, derives the name from Welsh **bedw**, 'birch trees', which would imply a Celtic compound *Betwo-rīxs*, 'birch-king' — a plausible formation but a proposal, not a settled etymology, and the father's name Bedrawc remains equally obscure.

The name's later career is a model of transmission. Geoffrey of Monmouth Latinized it as **Beduerus** (c. 1136); Wace and the French romances turned it into **Bedivers** and **Bedoier**; and Malory's **Bedivere** fixed the English form. The romance spelling preserves the Welsh sounds in continental dress — the w-vowel of the second syllable flattened to v — but the Welsh original is the earlier and the primary witness.

The ASCII form *bedwyr* loses nothing, because medieval Welsh orthography writes the name in plain Latin letters; the w and y that look like consonants to an English eye are Welsh vowel-letters, but they are ordinary characters of the Latin alphabet. The restoration is therefore a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Bedwyr** (patronymically Bedwyr fab Bedrawc) — Middle Welsh in the Insular-derived Welsh book-hand, attested from the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen onward, in *Pa gŵr?*, in the White Book and Red Book texts of *Culhwch ac Olwen*, and in the triad collections of the Red Book of Hergest. Welsh has no older monumental alphabet for this name: unlike Irish ogham, the Welsh epigraphic record preserves no inscription of Bedwyr, and none would be expected — the early inscribed stones of Wales are grave-markers in Latin and ogham, not narrative texts.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Medieval Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet; the spelling Bedwyr requires no diacritic, and the w and y that look like consonants to an English eye are Welsh vowel-letters — ordinary Latin characters.
- The name's meaning is unknown; Koch's derivation from Welsh bedw, 'birch trees' — implying *Betwo-rīxs*, 'birch-king' — is the standard proposal and remains debated.
- The continental forms (Beduerus, Bedivers, Bedivere) are adaptations of the Welsh original, not independent witnesses.
- The Unicode restoration Bedwyr is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

## Pronunciation

The modern Welsh pronunciation of the name is **/ˈbɛd.ʊɨr/** — Modern Welsh.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Bed-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b] and short open-mid front [ɛ], the stressed penult, as Welsh stress almost always falls on the syllable before the last
- **-dw-** — Voiced dental stop [d], then Welsh w as a full vowel: short close back [ʊ], the 'oo' of English 'book'
- **-yr** — Final-syllable Welsh y, the close central vowel [ɨ] (southern dialects relax it toward [ɪ]), closed by a tapped or trilled [r]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BED-weer' — read the w as the vowel 'oo', and let the final y sit between 'i' and 'u'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Middle Welsh** — Bedwyr fab Bedrawc, the spelling of the White Book and Red Book texts
- **Medieval Latin** — Beduerus, Geoffrey of Monmouth's form (c. 1136)
- **Old French / English** — Bedivers, Bedoier; Malory's Bedivere
- **Proto-Celtic (proposed)** — *Betwo-rīxs*, 'birch-king', Koch's tentative derivation from bedw, 'birch trees'

## Mythology

Bedwyr's dossier is compact and entirely medieval Welsh until Geoffrey of Monmouth: a poem's roster, a tale's episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes.

### The War-Band Remembered (Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen)

The poem known from its opening line as *Pa gŵr yv y porthaur?* — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh, preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. Halted at a fortress gate, Arthur recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names that proves the company.

### The One-Handed Spearman (Culhwch ac Olwen)

Calling the companions for the quest of Olwen, Arthur calls Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.' The court-list extends his household: Amren son of Bedwyr among the huntsmen, Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the maidens of the Island.

### The Beard of Dillus the Bearded (Culhwch ac Olwen)

No leash could hold Drudwyn, whelp of Greid son of Eri, save one made from the beard of Dillus Farfawc, plucked alive with wooden tweezers. As Cei and Bedwyr sat on a beacon cairn on the summit of Pumlumon, in the highest wind that ever was in the world, they spied smoke that did not bend with the wind and found the greatest robber who ever fled from Arthur at his fire. They let him eat and sleep, shaped the tweezers, dug the pit, plucked the beard, and slew him — and Arthur's mocking englyn over the leash so angered Cei that he never came to Arthur's aid again.

### The Sword of Gwrnach and the Cauldron of Diwrnach (Culhwch ac Olwen)

At Gwrnach the Giant's castle, from which no guest returned alive, Cei went in under a false craft — the best burnisher of swords in the world — and won Bedwyr admission by a sign: the head of his lance would leave its shaft, draw blood from the wind, and settle on its shaft again; Cei then beheaded the giant with his own polished sword. In Ireland, refused the cauldron of Diwrnach Wyddel, Bedwyr arose and seized it and set it on the back of Hygwyd, Arthur's cauldron-bearer, while Llenlleawg caught up Caledfwlch, and they fought their way back to the ship Prydwen.

### The Diadem Above the Three (Trioedd Ynys Prydein 21 · 26)
Continue.

The triads name Bedwyr twice, both times beside Cei. The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan son of Tallwch, Hueil son of Caw, and Cei son of Cynyr — and adds that one was battle-diademed above all three: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. The triad of the Three Powerful Swineherds is the tradition's joke at the war-band's expense: while Drystan kept March's swine, Arthur and March and Cei and Bedwyr were there, all four, yet got not so much as one pigling, neither by force, nor by deception, nor by stealth.

### Beduerus at Soissons (Historia Regum Britanniae XI)

Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin history (c. 1136) makes him Beduerus: Arthur's cupbearer and constable of Normandy, slain in the fighting before Soissons in the war against the emperor Lucius Tiberius, and buried at Bayeux — a city his ancestors had built — with the king's great lamentation. Pseudo-history, not Welsh tradition, but the hinge on which Welsh Bedwyr turns into romance Bedivere.

## Symbols & Iconography

Bedwyr's attributes are few, functional, and all attested in the Welsh texts — the regalia of a working companion rather than a crowned god:

- **The one-handed lance** — A lance whose single thrust produced a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances — one arm doing the work of nine
- **The battle-diadem** — The triad's crown above the crowned: one was battle-diademed above all three, and that was Bedwyr son of Bedrawc
- **Cavall, Arthur's hound** — The king's own dog entrusted to Bedwyr's hand in the hunting of Twrch Trwyth — trust made visible
- **The wooden tweezers** — The instrument of the Dillus episode on Pumlumon: the beard had to be plucked alive, for dead it would have been brittle, and no other leash could hold the hound Drudwyn
- **The sword cast back to the water** — In the later Malorian tradition, Bedivere is the last knight, who returns Excalibur to the lake and sees the arm in white samite catch it

## Archaeology & Evidence

Bedwyr is a textual hero: no inscription names him, and Welsh tradition offers no relic or shrine. His manuscript witnesses are exact. The poem *Pa gŵr?* survives uniquely in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 1), copied in the mid-thirteenth century and the oldest surviving manuscript wholly in Welsh. *Culhwch ac Olwen* survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and, in a fuller recension, in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, late fourteenth century), which also carries the great collection of the triads.

The one landscape witness is genuine: Pumlumon (Plynlimon) in Ceredigion, the mountain whose summit cairns the tale makes the lookout of Cei and Bedwyr in the Dillus episode, is a real massif of the Cambrian Mountains crowned with prehistoric cairns. Geoffrey of Monmouth's burial of Beduerus at Bayeux belongs to his Norman pseudo-history, not to any Welsh memory.

## Realm & Domain

**Bedwyr** is catalogued under the domain 'Knight, One-handed' — two words that fix his place in the tradition exactly: the companion-knight of the Welsh war-band, and the one-handed spearman whose missing arm the texts never explain and never count as loss.

### Knight

Bedwyr is the type of the Arthurian companion before romance invented the word for it: sworn to the war-band, bound to [[kai|Cei]] in the tradition's fixed pairing — the sources say 'Cei and Bedwyr', never the reverse — and entrusted with the tasks that decide the quest. In the Twrch Trwyth hunt, the greatest boar-hunt in Welsh literature, it is Bedwyr who leads Cavall, Arthur's own hound.

### One-handed

The single hand is the tradition's arithmetic of worth: though one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle, and his lance produced a wound equal to nine opposing lances. The triads carry the same measure in their own idiom — the one man battle-diademed above Drystan, Hueil, and Cei.

### The Companion of Cei

The pairing is itself a domain: at the gate of Gwrnach's castle, in the highest wind on Pumlumon, on the shoulders of the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, the two move as one instrument — Cei's cunning at the door, Bedwyr's hand on the prize.

## Across Cultures

Bedwyr's transmission is the clearest case in the Arthurian corpus of a Welsh hero passing whole into the continental tradition: Welsh Bedwyr becomes Geoffrey's Latin Beduerus, then the Bedivers and Bedoier of Old French romance, and at last Malory's Sir Bedivere — one continuous name-line from the Black Book of Carmarthen to Caxton's print shop.

Within Celtic comparison, the one-handed warrior who loses nothing of his worth has tempted scholars toward the Irish parallel of [[nuada|Nuadu]] of the Silver Hand, the king who lost his arm at Mag Tuired and ruled again by means of a silver one; the handbooks treat this as a shared Celtic motif of the maimed-but-undiminished champion, not a derivation of one figure from the other. What the Welsh tradition keeps distinct is the pairing: Cei and Bedwyr are a fixed couple — the sources name them in that order, never the reverse — a bond as elemental in early Welsh Arthurian lore as any kinship, set beside [[gawain|Gwalchmai]], Arthur's nephew, as the court's two immovables.

## Cultural Legacy

Bedwyr's afterlife runs under a French name. Wace's *Roman de Brut* and Layamon's *Brut* carried Geoffrey's Beduerus into the vernacular chronicles; the French romances made him Bedivere, one of the first and last of the Round Table; and Malory gave him the role the whole world now knows — the last knight alive with Arthur, commanded to cast Excalibur into the water, twice hiding it for its worth and twice rebuked, until at the third throw an arm clothed in white samite rose from the lake, caught the sword, brandished it thrice, and vanished. Tennyson's *Idylls of the King* sealed the image: it is to Bedivere that the dying Arthur speaks the great consolation — 'The old order changeth, yielding place to new' — before the barge bears him away.

Twentieth-century scholarship brought the Welsh original back into view: Bromwich's edition of the triads restored the battle-diadem to Bedwyr son of Bedrawc, and the standard handbooks now present the romance Bedivere as what he is — a Welsh heroic companion who had served Arthur in Welsh for perhaps three hundred years before French poetry heard of him. In Wales itself the name never left: Bedwyr remains a living Welsh given name.

## A Meditation

Bedwyr is the tradition's proof that loss is not the measure of a man. The texts hand him to us already one-handed — the wound is never narrated, never mourned, never explained — and then spend every remaining line insisting on the arithmetic of what is left: one arm that sheds blood faster than three warriors, one lance that wounds like nine, one diadem above the three crowned. The silence about the missing hand is the point: the Welsh tradition does not tell a story about a maimed warrior; it tells stories about the swiftest, surest companion Arthur has, who happens to fight with one arm.

And beneath the arithmetic stands the quieter fact: he never shrank from any enterprise on which Cei was bound. The tradition could have made him Arthur's mirror or Cei's rival; it made him Cei's shadow instead — the second name in every pair, the hand on the cauldron while the cunning works the gate. Loyalty, in the oldest Welsh telling, is not obedience to the crown but fidelity to a companion: the willingness to sit in the highest wind in the world, on a cairn on Pumlumon, because that is where the quest requires the two of you to sit.

# The many faces of Beli

No important name has only one face. **Beli** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Celtic transcription original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *beli* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

- **Domain of influence:** Light, Sun
- **Pantheon:** Celtic

## Overview

**Beli** (*beli*) — Light, Sun · Bright, shining — is Beli mawr, Beli the Great, son of Manogan: the ancestor-king who stands at the head of the Mabinogion's British dynasties. The tale of Lludd and Llefelys opens with him — king of the Island of Britain, father of Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw, and 'a fourth son called Llefelys' — and finishes him in a sentence; the Second Branch then watches his son Caswallawn take the crown from the children of Llŷr under a veil of illusion.

Beyond the tales, Beli's real dominion was genealogical. The Harleian genealogies carry the royal pedigrees of the Welsh kingdoms back to Beli mawr, and the convention held for centuries: descent from Beli the Great was the deepest legitimacy a British dynasty could print. Geoffrey of Monmouth Latinized him as Heli, father of Lud, Cassibelaunus, and Nennius, and through Geoffrey his house entered the bloodstream of European letters.

The name's traditional gloss is 'bright, shining', reached through its long-proposed connection with the continental Celtic god Belenos — Tertullian's god of the Noricans, the Apollo Belis of Aquileia — conventionally derived from the root *bhel-, 'to shine'. The derivation of Belenos itself is debated, and the identification of the Welsh ancestor with the god is a venerable possibility, not a proof; the lexicon records the gloss as the tradition gives it.

## The Name

The name is attested in Middle Welsh as **Beli**, characteristically with the epithet — *Beli mawr uab Manogan*, 'Beli the Great, son of Manogan' — in the Mabinogion and in the genealogical tracts. Geoffrey of Monmouth writes it in Latin as **Heli**, a form his translators later Englished as both Heli and Beli.

The traditional gloss is 'bright, shining', and it arrives by way of the continental theonym **Belenos / Belinus** — the god the Latin tradition equated with Apollo — whose name has conventionally been derived from Proto-Indo-European *bhel-, 'to shine'. The link between the Welsh ancestor and the god is one of the oldest proposals in Celtic scholarship and remains unproven; the etymology of Belenos itself is disputed, and rival derivations exist. This edition records the gloss as the tradition hands it down, with the uncertainty attached.

The name should also be distinguished from its homonyms. Geoffrey's **Belinus**, son of Dunvallo and brother of Brennius, is a different figure who shares nothing with Beli Mawr but the name; and several historical Welsh dynasts bore Beli as a personal name — Beli son of Rhun stands in the Gwynedd pedigree — without being the ancestor-king.

The ASCII form *beli* loses nothing, because the attested Welsh spelling is already plain Latin letters; the restoration is a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as **Beli** — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great codices of the Mabinogion, and in the genealogical collections preserved in Harley MS 3859 and its sister manuscripts. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet from the early medieval period; the spelling Beli requires no diacritic.
- Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin form Heli reflects the same name carried into the orthographic conventions of twelfth-century Anglo-Latin.
- The proposed connection with Gaulish Belenos is a question of etymology and mythography, not of attestation: no British inscription preserves the name in either form.
- The Unicode restoration Beli is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

One caution attaches to the record: the traditional gloss 'bright, shining' belongs to the Belenos connection and is recorded here as tradition, not as a demonstrated derivation of the Welsh name.

## Mythology

Beli has no adventure of his own: his story is his house. The Mabinogion knows him as the dead king whose sons inherit Britain, France, and the quarrels of the next generation; the pedigrees know him as the root; Geoffrey knows him as the father of the builder of London.

### The Four Sons of Beli (Mabinogion, Lludd a Llefelys)

The tale opens with the settlement of the island: Beli the Great, son of Manogan, was king of this island, and he had three sons — Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw — and, as the story tells, a fourth son called Llefelys. When Beli died, the kingdom of the Island of Britain fell to Lludd as the eldest; Lludd ruled prosperously, rebuilt the walls of London, and lived there for most of the year. Llefelys went to France, won the old king's only daughter, and inherited that kingdom in his turn. What follows — the three plagues, the counsel from the middle of the Channel — belongs to the sons; Beli's part is finished in the opening lines, which is precisely his function: the point from which legitimacy flows.

### Caswallawn's Veil (Mabinogion, Branwen ferch Llŷr)

While Brân the Blessed marched into Ireland, he left seven regents in Britain, his son Caradog at their head. Caswallawn son of Beli marched against them wearing a veil of illusion, so that no one could see him — only his sword killing. He slew the seven; Caradog died of a broken heart; and Caswallawn son of Beli became king in London. The branch never explains or excuses the usurpation: while the children of Llŷr spent themselves overseas, the children of Beli took the island.

### The Root of the Royal Trees (Harleian Genealogies)

The Harleian genealogies — the Welsh royal pedigrees preserved in British Library, Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) — carry the lines of the British kingdoms back generation by generation until they reach Beli mawr, who stands near the root of the trees. To claim a throne in early Wales was in part to publish a pedigree, and the pedigrees converge on him; the convention held for centuries in the genealogical tracts.

### Heli, Father of Lud (Geoffrey of Monmouth)

Geoffrey's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) carried Beli into Latin as Heli, father of Lud, Cassibelaunus, and Nennius. Lud rebuilt Trinovantum with noble walls and renamed it Kaerlud — whence London, Geoffrey says, and the gate called Ludgate; Cassibelaunus became the enemy of Caesar. Through the Historia, one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages, Beli's house entered European letters.

### The Bright One Behind the King (Tertullian; Herodian)

Around the year 200 Tertullian lists the local gods of the provinces and gives the Noricans Belenus; a generation later Herodian tells how, at the siege of Aquileia in 238, the citizens credited their deliverance to Apollo, the god the region worshipped under the name Belis. The altars agree — dedications Belino Augusto sacrum cluster at Aquileia and across the eastern Alpine provinces. Whether the Welsh ancestor descends from this 'bright, shining' god is the standing question of Beli scholarship; no text performs the identification, and the honest verdict is the one the handbooks give: a venerable possibility, unproven.

## Symbols & Iconography
Continue.

Beli's attributes are institutional rather than mythic — the regalia of a founding king rather than the wonders of a tale:

- **The Island of Britain** — The single realm he held and his sons inherited; kingship imagined whole before it was ever divided
- **The family tree** — The pedigrees of the Welsh dynasties growing back to one root; ancestry as the ground of legitimacy
- **The veil of illusion** — Caswallawn's invisible cloak in the Second Branch, the house of Beli taking the crown unseen
- **The walled city** — London, rebuilt by his son Lludd, the memory of the dynasty fixed in stone and street-names
- **The sun's brightness** — The traditional gloss of the name, carried from the Belenos inscriptions into the Welsh ancestor

## Archaeology & Evidence

Beli is a textual figure: no inscription, image, or votive object from Britain names him, and no cult site is his. His witnesses are codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410) for the Mabinogion tales, and British Library Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) for the genealogies that root the Welsh dynasties in him.

The material evidence belongs to his proposed continental cognate: the dedications Belino Augusto sacrum from Aquileia and the eastern Alps are real stones with a real theonym — the strongest archaeological fact in the whole dossier, and the reason the 'bright, shining' gloss will not go away. But they are comparative evidence only: no altar from the Celtic provinces can be read as addressed to the Welsh ancestor-king himself.

## Realm & Domain

**Beli** is catalogued under the domain 'Light, Sun' — the name's traditional solar reading, inherited from its long-proposed connection with the 'bright, shining' god Belenos. His attested role in the texts is something adjacent: the luminous first term of a dynasty, the light at the root of the tree rather than a god in the sky.

### Light

The traditional gloss of the name — 'bright, shining' — reaches Beli through Belenos, the continental god the Latin sources equated with Apollo. Whether the Welsh ancestor descends from the god is unproven, but the gloss is old, and it fits the figure's function: he is the name the whole tradition is lit from.

### Sun

No Welsh text gives Beli a solar myth — there is no chariot, no journey, no setting. The solar reading lives entirely in the etymology and in the continental altars. What the Welsh record offers instead is the genealogical counterpart of a sun: the single source from which the royal lines radiate, the Harleian pedigrees climbing back to Beli mawr as to a first light.

### The Kingship the Domain Implies

What the texts actually give Beli is the Island of Britain: its crown, its walled city, and the sons who inherit both. If a solar god stands behind him, the Welsh tradition has long since dimmed the god into the ancestor — and the ancestor is the figure the record can defend.

## Across Cultures

Beli's whole cross-cultural argument is the Belenos question. The continental god is attested from Aquileia to Noricum, glossed by the ancients as a Celtic Apollo, and derived by tradition from *bhel-, 'to shine'; the Welsh Beli Mawr matches the name nearly perfectly, and from O'Rahilly onward scholars have set the Irish ancestor-figure Bile beside both, proposing a single Celtic 'bright one' dimmed into three literatures as three ancestors. Mac Cana and Koch record the comparison; neither certifies it.

Within the Welsh corpus his closest kin are the other fountainheads of dynasty: [[don|Dôn]], mother of the Children of Dôn, and the house of Llŷr, whose sons Brân and [[manawydan|Manawydan]] lose the island's crown to Beli's son Caswallawn in the Second Branch. Two distinctions are worth keeping: Geoffrey's Belinus, son of Dunvallo and brother of Brennius, is a different figure who shares nothing with Beli Mawr but the name; and the historical Welsh dynasts called Beli — Beli son of Rhun stands in the Gwynedd pedigree — are bearers of the name, not the ancestor-king.

## Cultural Legacy

Beli's afterlife is genealogical before it is literary. The medieval pedigrees made descent from Beli Mawr the deepest claim a British dynasty could print, and the convention outlived the Middle Ages: Tudor and Stuart antiquaries, eager to trace the crown to British and Trojan roots, found Beli waiting at the root of the trees Geoffrey had Latinized. Through Geoffrey's Heli he fathered the legend of London itself — Lud's town, Lud's gate, the name written into the city's streets — and through his son Cassibelaunus he stands two generations above Shakespeare's Cymbeline, whose Britain is still Beli's island.

In modern Wales the name persists quietly: Beli remains a Welsh personal name, and Beli Mawr keeps his place in the national memory as the grandfather of kings. Modern Celtic pagan and Druid practice honors the ancestral Belenus beside him, keeping the old question — king or bright god — alive rather than answered.

## A Meditation

Beli is the patron of everything that matters most and does least: the dead father, the founding reign, the name at the root of the tree. He fights no monster, wins no bride, casts no spell; the Mabinogion finishes him in a sentence, and then builds a world on him. His sons inherit his island and quarrel over it; his house takes the crown under a veil of illusion; the pedigrees spend a thousand years climbing back to him.

That is how ancestry actually works — the founder is never the hero of the story, only its premise. Beli asks the genealogist's hard question of every institution and every family: not what have you done, but what are you descended from, and does the root still hold. And the name itself holds its own question: whether the bright one, the shining god of the continental altars, lies behind the sober Welsh king. Some roots run deeper than the record can follow. Beli is the place where Britain's goes dark.
