## A Meditation

Freyja holds two things the world keeps trying to separate. She is the goddess of love — desire, gold, the necklace, the weeping for Óðr — and she is a commander of the dead, choosing half the slain before Óðinn takes his half. The Edda refuses the split: the same figure who weeps tears of red gold rides to battle; the same word that means ‘lady’ heads a war-dead of her own.

Her refusals are as load-bearing as her powers. Offered to Þrymr as a bride-price, she does not argue; the hall shakes and the necklace bursts. Charged by Loki with her lovers, the tradition answers through her father: it is no shame. The corpus never lets her be traded, commanded, or shamed — only impersonated, invoked, and followed. To say her name in Old Norse was simply to say ‘the lady’: the title and the goddess are one word, and the one word was always enough.

No important name has only one face. **Freyr** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. ## Overview

**Freyr** (*freyr*) — Fertility, Sunshine, Rain · Lord — is the Vanir god who became the Æsir's own lord of the growing world: son of [[njordr|Njǫrðr]], brother of [[freyja|Freyja]], ruler of rain and sunshine and the fruit of the earth, the god Snorri says it is good to call on for *ár ok frið* — harvest and peace.

Old Norse *Freyr* descends from Proto-Germanic *frawjaz* ‘lord’ — the same word as Gothic *frauja* and Old English *frēa* — and forms a title-pair with *Freyja* ‘lady’. His mythology is the corpus's clearest economy of sacrifice: the self-wielding sword given to Skírnir as the price of Gerðr's love, the improvised antler that killed the giant Beli, and the fatal absence of that sword when he faces [[surtr|Surtr]] at Ragnarök. To the Swedes of Heimskringla he is also the euhemerized King Freyr of Uppsala, the peace-years king of the Yngling line.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Freyr** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography, never about the god's standing. The name also travels under older bynames. Lokasenna names him *Ingunar-Freyr*, and Ynglingatal and the Skáldskaparmál tradition give *Yngvi-Freyr* — the element scholars connect, with due caution, to the Ing of the Old English Rune Poem and the Inguaeones of Tacitus.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The word is the common noun *freyr* ‘lord’, from Proto-Germanic *frawjaz*, with the nominative singular ending *-r*.
- The diphthong *ey* descends from older *au* (still visible in a normalized younger-futhark carving, ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ *frauR*); the manuscripts' *ey* is the smoothed Old Icelandic form.
- Normalized Old Norse writes the name in plain ASCII — no diacritic, no thorn or eth — so the Unicode restoration **Freyr** is letter-for-letter the manuscript form, capitalized.
- Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: freyr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈfrœy.r̩/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Fr-** — Voiceless labiodental [f] and trilled [r], a common Old Norse onset cluster
- **-ey-** — The falling diphthong /œy/, born by umlaut and monophthong-smoothing from an older *au*; it sits between the ‘oy’ of English *boy* and the ‘ay’ of *day*, and survives in modern Icelandic as /ei/ (Icelanders say ‘FRAY-ir’)
- **-r** — The syllabic trill [r̩] of the nominative masculine ending, carrying its own light beat

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘FRAY-ur’ — one syllable for the diphthong, then the light final trill.

- **Proto-Germanic** — *frawjaz*, ‘lord’
- **Younger Futhark (normalized)** — ᚠᚱᛅᚢᛦ, frauR, the Viking-Age carving, keeping the older *au* before it smoothed to ey
- **Gothic** — frauja, ‘lord’, the Gospels' word for the Lord
- **Old English** — frēa, the poetic ‘lord’ of Beowulf's kings
- **Modern Icelandic** — Freyr, the name's unbroken living form

## Mythology

Freyr's surviving mythology is built on a single economy — what the lord of plenty gives away — told across the two Eddas and the kings' sagas with unusual coherence.

### The Tooth-Gift (Grímnismál 5)

The gods gave Álfheimr to Freyr as a tooth-gift — the present made to a child when its first tooth appears. The detail is the Edda's way of saying the elf-realm has always been his; Snorri pairs it with the fixed formula of his office: rule over rain, sunshine, and the fruit of the earth, and the governing of men's prosperity.

### The Price of Gerðr (Skírnismál)

Seated in Hliðskjálf, Óðinn's all-seeing high seat, Freyr looked north into Jǫtunheimr and saw Gerðr, daughter of the giant Gymir, whose white arms lit sky and sea as she walked from hall to bower. The longing that followed was a sickness: he would not eat, sleep, or speak. [[njordr|Njǫrðr]] sent the servant Skírnir to bargain the cause out of him, and Skírnir named his price for the wooing-errand — Freyr's horse and his sword, the one that fights by itself if he is wise who wields it. Freyr paid both on the spot. Skírnir rode through the magic flame, broke Gerðr's refusal with gifts, runes, and threats, and won her promise to meet Freyr in the grove Barri nine nights hence. The poem closes on the waiting god: ‘Long is one night, longer is two — how shall I endure three?’

### The Gifts of the Dwarfs (Skáldskaparmál)

Two of the six treasures of the gods are Freyr's. Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, was made by the sons of Ívaldi — big enough for all the Æsir with their war-gear, always granted a fair wind, foldable into a pouch. Gullinbursti, the golden-bristled boar, came from the same wager between Loki and the smith Brokkr that produced [[thor|Þórr]]'s hammer. Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa, carved on a hall's panels in Iceland about 983 and quoted by Snorri, remembers Freyr riding the boar to Baldr's funeral; Gylfaginning gives him a chariot drawn by Gullinbursti for the same journey.

### Swordless Against Surtr (Vǫluspá 52–53; Gylfaginning 51)

The Edda keeps the ledger. In Lokasenna, [[tyr|Týr]] throws the old bargain in Freyr's face: with gold you bought Gymir's daughter and sold your sword — when Muspell's sons ride through the dark wood you will not know what to fight with. Gylfaginning recalls that Freyr once killed the giant Beli with a hart's antler and could have slain him with his fist; but at Ragnarök improvisation ends. Freyr goes against [[surtr|Surtr]], and his death, Snorri says, comes the harder because he lacks the good sword he gave Skírnir. Vǫluspá's seeress watches the shining lord fall before the fire.

### The King Who Would Not Die (Ynglinga saga 10–13)

Heimskringla's euhemerized Freyr is king of the Swedes at Uppsala after Njǫrðr: he built the great temple, gathered the land-rents and the wealth of Uppsala into his own hand, and in his days began the Fróði-peace, the peace-years of good seasons the Swedes credited to their king. When he died, his men concealed it: they set him in a mound with three holes, told the people he lived, and for three years the tribute — gold, silver, copper — was poured down into the mound while the peace held. Afterwards the Swedes still would not burn him; they called him the god of the world and sacrificed to him for peace and good seasons.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography of Freyr is the richest of any Vanir god — a full set of attributes fixed by the Eddas and the cult reports alike:

- **Gullinbursti** — The golden-bristled boar forged by Brokkr and Sindri, faster than any horse through air and water, its bristles lighting night to day; Freyr rode it — or drove behind it — to [[baldr|Baldr]]'s pyre
- **Skíðblaðnir** — The best of ships, built by the sons of Ívaldi: fair wind at every hoisting, room for all the Æsir armed, and it folds like cloth into a pouch
- **The self-wielding sword** — The blade that fights by itself for the wise, surrendered to Skírnir as the price of the errand to Gerðr
- **The hart's antler** — The improvised weapon with which he killed the giant Beli bare-handed; the sign of the swordless god
- **Álfheimr** — The realm of the elves, given him by the gods as a tooth-gift in the first days
- **The phallus** — The cult attribute Adam of Bremen reports at Uppsala and the Rällinge statuette displays: fertility written on the body of the god

## Archaeology & Evidence

Freyr is one of the few Norse gods with a plausible cult-image in the ground. The Rällinge statuette — a small seated bronze of the Viking Age, found in 1904 at Rällinge, Lunda parish, Södermanland, Sweden — shows a cross-legged, bearded, unmistakably ithyphallic figure and has been identified as Freyr since its discovery; it matches Adam of Bremen's description of the Uppsala *Fricco* with striking economy.

Uppsala itself anchors the cult landscape: Adam describes the great temple, its golden chain, and its triad of Thor, Wodan, and Fricco around 1075, and the royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala still stand where Ynglinga saga sets King Freyr's own mound and the *Uppsala auðr*. The theophoric place-name record — hundreds of Frøy-/Frö- names, weighted to groves and fields — is the strongest indirect witness of a working fertility cult. Against all this, the runic corpus is silent: no surviving inscription invokes the god by name. The literary witnesses are the Codex Regius poems (Skírnismál, Grímnismál, Lokasenna, Vǫluspá) and the quotation of Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983) in Skáldskaparmál, which proves the boar-riding Freyr was already a fixture of pre-Christian hall decoration a generation before the conversion of Iceland.

## Realm & Domain

**Freyr** is the god of the peace-years: the Vanir lord whose portfolio Snorri fixes in a single sentence — rain and sunshine, the fruit of the earth, the prosperity of men — and whom the Swedes remembered as the king in whose days the Fróði-peace began.

### Harvest

‘He rules over rain and sunshine, and therewith the fruit of the earth’; it is good to call on him for harvest — *ár*. The golden-bristled boar and the elf-realm tooth-gift belong to the same shining, growing world.

### Prosperity

Snorri adds: ‘he also governs the prosperity of men’. The euhemerized tradition turns that portfolio into economics — King Freyr gathers the land-rents and the *Uppsala auðr*, the wealth of Uppsala, into his own hand, and his mound swallows three years of tribute.

### Kingship

Yngvi-Freyr stands at the fountainhead of the Ynglings, the dynasty of Uppsala from which medieval Norway's and Sweden's kings traced their lines; his reign is the North's canonical portrait of sacral kingship, the king as guarantee of season and peace.

## Across Cultures

Freyr's name is a title, and titles travel farther than theonyms. His Proto-Germanic *frawjaz* ‘lord’ is Gothic *frauja* — the word Ulfilas's Bible uses for the Lord — and the Old English poetic *frēa*, the ‘lord’ of Beowulf's kings; his sister [[freyja|Freyja]] is the same word in the feminine.

The older debate runs through his bynames. Lokasenna calls him *Ingunar-Freyr*; Ynglingatal and Snorri derive the Yngling dynasty from *Yngvi-Freyr*. Since Grimm, scholars have connected that Ing-element with the Inguaeones of Tacitus's Germania 2 — the peoples descended from Mannus through Ing — and with the Ing of the Old English Rune Poem, ‘first among the East Danes seen by men’ before he went east over the wave. The equation Ing = Yngvi = Freyr is argued, not proven; Simek counsels caution, and the manuscripts do not settle it. What the outside world saw plainly is recorded by Adam of Bremen: at Uppsala the Swedes called the god *Fricco*, granted him *pacem voluptatemque* — peace and pleasure — and set him ithyphallic between Thor and Wodan, a Germanic Priapus inside a triad of his own. Within the corpus his closest kin are [[njordr|Njǫrðr]] his father and [[freyja|Freyja]] his twin in title — the Vanir triad of wealth, sea, and season.

## Cultural Legacy

Freyr never left the North. His cult geography survives on the map in hundreds of theophoric place-names — Frøysland, Frøsvoll, Frösåker, Fröslunda and their kin across Norway and Sweden — the densest fertility-god landscape in Scandinavian onomastics, many compounded with ‘grove’, ‘field’, and ‘meadow’. The name itself lives on as a Scandinavian given name: Freyr in Iceland, Frej in Denmark and Sweden.

His historical afterlife is the Yngling one: medieval Norwegian and Swedish royal genealogies traced their lines through the Ynglings of Uppsala to Yngvi-Freyr, making the peace-years king the dynastic ancestor of two kingdoms, and Snorri's portrait became the North's standing image of the good reign — the king whose death the realm refused to admit. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep him at the centre of harvest and fertility blóts under the old formula *ár ok frið*, and the golden boar runs through modern jewellery, fantasy, and games as the sun-animal of the Vanir.

## A Meditation

Freyr is the god who teaches what lordship costs. His name is not a name at all but the word ‘Lord’ itself — every king and every master borrowing his title for as long as the peace holds. And the peace holds only by giving: the sword for the bride, the tribute for the mound, the life for the world at Ragnarök.

The Edda's arithmetic is merciless — the self-wielding sword is the one thing that cannot be given away and kept — but Freyr gives it anyway, for love, in a single scene, without a regret the poems record. The tradition honours him not for the fight he loses but for the peace-years he bought while he could: rain and sunshine in their season, the fruit of the earth, the prosperity of men. The lord of plenty is the god of the gift you cannot take back.

# Pronouncing Frigg: a guide for the curious

Saying **Frigg** aloud is harder than reading it on a screen, and more rewarding. The restored spelling is a compressed pronunciation guide: every accent and macron is an instruction. This post unpacks those instructions — the reconstructed sound, the phoneme-by-phoneme record, the kindred forms in neighboring languages — and then zooms out to the full record around the name: its Younger Futhark writing, its mythology, its cult, and its modern life as a Unicode domain. ## Overview

**Frigg** (*frigg*) — Marriage, Motherhood, Queenship · Queen of the Æsir, the Knower Who Speaks Not — is the foremost of the ásynjur: daughter of Fjörgynn, wife of [[odinn|Óðinn]], mother of [[baldr|Baldr]], and the one figure in the Norse corpus said to know all fate while prophesying none of it.

Her dossier is short and dense. Snorri gives her rank and household — her hall Fensalir, her handmaid [[fulla|Fulla]], her messenger Gná on the horse Hófvarpnir, her protector-aspect Hlín — and the prose fact that she knows men's fates though she says nothing of them. The Poetic Edda gives her the doctrine in verse: Freyja's answer to [[loki|Loki]] in Lokasenna, that Frigg knows all fate though she does not speak it; and the heaviest single line of Völuspá, 'then Frigg wept in Fensalir over Valhöll's woe'. Her one great act is the oath: when Baldr dreams of death, she exacts from all creation the promise not to harm him, omitting only the mistletoe as too young to swear — the gap through which the doom enters.

## The Name

The name is attested in Old Norse as **Frigg** (nominative; genitive *Friggjar*). Its etymology is among the more secure in the pantheon: Proto-Germanic *Frijjō*, 'the beloved one', from the verbal root *frijōn* 'to love' — the same Indo-European stock (*priH-) that gives Sanskrit *priyā́* 'beloved' and, on the Germanic side, English *friend* and *free*. The double-g of the Old Norse form is the assimilated survival of the stem plus the old nominative ending: *Frijjō-r* contracted into the geminate.

The continental record keeps the name's family. Paul the Deacon, writing the Langobard origin legend in the eighth century, calls the wife of Godan **Frea** — the Langobardic form of the same name; Old High German knows *Frija*; and Old English preserves *Frīg*, chiefly as a fossil in the weekday *Frīgedæg*, Friday, the Germanic translation of dies Veneris.

The ASCII form is not a compromise here: normalized Old Norse *Frigg* is already written in plain ASCII letters. There is no diacritic, no thorn or eth, no vowel-length mark for the early domain-name system to have stripped. The name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — which is a statement about orthography, never about the goddess.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Frigg** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the Codex Regius and Uppsala codices of the Prose Edda, recording material centuries older. Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this theonym survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The stem is Proto-Germanic *Frijjō* 'the beloved one', from the root *frijōn* 'to love'; the old nominative ending assimilated into the final geminate, giving Old Norse Frigg (genitive Friggjar).
- Old Norse orthography writes the name in plain Latin letters with no diacritic: the double-g is ordinary text, not a special character.
- In the Younger Futhark the name would be carved ᚠᚱᛁᚴ (f-r-i-k, the k-rune writing the geminate gg) — a normalized reconstruction, since no carved attestation survives.
- The Unicode restoration Frigg is therefore identical to the ASCII input apart from the capital; nothing was lost in transit, which is why the name sits in Tier 2.

Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: **frigg.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release** — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈfriɡː/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Fr-** — Voiceless labiodental [f] and trilled [r]; the cluster is firm at the head of the word, stressed as the single syllable of the name
- **-i-** — Short close front [i], held brief; the vowel of English 'bit', not a long ī
- **-gg** — Long voiced velar stop [ɡː], the true geminate: the consonant is held and released, as in modern Icelandic Frigg; the old nominative ending is swallowed into this double-g

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'FRIG' with the g held long — rhymes with 'big', the r lightly trilled, the double-g pressed and released.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Frigg, wife of Óðinn and foremost of the ásynjur
- **Proto-Germanic** — *Frijjō, 'the beloved one'
- **Langobardic** — Frea, wife of Godan in Paul the Deacon's Historia Langobardorum
- **Old English** — Frīg, fossilized in Frīgedæg, Friday
- **Modern Icelandic** — Frigg, unchanged in spelling

Frigg is Tier 2 because the Old Norse form is already plain ASCII: nothing distinctive is lost in transit. The queen of the gods carries a name so plain that only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

## Mythology

Frigg's mythology is the mythology of the one who knew first: the oath she almost completed, the grief she almost prevented, the silence she keeps about everything else.

### The Oath of All Things (Gylfaginning 49)

When [[baldr|Baldr]] dreams baleful dreams for his life, Frigg fights the future with an oath, exacted from all things — fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poison, serpents — that they will not harm her son. Only the mistletoe, growing west of Valhöll, seemed too young to demand the oath of. The completeness of the list is the point: Snorri enumerates creation itself, and the catastrophe enters through the one thing a mother's thoroughness could not imagine mattering.

### The Tears in Fensalir (Gylfaginning 49 · Völuspá 33)

[[loki|Loki]], in a woman's shape, comes to Fensalir and draws the single omission out of Frigg herself. When blind [[hodr|Höðr]]'s guided throw falls and Baldr lies dead, it is Frigg who finds the first voice in the silent hall and asks who among the Æsir will ride to Hel and offer ransom — the grief-struck mother still doing strategy. Völuspá gives her the briefest and heaviest line in the poem: 'Then Frigg wept in Fensalir over Valhöll's woe.' And when [[hermod|Hermóðr]] rides back from the dead, he carries a gift addressed to her: from [[nanna|Nanna]], her son's wife who died of grief on the pyre, a linen robe — one bereaved woman remembering another, out of Hel itself.

### She Knows All Fate (Lokasenna 26–30 · Gylfaginning 20)

In the flyting, Loki turns his slander on the queen — his taunts are the poem's business, not the tradition's verdict — and [[freyja|Freyja]] answers with the line that defines her: 'Frigg knows, I think, all fate, though she does not speak it.' Snorri repeats the same fact as plain prose: she knows the fates of men, though she prophesies nothing.

### The Foster-Mother's Wager (Grímnismál, prose prologue)

[[odinn|Óðinn]] and Frigg foster two shipwrecked princes, Agnarr and Geirröðr; Óðinn backs Agnarr, Frigg backs Geirröðr, and Geirröðr takes the throne. When Óðinn boasts of his foster-son's hospitality, Frigg calls it false, and the wager is laid. She sends Fulla to warn the king that a dangerous wizard is coming, easily known because no dog will leap at him; Óðinn arrives, is seized, and hangs tortured between two fires for eight nights — outmaneuvered by his own wife, until the whole poem of Grimnir's sayings pours out of his captivity. It is the one myth where the queen moves the plot against the Allfather, and she wins the move.

### Frea and the Naming of the Longbeards (Paul the Deacon 1.8)
Continue.

The goddess's clearest continental appearance is Latin and eighth-century. Frea, Godan's wife — the Langobardic form of Frigg — counsels the outnumbered Winnili: at sunrise the women are to let down their hair around their faces like beards and stand with their husbands. At dawn she turns Godan's bed toward the east and wakes him; he sees the bearded women and asks, 'Who are these longbeards?' Frea answers: you have given them a name — now give them the victory. Godan grants both, and the Winnili become the Langobardi. The tale is an origin-legend, but it proves the migration-age mainland knew a goddess Frea at Godan's side, counsellor and kingmaker, centuries before the Icelandic Eddas wrote her as Frigg.

## Symbols & Iconography

Frigg's attributes are domestic and funerary rather than martial — the corpus fixes her by her hall, her women, and the one unsworn plant:

- **Fensalir** — 'The fen-halls', her dwelling and the Edda's only named home for her; Völuspá makes it the address of her weeping
- **The unsworn mistletoe** — The one shoot too young for the oath: the symbol of the gap in all thoroughness, slender and fatal
- **Fulla's casket** — [[fulla|Fulla]] carries Frigg's eski, minds her footwear, and shares her secret counsels: the kept knowledge of the queen made portable
- **Gná and Hófvarpnir** — Her messenger and the 'hoof-thrower' horse that crosses air and sea: the queen's word carried between worlds, a female mirror of [[sleipnir|Sleipnir]]'s errands
- **The linen robe from Hel** — [[nanna|Nanna]]'s gift, sent back with [[hermod|Hermóðr]]: a wife's token to the mother-in-law, carried out of the land of the dead
- **Frigga's distaff** — Orion's belt in Scandinavian folk astronomy, noted by Grimm: the later ages giving the queen the spindle the Eddas forgot

## Archaeology & Evidence

Frigg is an essentially textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and the Scandinavian place-name evidence sometimes claimed for her is contested by the place-name scholars. Her material footprint is calendrical and linguistic — the weekday itself. The substitution of Frigg for Venus in the Germanic translation of the seven-day week (Old English Frīgedæg, Old Norse frjádagr) is the fossil of the interpretatio romana, preserved in every modern Germanic language.

The narrative witnesses are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the Codex Regius and Uppsala manuscripts of Snorri's Edda, thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Icelandic codices recording far older material. Her continental attestation, Paul the Deacon's Historia Langobardorum, descends in a rich manuscript tradition from the late eighth-century original. Scandinavian folk astronomy, recorded by nineteenth-century collectors and noted by Grimm, kept the name Friggerock — 'Frigga's distaff' — for the three stars of Orion's belt: the nearest thing to a living material tradition attached to her, and the honest root of the later cloud-weaver image.

## Realm & Domain

**Frigg** is catalogued under Marriage, Motherhood, Queenship — three provinces the sources assign her without ornament: she is Óðinn's wife and equal in counsel, Baldr's mother and the engineer of his protection, and the pantheon's silent keeper of fate.

### Marriage

Gylfaginning numbers her first among the ásynjur as Óðinn's wife, and the Grímnismál prologue shows the marriage as a working partnership of wagers and stratagems — the one myth where she outmaneuvers the Allfather at his own game of disguises.

### Motherhood

Her motherhood defines the pantheon's central tragedy: the oath of all things is a mother's answer to a prophecy, and Völuspá's single line — Frigg weeping in Fensalir — is the tradition's image of grief foreseen and powerless.

### Foresight

Lokasenna and Gylfaginning agree on the fact: she knows all fate and prophesies nothing. In a mythology where knowledge is Óðinn's obsession, bought with an eye and a hanging, Frigg possesses it without price — and her power is exactly her silence.

### Queenship

Her household is a court in miniature: [[fulla|Fulla]] the confidante with the golden snood, Gná the messenger riding Hófvarpnir through air and sea, Hlín set to guard those Frigg wills to save.

## Across Cultures

The Roman interpretatio fixed Frigg's identity for posterity through the calendar: when the Germanic peoples translated the seven-day week, dies Veneris — Venus's day — became Frigg's day, Old English Frīgedæg, Old Norse frjádagr, whence Friday. The equation is Venus-as-consort: the wife of the chief god takes the day of the goddess of love. Greek comparison runs to [[hera|Hera]], the queen and goddess of marriage, but the structural fit is imperfect — Frigg keeps a seeress's knowledge Hera never claims.

The deepest syncretic debate is internal. Since Jacob Grimm, scholars have asked whether Frigg and [[freyja|Freyja]] were originally one goddess: both wear falcon-cloaks, both are sought by giants, both weep for absent mates, and their husbands' names (Óðinn, Óðr) look like doubles. The names themselves, however, are different words — *Frijjō* 'beloved' against *frawjǭ* 'lady' — and the handbooks (Simek, Orchard, Lindow) print the question open rather than settled.

Her firm continental witnesses are two. Paul the Deacon's Frea stands at Godan's side in the Langobard origin legend, counselling the stratagem of the beards. Saxo Grammaticus, euhemerizing in the Gesta Danorum, gives a Queen Frigga who strips gold from Óðinn's statue to gild herself and disgraces the marriage — a scandal-story that belongs to Saxo's literary workshop, instructive about thirteenth-century Danish readings of the goddess but not about her cult.

## Cultural Legacy

Frigg's most durable legacy is the fifth weekday: Friday carries her name in every Germanic language, the Germanic answer to the day of Venus — a goddess fossilized in the calendar of half the modern world.

The Victorian revival made her the weeping mother of the North: Matthew Arnold's 'Balder Dead' (1855) gives her long grieving speeches the Eddas only imply. The same century's folklore collectors recorded 'Frigga's distaff' (Swedish Friggerock) as the folk name of Orion's belt, and from that spindle the romantic image of the cloud-weaving queen descends — an image the Eddas themselves never draw, and one this temple presents as the later, lovely accretion it is. Wagner recast her as Fricka in the Ring, the severe guardian of marriage and the operatic portrait most moderns know first.

Modern Heathenry honors her as goddess of hearth, household, and the keeping of frith — the peace-bond of the hall — and modern fantasy keeps her at Óðinn's side. Her name never needed restoring: it never left the week.

## A Meditation

Frigg is the patron of the knowledge that cannot be used. She knows all fate and speaks none of it — not from coldness, but because the Edda understands what foresight costs: she sees the mistletoe coming and still must live the days before it falls.

Her one permitted weapon is thoroughness, and she wields it to the limit of the world — fire, water, iron, stone, sickness, serpent, all sworn — and the future enters through the single twig too young to swear. What the tradition leaves her is not failure but a harder thing: the discipline of the one who knows. Every keeper of unwelcome certainty — the parent who sees, the friend who cannot say, the expert whose warning would only spread the panic — works in Fensalir, keeping counsel with a knowledge that has nowhere to go.

# The hidden history behind Fuji

Behind the modern ASCII form *fuji* hides a much longer story. **Fuji** reaches back through manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral tradition long before it ever touched a keyboard, and every mark in the restored spelling is a receipt from that journey. In what follows we trace the name from its Japanese characters attestations through its mythology, its cult, its symbols, and its afterlife in other cultures — and we show how the PuniCodex project turned that philological record into a Unicode domain that resolves today. The history was never lost. It was only waiting for the infrastructure to catch up.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Fuji
- **ASCII form:** fuji
- **Meaning:** "Wealthy warrior"
- **Domain of influence:** Sacred Mountain
- **Pantheon:** Japanese

## Overview

**Fuji** (*fuji*) — Sacred Mountain — belongs to the Japanese tradition. The name means "Wealthy warrior".

Mount Fuji is the sacred mountain of Japan, an object of worship since at least the Nara period and the most reproduced image of the country.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Fuji**. The plain ASCII form *fuji* is the modern Hepburn romanization; the restoration capitalizes the conventional spelling. Because the Japanese source script uses logographic characters whose distinctive visual form cannot be conveyed in the basic Latin alphabet, and because no diacritic or special letter is added in this restoration, the name is placed in Tier 2. The Unicode form remains the philologically complete reference, while the ASCII spelling is a practical convenience for the domain-name system.

## The Name

The name is attested in Japanese characters as **富士**. Etymologically it means "Wealthy warrior".

The name Fuji is of uncertain etymology. One influential theory derives it from the Ainu *fuchi* or *huchi*, meaning "fire" or "old woman," referring to the volcano's fire and the fire goddess. Another derives it from Old Japanese *fushi* or *fuji*, a wisteria-like plant, or from a phrase meaning "wealthy warrior." The mountain has been an object of worship since at least the Nara period.

The ASCII form *fuji* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry Japanese characters or diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Fuji** gives the conventional Hepburn romanization with initial capitalization, the standard scholarly way to cite a proper name in romanized Japanese. The name is Tier 2 because the restoration does not add a distinctive diacritic or special letter absent from the ASCII form.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **f** → **F** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **j** → **j** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is written in Japanese characters as **富士** — Japanese logographic and syllabic script (kanji plus kana where attested), attested in the classical Japanese sources. The script is written top-to-bottom in traditional contexts and left-to-right in modern reproductions.

The scholarly transliteration is *Fuji* (Hepburn romanization with initial capitalization), giving the normalized reading //ɸɯ.ʑi//.

The characters 富士 are *ateji*, now read for their auspicious meanings: 富 (wealth) and 士 (warrior, gentleman). The mountain's name predates the writing system and was assigned these graphs because of their sound and favorable associations.

## Pronunciation

The conventional reading of the name is **/ɸɯ.ʑi/** — Modern Japanese (Standard Japanese).

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'FUJI' — pronounce each vowel clearly and avoid English diphthongs. Japanese is mora-timed, so each syllable receives roughly equal weight.

Fuji is Tier 2 because the ASCII form *fuji* already represents the same phonemic sequence; no stress mark, length mark, or distinctive letter is required to recover the spoken name.

## Mythology

The *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki* connect the volcano to the fire deity Kagutsuchi: when Izanagi killed Kagutsuchi with his sword, the blood that fell on the rocks created other kami, and the fire god's body was said to be buried or transformed into mountains. Later tradition identifies the mountain itself as the abode of the kami *Konohana-sakuya-hime* and *Ōyamatsumi*, and the object of the *Asama* or *Sengen* cult. The *Konjaku Monogatari* and *Fuji-kō* literature describe ecstatic ascents and visions of paradise from the summit.

### The Name and Its Power (Kojiki / Nihon Shoki)

The name Fuji is explained in folk etymology as 'without equal' (*fushi*) or 'inexhaustible' (*fuji*). The mountain was long identified with a female kami, the deity of the volcano, and with Sengen Daimyōjin, a syncretic Buddhist-Shinto figure who governed fire and fertility. Its eruptions were interpreted as the anger or fertility of the divine.

### Fuji as Lotus Mandala (Buddhist cult)

Medieval Buddhism imagined Fuji as a lotus mandala. The *Fuji-kō* confraternities of the Edo period climbed the mountain in white robes, reciting sutras and performing ritual circumambulations. The summit was a boundary between the human world and a Buddhist paradise, and the crater itself was sometimes identified with the Pure Land.

### The Floating World's Mountain (Art and nation)

Katsushika Hokusai's *Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji* and Utagawa Hiroshige's travel series fixed Fuji's image in global consciousness. It appears in calm seas, behind thunder, above villages, and through waves — always the same mountain, always changing with the viewer's place in the world.

## Symbols & Iconography

- **Snow-capped cone** — the symmetrical volcanic form, icon of Japan par excellence.
- **Sakura and wisteria** — floral symbols associated with the Fuji cult and spring pilgrimage.
- **Lava caves and springs** — the mountain's fire and water are both sacred; the *Oshino Hakkai* springs are thought to be melted snow from Fuji.
- **Red *torii* and *sōmen*** — pilgrims wear white robes and conical hats, carrying a staff and bell.

- **Torii and shrine markers** — The network of shrines, especially Sengen shrines, that manage the mountain's cult
- **Crater and rising sun** — The summit caldera and the dawn viewed from it, central to pilgrimage experience
- **Pilgrim's staff** — The walking stick and stamped robe of those who climbed the sacred slopes

## Archaeology & Evidence

The summit of Fuji preserves more than a hundred *okunoin* sacred sites, shrines, and the Konohana-sakuya-hime shrine rebuilt in the modern period. The *Yoshida-guchi* and *Subashiri* trail systems, the *Ōmuro* sect headquarters, and numerous *Fujizuka* mounds in the Kantō plain provide a dense archaeological and landscape record of the Fuji cult.

## Realm & Domain

Mount Fuji is the sacred mountain of Japan, the highest peak in the country, and a *shintai* — a natural body in which a kami dwells. Its domain encompasses fire, water, fertility, and the boundary between this world and the other world. Pilgrimage (*Fuji-kō*) and the veneration of the mountain as a deity (*Sengen*) have shaped Japanese religion, art, and literature for more than a thousand years.

### Volcano Deity

As a living volcano, Fuji has been feared and worshipped as a source of both destruction and fertility.

### Pilgrimage Peak

For centuries pilgrims climbed to the summit, where shrines and lodges marked the path.

### National Symbol

Its image identifies Japan in art, currency, passports, and global imagination.

### Artistic Muse

Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views made Fuji an icon of world art.

## Across Cultures

Fuji worship blends Shinto (*Sengen* or *Asama* shrines), Buddhism (*Fuji-san* cults and the founder Hasegawa Kakugyō), and folk asceticism. The *Fuji-kō* confraternities of the Edo period, founded by Kakugyō and later systematized by Jikigyō Miroku, organized mass pilgrimages and built miniature Fujis (*Fujizuka*) in towns across Japan. The mountain also attracted *Shugendō* practitioners, who saw it as an axis mundi.

## Cultural Legacy

Mount Fuji is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the most reproduced image in Japanese art, from Hokusai's *Thirty-Six Views* to contemporary postcards and corporate logos. It continues to be climbed by hundreds of thousands of pilgrims and tourists each summer and remains the national symbol of Japan.

- The compound appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki as one of the kami born from Izanagi's purification.
- The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves vowel length; the kanji form is not used as a domain because CJK scripts are not supported in the .com IDN table.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɸɯː.dʑiɴ/** — Modern Standard Japanese (Hepburn).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Fū-** — Voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] (like a soft 'f' made with both lips) plus long close back rounded [ɯː]; the macron marks length, giving Tier-1 status
- **-jin** — Voiced alveolo-palatal affricate [dʑ] plus close front [i] and moraic nasal [ɴ]; the final -n is a uvular nasal

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'FOO-jin' — the first syllable is long and breezy, with lips almost touching for the 'f'; the final 'jin' is quick with a soft 'j'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — 風神 (fūjin), 'wind god,' from fū 'wind' + shin/jin 'god'
- **Chinese antecedent** — Fengshen (風神), the Chinese wind deity; Fūjin is a Japanese adaptation
- **Pairing** — Raijin (雷神), the thunder god, his frequent companion in art and temple architecture

Fūjin is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. The name is a straightforward Sino-Japanese compound: 風 (fū, 'wind') + 神 (jin, 'god/spirit'). He is typically paired with Raijin, the thunder god, in Japanese temple and popular art.

## Mythology

Fūjin's mythology is grounded in the creation narratives of the *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, in popular Buddhist iconography, and in the visual tradition of Japanese screen painting. He is both a primordial force and a temple guardian.

### The Birth of the Wind Kami (Kojiki / Nihon Shoki)

The *Kojiki*'s birth-of-the-kami sequence includes Shinatsuhiko-no-mikoto, the wind deity born to Izanagi and Izanami among the elemental gods that follow the making of the islands. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older wind kami, fixed in Japanese art from the medieval period onward.

### Wind in the Age of the Gods (Nihon Shoki)

The *Nihon Shoki* gives the wind its own etiology: in an alternate account of the creation, Izanagi blows away the mist that wraps the new-made land, and from that breath the wind kami Shinatsuhiko is born — wind as the first clearing of the world. The name Fūjin itself is the later Sino-Japanese label under which the native wind kami were merged with the Buddhist wind deva.

### Guardian of the Four Heavens (Buddhist iconography)

In esoteric Buddhism the wind god is Fūten, one of the Twelve Devas (*jūniten*) who guard the directions; protector of the north-west, he adapts the Indian wind god Vāyu transmitted through the mandalas of esoteric ritual. Temples across Japan, above all Sanjūsangen-dō in Kyōto, house famous depictions of Fūjin and Raijin as muscular, wind-whipped guardians of the Dharma.

### The Birth of Fūjin (Kojiki / Nihon Shoki)

The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin. In the *Kojiki*'s birth-of-the-kami sequence, Shinatsuhiko-no-mikoto, the wind deity, is born to Izanagi and Izanami among the elemental gods that follow the making of the islands. The *Nihon Shoki* adds its own etiology: Izanagi blows away the morning mist that wraps the new-made land, and from that breath the wind kami is born. The thunder kami, by contrast, are born from Izanami's corpse after her death in the birth of the fire god — neither wind nor thunder kami are products of Izanagi's later purification at the misogi. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older wind kami.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Fūjin concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Wind bag (fūtaku)** — The sack from which all winds are released, his most distinctive attribute
- **Leopard skin** — His wild garment, marking him as a powerful, untamed kami
- **Green or red skin** — His demonic complexion, shared with other fierce protective deities
- **Streaming hair** — The visual sign of wind in motion, often rendered with exaggerated dynamism
- **Temple gate pairing with Raijin** — The *fūjin-raijin-zu* motif that protects Buddhist temples from harmful influences

## Archaeology & Evidence

Fūjin is best known from Japanese painting and sculpture rather than from archaeological contexts alone. The oldest surviving depictions appear in Heian- and Kamakura-period Buddhist iconography, where he serves as a guardian deity. The most famous visual testimony is the pair of folding screens by Tawaraya Sōtatsu (early 17th century), now at the Kyoto National Museum and Kenninji temple, which depict Fūjin and Raijin in gold-leaf clouds. Temple sculptures and ema (votive plaques) across Japan preserve popular representations of the wind god, while the textual record in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki anchors his mythological origins in the creation age.

## Realm & Domain

**Fūjin** is the wind made wild. In Japanese art he appears as a fierce demon, hair streaming, clad in a leopard-skin loincloth, carrying a vast bag of winds on his shoulders. When he opens it, gales tear through forests, scatter roofs, and flatten fields; when he closes it, the air grows still. He is one of the oldest kami in the Japanese pantheon, a destructive force that is also necessary for pollination, dispersal of seeds, and the cleansing of stale air.

He is the brother or counterpart of Raijin, the thunder god, and the two are often depicted together at temple gates, where their terrifying presence keeps danger away from sacred ground.

### Bag of Winds

He carries a great sack (fūtaku) slung over his shoulders; opening it releases the winds of the world.

### Demon Guardian

His fierce face and muscular body mark him as one of the powerful oni-like kami who protect temples.

### Companion of Raijin

He is paired with the thunder god at temple gates and in screen paintings, storm and wind as twin forces.

### Cosmic Breath

Beyond destruction, wind is the breath that moves pollen, carries clouds, and clears the air for new growth.

## Across Cultures
Continue.

Fūjin descends from the Chinese wind deity Fengshen, transmitted to Japan along with Buddhism and continental iconography. He also resembles wind gods across Eurasia, from the Greek Boreas and the Vedic Vāta to the Central Asian wind demons depicted on Silk Road textiles. In Japan, however, he became thoroughly domesticated as a kami, paired with Raijin and rendered in a distinctive visual style by artists such as Tawaraya Sōtatsu and Ogata Kōrin. The Japanese fascination with storms — wind, rain, thunder, lightning — produced one of the most dynamic bodies of religious painting in East Asia, with Fūjin and Raijin at its center.

Within the Japanese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[jizo|Jizō]], [[kobe|Kōbe]], [[kyoto|Kyōto]], [[nikko|Nikkō]], [[osaka|Ōsaka]],.

## Cultural Legacy

Fūjin remains one of Japan's most recognizable kami. The folding screens (*byōbu*) depicting Fūjin and Raijin by Tawaraya Sōtatsu are national treasures and icons of Japanese art. Temples still display the pair at gates and in festival processions, and Fūjin appears in manga, anime, video games, and advertising as a symbol of overwhelming natural force. His name is invoked in discussions of typhoons and seasonal winds, and the visual motif of a figure with a wind bag has become a global shorthand for the wind itself. The Unicode restoration *Fūjin* preserves the long vowel that the plain ASCII form *fujin* cannot carry — the same macron that distinguishes the god's name (風神) from its commonest homophone, *fujin* (婦人), 'a lady'.

## A Meditation

Fūjin is the god of the air we cannot see but cannot live without. His bag of winds contains both destruction and renewal: the gale that uproots trees also scatters seeds, the storm that sinks ships also clears the sky. He is a reminder that the atmosphere is not empty space but a living force.

To contemplate Fūjin is to feel the wind as sacred. Every breath, every gust, every seasonal shift becomes a meeting with an ancient power. He does not ask for worship in stillness; he is worshipped in motion, in the visible effects of the invisible.

The *Engishiki* preserves the prayers of farmers who asked the wind kami of Tatsuta and Hirose to spare the ripening grain; twice in the thirteenth century, the memory of the nation says, the answer came as the *kamikaze* that scattered the Mongol fleets. Fūjin's bag thus holds both the gale that is begged to pass and the gale that is begged to come — and the contemplation of wind ends in the recognition that every breath is borrowed from a power no one owns.

# The many faces of Fulla

No important name has only one face. **Fulla** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Younger Futhark original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *fulla* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Fulla
- **ASCII form:** fulla
- **Meaning:** "Bountiful"
- **Domain of influence:** Abundance, Secrets
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᚠᚢᛚᛚᛅ (Younger Futhark)

## Overview

**Fulla** (*fulla*) — Abundance, Secrets · Frigg's Handmaid, the Keeper of the Casket — is the most trusted figure in the queen's hall: the virgin ásynja who goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head, who carries Frigg's little box, looks after her shoes, and shares her secret counsels.

Old Norse *Fulla* is a transparent formation on *fullr* 'full' — the same word as English 'full' and German 'voll' — so the name means 'Fullness, Plenty': an abstract noun worn as a personal name, like her sister ásynjur Sjǫfn ('affection') and Lofn ('praise, permission'). Her dossier is four precise notices: Snorri's portrait in Gylfaginning 35, her errand to King Geirröðr in the prose introduction to Grímnismál, the finger-ring Nanna sends her from Hel in Gylfaginning 49, and — if the identification holds — her continental echo as Volla, sister of Friia, in the Second Merseburg Charm.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Fulla** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the goddess. This temple is domain-less: the plain-ASCII fulla.com is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release; no form of the name is claimed.

## The Name

The name is attested in Old Norse as **Fulla** — a feminine weak noun formed directly on the adjective *fullr* 'full', hence 'Fullness, Plenty, the Bountiful one'. It belongs to the family of abstract-noun goddess-names in Gylfaginning's catalogue of the ásynjur: Sjǫfn from *sjafni* 'affection', Lofn from *lof* 'praise, permission', Vár from *várar* 'vows' — qualities and states given names and errands of their own. The name answers her office exactly: the keeper of the queen's treasure-box is herself called Plenty.

The ASCII form and the restored form are identical because the normalized Old Norse spelling carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter: five plain Latin letters. The mechanical tier rule therefore classifies the name Tier 2 — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses. This is an orthographic report, not a judgment of standing.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **f** → **F** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

No form of the name is held in the collection: the plain-ASCII fulla.com is registered outside the project and watched for release.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Fulla** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius (the Grímnismál prose) and the Prose Edda codices, recording material centuries older. Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this theonym survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a feminine weak noun formed on the adjective *fullr* 'full'; as an a-stem it carries no nominative *-r*, which is why the name ends in plain -a.
- The double l is a true geminate /lː/; the Younger Futhark rendering ᚠᚢᛚᛅ writes it with a single ᛚ, as the runic row does not mark consonant length.
- The vowels are short: no length marks appear in normalized Old Norse orthography, and none are restored.
- The Unicode restoration **Fulla** is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital: the name carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, and is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

The temple claims no domain: the plain-ASCII fulla.com is held by a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈful.la/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Fu-** — Voiceless labiodental [f], short close rounded [u] as in English *put*; stressed first syllable, as in every Old Norse word
- **-lla** — A true geminate [lː], the double l held twice as long as a single l, then a short open [a]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'FULL-ah' — but with the vowel of *put*, not *pool*, and the l genuinely doubled, two even syllables with the weight on the first.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Fulla, Frigg's handmaid; from *fullr*, 'full'
- **Old High German** — Volla, Friia's sister in the Second Merseburg Charm, widely read as the same figure
- **Proto-Germanic** — *fullaz, 'full' — the ancestor of English 'full', German 'voll', Gothic fulls, and Norse fullr
- **Owned form** — None; the temple claims no domain, and fulla.com is held outside the collection

Fulla is Tier 2 by rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII, and the restoration loses nothing in transit. The doubled l — which the runic row would write with a single ᛚ — is the one feature no plain spelling can show.

## Mythology

Fulla has no saga of her own: her mythology is four precise notices, and every one of them places her at [[frigg|Frigg]]'s side. What the tradition lost in narrative it kept in definition — no goddess in the Edda is more exactly described in a single sentence.

### The Keeper of the Casket (Gylfaginning 35)

Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur gives Fulla her entire portrait at once: 'Fulla is a virgin and goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head; she carries Frigg's eski, looks after her footwear, and shares her secret counsels with her.' The three duties descend in rank and rise in intimacy — the box is treasure, the shoes are service, the counsels are trust itself. She is named immediately after Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, and the pairing has stuck: where Gná carries the queen's words out through the worlds, Fulla keeps the queen's words that never leave the hall.

### The Warning to Geirröðr (Grímnismál, prose)

Her one errand in the Poetic Edda is given in prose. [[odinn|Óðinn]] and Frigg had quarrelled over their foster-sons: Frigg accused King Geirröðr, Óðinn's favourite, of being so stingy he tortured his guests, and Óðinn laid a wager and set off disguised to test him. Frigg sent her handmaid Fulla to Geirröðr ahead of him, to warn the king to beware of a sorcerer coming to bewitch him — with the token that no dog, however fierce, would leap at the man. The warning is the trap: Geirröðr seized the stranger, named Grímnir, and tortured him between two fires, and out of that fire the god spoke the whole catalogue of the worlds. Fulla appears only to deliver the message and vanish, but the wager, the torture, and the poem's entire revelation turn on her errand.

### The Ring from Hel (Gylfaginning 49)

When Hermóðr rode nine nights to ransom [[baldr|Baldr]] and came home with the tidings, he brought tokens from the dead: Baldr sent back the ring Draupnir to Óðinn, and [[nanna|Nanna]] — Baldr's wife, who had died of grief on his pyre — sent gifts out of Hel to the two women of Frigg's hall: a linen headdress for Frigg, and a finger-ring for Fulla. When a dead goddess thinks of Ásgarðr's household, she thinks of the queen and of the queen's handmaid by name.

### Volla, Friia's Sister (Second Merseburg Charm)

The one continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German: Phol and Wodan rode to the wood, Balder's foal wrenched its foot, and the goddesses chant over it in sequence — Sinthgunt, Sunna her sister; Friia, Volla her sister; and at last Wodan, who knows how. Since Jacob Grimm, Volla — Friia's sister — has widely been read as Fulla: the name is the exact Old High German form of the same word, and the charm puts her, precisely as the Edda does, at Friia's right hand. The identification is argued, not proven.

## Symbols & Iconography

Fulla's iconography is the iconography of trust — Snorri fixes her appearance and office in a single sentence, and the tradition never adds to it:

- **The eski** — Frigg's little casket, which Fulla carries: the portable treasury of the queen of the gods, and the clearest badge of her office
- **The golden band** — the gold snood she wears about her loose hair: unmarried freedom dressed in plenty, and Snorri's one detail of dress
- **The loose hair itself** — the virgin's unbound hair, the visible sign of her status in a hall of married goddesses
- **Frigg's shoes** — the queen's footwear in her keeping: the humblest duty in the catalogue, and the surest sign of a servant admitted to every chamber
- **The finger-ring from Hel** — Nanna's gift, carried back by [[hermod|Hermóðr]]: a token from the dead addressed, of all the ásynjur, to her

## Archaeology & Evidence
Continue.

Fulla is an entirely textual goddess: no cult site, toponym, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the runic corpus is silent — unsurprising for a figure the sources place inside the queen's household rather than in the public cult. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Grímnismál prose, which preserves her one errand, survives in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); her portrait in Gylfaginning 35 and her ring in Gylfaginning 49 come with the Prose Edda codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; and her name recurs in the þulur, the metrical name-lists appended to Skáldskaparmál.

The one continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, copied into a theological manuscript at Fulda in the tenth century and now in the Merseburg cathedral library: its Volla, sister of Friia, is the only attestation of the figure outside Iceland and, if the identification holds, the oldest by centuries. Against this single Carolingian-era survival, the whole archaeological record — the Migration-Age gold of the period's hoards, the picture stones, the amulets — offers atmosphere rather than attribution: golden bands are abundant in the ground, but none can be assigned to Fulla.

## Realm & Domain

**Fulla** is catalogued under Abundance, Secrets — and the sources earn both terms of it: her name is Fullness itself, and her defining duty is the keeping of what the queen does not say aloud.

### Abundance

Her name is the abstract noun of *fullr*, 'full': Plenty given a person, a golden band, and a casket to carry — the goddess in whose keeping the queen's portable wealth actually lives.

### Secrets

She shares Frigg's *leyniráðagørðir*, the queen's secret deliberations: of the three duties in her portrait, the counsels are the one that admits her past every door.

### Fidelity and Service

The casket and the shoes are the badges of the trusted chamber-servant — the lowest duties of the hall held, in her case, at the highest level of confidence.

### The Queen's Hall

Every notice the tradition keeps of her places her at Frigg's side: named beside Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, in the catalogue of the ásynjur, and remembered beside the queen herself when Nanna's gifts come back from Hel.

## Across Cultures

Fulla's cross-border life runs through one word and one relationship. The word is *fullr*: Proto-Germanic *fullaz* gives English 'full', German 'voll', Gothic fulls, and Old Norse Fulla — a goddess whose name is the ordinary adjective turned abstract noun, 'Fullness'. The relationship is the one the Merseburg Charm preserves: Volla beside Friia, as Fulla beside Frigg — and since Grimm the identification of the two has been the standing reading, with Simek registering both the fit and the doubt.

The deeper question is what kind of being she is. Gylfaginning's ásynjur catalogue is full of abstract-noun goddesses — Sjǫfn, Lofn, Vár — and scholars have long suspected that Fulla, Gná, and their sisters are facets of Frigg herself: the queen's plenitude and far-ranging given names and errands of their own. Whether she began as an independent goddess of plenty or as an aspect that walked off on its own, the sources keep her a person: she receives a ring, runs an errand, and wears her own gold. Within the corpus, her closest kin are the figures of Frigg's household: [[frigg|Frigg]] herself, [[nanna|Nanna]], who sends her the ring, and the other ásynjur of Snorri's catalogue, among them [[syn|Syn]], who guards the door against those who should not enter, and [[eir|Eir]], the best of physicians.

## Cultural Legacy

Fulla's afterlife is scholarly and liturgical rather than popular. Grimm devoted sustained attention to her and Volla in Teutonic Mythology, and every handbook since — Simek, Orchard, Lindow — keeps her as the standing example of the abstract-noun ásynja: the goddess whose name tells you exactly what she is. Her image — loose hair, golden band, the queen's casket on her arm — became the fixed picture of the trusted northern handmaid, and she enters nearly every retelling of the Baldr cycle by virtue of one finger-ring.

In contemporary practice, modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep her at Frigg's side as a goddess of plenty, household trust, and well-kept secrets, invoked where abundance must be held in confidence. She never became a pop-culture figure; she remained what the Edda made her — the most trusted person in the queen's hall, and the tradition's proof that even abundance has a keeper.

## A Meditation

Fulla is the goddess of what is held in trust. Every detail of her portrait is a form of custody: the casket she carries but does not own, the shoes she tends but does not wear, the counsels she shares but does not speak. Even her name works this way — Fullness is not a thing she does but a thing she keeps.

The tradition gives her no adventure because her office is the adventure's opposite: Gná rides out with the queen's words; Fulla stays, and what is entrusted to her stays with her. Nanna's ring from Hel is the tradition's own verdict on that office — when the dead send gifts home, they send one to the keeper. In a mythology that ends in fire and betrayal, Fulla is the quiet counterweight: the proof that some things, once entrusted, are simply kept.

# The many faces of Fúxī

No important name has only one face. **Fúxī** appears as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and its roots, the Chinese characters original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *fuxi* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Fúxī
- **ASCII form:** fuxi
- **Meaning:** "Hidden one"
- **Domain of influence:** Culture, Writing, Divination
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 伏羲 (Chinese characters)
- **Live domain:** fúxī.com

## Overview

**Fúxī** (*fuxi*) — The First Teacher — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Culture, Writing, Divination". The name means "Hidden one".

Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Fúxī** and serves its temple at [fúxī.com](https://xn--fx-rka1r.com). The restoration preserves the accent on ú and the macron on ī — distinctive features the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *fuxi* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Chinese characters as **伏羲**. Etymologically it means "Hidden one".

The ASCII form *fuxi* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Fúxī** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. ## The Original Script

The name is written in Chinese characters as **伏羲**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *fuxi* and the PuniCodex restoration **Fúxī** are measured: the restoration preserves both its pitch accent and its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

Written 伏羲: fú (subdue; the man-radical with the hound) plus xī (the ancient graph for sacrificial breath). The compound is attested from Warring States texts onward — the name predates any agreed reading of it, which is itself a mark of antiquity.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/fu˧˥ ɕi˥/** — Mandarin (Hanyu Pinyin with tones).

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: foo-shee, rising tone on fu, high level on xi.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 伏羲
- **Variant writing** — 庖犧 (Páoxī)
- **Owned form** — Fúxī

Fúxī 伏羲 carries the rising tone on both syllables in Mandarin; older romanizations write Fu-hsi. The first graph 伏 suggests "to subdue, to prostrate," the second 羲 a sacrificial term — a name older than its etymologies, borne by the first of the Three August Ones. The older romanization Fu-hsi records the same syllables; pinyin's x is the alveolo-palatal fricative of modern Mandarin.

## Mythology

Fúxī's myths are all acts of notation: he does not fight or flee — he observes, abstracts, and teaches. He is the culture-bringer as draftsman.

### Reading the World (The Diagram)

The Yìjīng's Great Treatise records the founding act: Fúxī looked up and contemplated the images of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth, contemplated the markings of birds and beasts and the order of the near at hand — and from all three made the eight trigrams, "to comprehend the powers of the spirits and to classify the natures of the ten thousand things." Writing, mathematics, and divination begin as one gesture of attention.

### The Dragon-Horse's Map (The River)

Later tradition gives the revelation a courier: a dragon-horse rose from the Yellow River bearing on its back the Hétú, the River Chart — the arrangement of numbers and marks from which Fúxī drew the trigrams. Paired with the Luò River Writing that inspired the Great Plan, the Chart made the Yellow River itself the first text of Chinese civilization.

### The Brother-Sister Marriage (The Flood)

In the flood myth recorded among the Miao and in Tang collections, Fúxī and Nǚwā alone survive the waters, taking refuge on Mount Kūnlún. Brother and sister, they divine heaven's will by rolling millstones and watching smoke columns join — and consent to marry, repopulating the drowned world. The myth explains both marriage's institution and humanity's second beginning.

### Nets, Music, and Domestication (The Arts)

The tradition credits him with the survival-arts in sequence: knotting cords into nets for fishing and hunting, keeping domestic animals (hence one reading of his name, "subduer of beasts"), making the thirty-five-stringed se zither, and fixing the marriage rites. Civilization, in his legend, is a curriculum — and he is its whole faculty.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Fúxī concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The trigrams** — Pattern abstracted from nature — the seed of all Chinese correlative thought
- **The carpenter's square** — His emblem in Han art: the earth-measurer's tool (Nǚwā holds the compass of heaven)
- **The dragon-horse** — The creature from the Yellow River whose markings revealed the diagram

## Archaeology & Evidence

The Wu Liang shrine reliefs (2nd century CE, Shandong) show Fúxī and Nǚwā with serpent bodies entwined, square and compass raised — the canonical image, replicated across Han tomb art from Sichuan to Xinjiang (the famous Astana cemetery banner). The myth's textual archaeology runs from the Zhuangzi and Xunzi mentions to the Tang's flood-cycle records: a steady accretion from sage-king to cosmic progenitor, all preserved in the transmitted classics.

His cult anchored in the northwest: the **Fúxī temple at Tianshui** (Gansu), founded under the Ming, claims his birthplace and keeps his statue with the trigrams; the city still holds his festival. The **Huáiyáng** tomb-temple in Henan — the Tàihào Líng, 'tomb of the Great Bright One' — has drawn one of China's largest temple fairs for centuries, a month of pilgrimage in the second lunar month. Both sites make the same claim the classics do: that the pattern-reader of the Yellow River was buried and is honoured on its banks.

## Realm & Domain

Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.

### The Eight Trigrams

Bāguà: broken and unbroken lines in threes — the binary alphabet of the Yìjīng, attributed to his observation.

### The Net

He taught the people to knot cords into nets — fishing, hunting, and the technology of the snare.

### The Serpent Bodies

Han art shows him and Nǚwā as serpents intertwined — the primal pair, measuring square and compass in hand.

### Marriage

He instituted the rites of marriage and the bride-price of deer skins — order after the flood.

## Across Cultures

He heads most lists of the Three August Ones (Sānhuáng), paired inseparably with Nǚwā — their intertwined serpent forms in Han art echoing, scholars note, the union of measure and generation. Daoist tradition absorbed him as a revealer of the trigrams to the immortal lineages; Confucian tradition kept him as the first historian of pattern. The serpent-pair iconography has been compared by art historians with intertwined pairs from Egypt to India — diffusion debated, the resemblance celebrated.

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], [[long|Lóng]], [[mengpo|Méngpó]], [[nuwa|Nǚwā]], and [[pangu|Pángǔ]].

## Cultural Legacy

Every reading of the Yìjīng — the book that shaped Confucian statecraft, Daoist alchemy, and Leibniz's binary arithmetic — begins with his act of looking. The eight trigrams appear on the flag of South Korea; the River Chart structures a millennium of cosmological diagrams; and "Fúxī" remains the standard icon for the inventor-ancestor in Chinese cultural memory, the answer to the question of where pattern-thinking began.

## A Meditation

Fúxī is the patron of the second look — the one that sees not the thing but the pattern. His trigrams are only broken and unbroken lines, yet a civilization read everything in them for three thousand years. He asks the observer's question: what in the world are you willing to look at long enough that it begins, at last, to read back?

Leibniz saw the trigrams and recognized binary arithmetic; the information age looked again and found the whole grammar of bits — the broken and unbroken line as zero and one. Whether or not the old sage intended the code, his lesson stands: the world's patterns are legible to whoever looks long enough, and three lines, honestly observed, can hold a civilization's worth of distinctions. The first technology was attention.

The tradition says he looked at the horse's markings and the turtle's shell and saw not omen but order — the world already written, waiting for a reader. Every analysis since, from the Yìjīng's commentaries to the database schema, is his gesture repeated: reduce the world to its honest marks, and the marks will begin to answer.
