Old Norse *Magni* is the common noun *magn*/*megn* 'strength, might' made personal: 'the strong one'. The sources know him in two scenes and a promise — the lifting at Grjótúnagarðar, the gift of the gold-maned horse Gullfaxi that Óðinn reproved, and the prophecy of *Vafþrúðnismál* that after Ragnarǫk Magni and his brother Móði shall have Mjǫllnir, the hammer of their fallen father.

## The Name

The name is attested in Old Norse as **Magni** (nominative; genitive *Magna*, as in Hárbarðsljóð 53: *Magna faðir*, 'Magni's father'). It is a transparent formation on the Old Norse common noun *magn*/*megn* 'strength, might, main' — hence 'the strong one' — from Proto-Germanic *maginą 'strength, power'. The same root gives Old English *mægen* 'strength, force' (surviving in the phrase 'with might and main') and stands beside the verb *magan* 'be able', the ancestor of English *may* and *might*.

Unlike Þórr or Baldr, the name ends in *-i*: it is a weak ja-stem formation, so it carries no nominative *-r*. The ASCII fallback *magni* therefore loses nothing at all — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no ending — and the mechanical tier rule places the name in Tier 2 on a purely orthographic report.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

No domain is held for this name. Because *Magni* is pure ASCII, *magni.com* was registered long ago in the ordinary way and is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection; the project watches it for release, and this temple claims no address it does not own.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Magni** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and of the Prose Edda, recording material centuries older. Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the younger futhark; the god's name is not attested in runes, but as a human name Magni does occur in the inscriptional record, so the runic rendering is more than a theoretical exercise.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a ja-stem formation on *magn*/*megn* 'strength', ending in *-i*; there is no nominative *-r* as in Þórr or Baldr.
- Old Norse orthography writes no diacritic in this name: five plain Latin letters.
- In the Younger Futhark the name runs ᛘᛅᚴᚾᛁ (m-a-k-n-i); the ᚴ rune writes both k and g, and the short a and i need no qualification.
- The ASCII form *magni* therefore loses nothing — the restoration differs from the input only by the capital, which is why the mechanical rule places the name in Tier 2.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈmɑɣ.ni/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ma-** — Voiced bilabial nasal [m] and short open back [ɑ]; stress falls on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word
- **-gni** — The medial g is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ], softer than the English stop; then dental nasal [n] and short close [i]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'MAHG-ni' — a short open 'ah', the g softened between the vowels. Modern Icelandic, where the name is still living, hardens the g to [k]: 'MAHK-ni'.

- **Modern Icelandic** — Magni, unchanged in spelling for a thousand years

## Mythology

Magni's mythology is two scenes and a promise, told across both Eddas with unusual economy: the lifting of Hrungnir's leg, the gift of Gullfaxi, and the inheritance of the hammer after the end of the world.

### The Duel at Grjótúnagarðar (Skáldskaparmál 17)

The background is one of [[thor|Þórr]]'s greatest fights. The stone-hearted giant [[hrungnir|Hrungnir]] rode his gold-maned stallion Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr on the heels of [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s wager over whose horse was fastest; feasted, he drank and boasted he would carry off Valhǫll and kill every god but Freyja and [[sif|Sif]]. Þórr was summoned, and the duel was set at Grjótúnagarðar, the stone courts. The giants built Hrungnir a companion of clay, Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall and with a mare's heart that failed him; Hrungnir himself came with heart, shield, and weapon all of stone. Þjálfi tricked him into standing on his shield, and Þórr hurled Mjǫllnir through the raised whetstone — a shard lodged in Þórr's own head — and Hrungnir crashed forward, his leg across Þórr's neck.

### Three Nights Old (Skáldskaparmál 17)

Þjálfi could not lift the leg, and when all the Æsir had come, none of them could move it either. Then Magni arrived — the son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa, and he was three nights old — and he flung the leg off his father, saying it was a shame he had not come sooner: he thought he could have struck the giant dead with his bare fist. Þórr gave him Gullfaxi, the horse Hrungnir had ridden; Óðinn said Þórr did wrong to give so fine a horse to the son of a giantess and not to his own father. It is the whole of Magni's boyhood in one scene — and the only childhood the Edda gives any of the gods.

### The Hammer After (Vafþrúðnismál 51)

In the wisdom-contest, when Óðinn has wrung the fates of the gods from the giant Vafþrúðnir, one answer carries the brothers past the end of the world: 'Móði and Magni shall have Mjöllnir when Vingnir's fighting is done.' Vingnir is Þórr's own name. The prophecy does not flinch from what it costs — the father falls — and it states the inheritance plainly: the weapon passing whole into the hands of the sons.

### The Sons at Íðavöllr (Gylfaginning 51, 53)

At [[ragnarok|Ragnarǫk]] Þórr meets [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], the Midgard serpent, and strikes it dead — and walks nine paces before he falls to its venom. But the world does not end there: in Snorri's vision of the green earth after the fire, the survivors gather at Íðavöllr — Baldr and Höðr return from Hel, reconciled, and 'Þórr's sons Móði and Magni shall come there, and they shall have Mjöllnir.' The hammer survives the god.

### The Father's Boast (Hárbarðsljóð 53)

The Poetic Edda's other notice of Magni is genealogical: trading insults with the disguised ferryman, Þórr names himself at full strength — 'I am Óðinn's son, Meili's brother, and Magni's father' (*Magna faðir*). Of all his titles, the name he closes with is his son's. Skáldskaparmál's kennings agree, styling Þórr 'father of Magni and [[modi|Móði]] and [[thrud|Þrúðr]]'.

## Symbols & Iconography

Magni's iconography is narrative rather than cultic — the corpus gives him no temple and no regalia of his own, but his two scenes fixed a small set of attributes:

- **Hrungnir's leg** — The stone giant's fallen limb across Þórr's neck: the weight no god could move, and the boy's single feat
- **Gullfaxi** — 'Gold-mane', Hrungnir's stallion, given to Magni as the prize of the lifting — the gift that drew Óðinn's reproof: so fine a horse should not go to a giantess's son
- **Mjǫllnir** — Not yet his: the hammer he inherits with Móði after Ragnarǫk, the one treasure of the old world promised to the new
- **The whetstone shard** — The fragment of Hrungnir's weapon lodged in Þórr's head at the same duel: the scar that remained when the leg was lifted
- **Móði** — 'Wrath', his brother, named with him in both inheritance passages: the Edda never lets the heirs be counted singly

## Archaeology & Evidence

Magni is a purely textual figure: no runestone invokes him as a god, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely tied to his cult, and no picture stone has been convincingly read as the lifting of Hrungnir's leg. The material record keeps only his name's raw material: *Magni* occurs as an ordinary human personal name in Viking-Age runic inscriptions, built on the same *magn* 'strength' element that names the god.

**Magni** is catalogued under Strength, Son of Thor — and both halves of the domain are simply the content of his myth.

### Strength

His name is the common noun for strength itself, and his one feat is pure strength: lifting Hrungnir's stone leg off his father when the assembled Æsir could not.

### Son of Þórr

Skáldskaparmál's kennings for Þórr begin with his fatherhood — 'father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr' — and Hárbarðsljóð closes Þórr's self-naming with the same fact: *Magna faðir*.

### The Inheritance

Vafþrúðnismál 51 and Gylfaginning 53 agree: after Ragnarǫk, Magni and his brother Móði shall have Mjǫllnir — the hammer passing whole from the fallen father into the renewed world.

### Youth

He does it all at three nights old: the Edda's only divine childhood, and the proof the tradition offers that strength answers to nature, not to age.

## Across Cultures

Magni's scene belongs to one of the oldest hero-patterns in the Indo-European world: the prodigious infant. Greek tradition sets it at the beginning of [[herakles|Hēraklēs]]' life — the baby strangling the serpents in his cradle, told by Apollodorus and sung by Pindar in the first Nemean ode — and Irish tradition builds the boyhood deeds of [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]] on the same armature, the *macgnímrada* of the Táin, where a child performs the feats of grown champions. The North compressed the whole pattern into a single sentence: three nights old, and already the strongest person in the story. The comparison is one of motif, not borrowing — Simek and Lindow treat Magni as a native figure of the Þórr-complex, and no line of transmission is needed.

His name, meanwhile, is ordinary Germanic vocabulary: *maginą, 'strength', an element that built personal names across the North — so the strongest boy in the Edda wears the plainest possible label. Within the corpus, his closest kin are [[modi|Móði]], the brother named beside him in both inheritance passages, and [[thor|Þórr]], the father whose deed he completes and whose weapon he carries out of the fire.

## Cultural Legacy

Magni's afterlife ran quiet for centuries: the Icelandic given name *Magni* never died out, and Victorian mythographies kept the Hrungnir duel in circulation as one of Þórr's set-pieces — the Kearys' *The Heroes of Asgard* (1857) retold it for generations of children.

The twenty-first century put the brothers back on stage. Marvel Comics introduced Magni Thorson, a future son of Thor, in the 'Reigning' storyline of *Thor* in the early 2000s; and Santa Monica Studio's *God of War* (2018) cast Magni and Modi as their father's enforcers, carrying the pair to an audience far larger than the Edda's. Modern Heathenry keeps him among the sons of the Æsir honored for the survival of the world after Ragnarǫk — the generation for whom the hammer is kept.

## A Meditation

Magni is the Edda's answer to the question every parent eventually asks: will anyone be strong enough when I cannot stand up? The myth answers it twice. Once at Grjótúnagarðar, where the whole company of the gods heaves at a dead giant's leg and fails, and a three-night-old boy walks up and does it — strength, the story insists, is not a function of age or rank, and help can arrive from the person everyone overlooked.

And once at the end of the world, where the father kills the serpent, walks nine paces, and falls — and the hammer is not buried with him. Móði and Magni carry Mjǫllnir into the green world. The Edda does not promise that the strong live forever. It promises that strength, like the hammer, is inheritable.

## Mythology

The mythology of Mago is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

### Mago Shapes the Land (Creation myth)

In Korean folktales, Mago Halmi is so enormous that her body becomes the landscape. Her urine forms rivers, her sighs become wind, and her skirt covers mountains. She creates the topography of Korea through her movements and labour.

### The Skirt That Covered Mountains (Skirt motif)

A widespread motif tells how Mago spread her skirt to cover or move mountains, creating valleys and peaks. The motif links female creative power to textile work and to the shaping of the earth.

### Mago in the Gut (Ritual presence)

Shamans invoke Mago as a primordial mother who can restore order, heal illness, and bless the community. Her presence in ritual connects the immediate concerns of the living to the deep time of cosmic creation.

# Makemake: The Creator of Rapa Nui and Lord of the Bird-Man

On the most isolated inhabited island on Earth, a god named **Makemake** presided over creation, fertility, and one of the most extraordinary ritual competitions ever recorded. Rapa Nui, known to the wider world as Easter Island, is famous for its moai statues, but its religious life reached a climax in the bird-man cult of Orongo, where human representatives competed to retrieve the first egg of the sooty tern from a nearby islet. Makemake was the deity at the center of that cult, the creator who gave life to the island and the power who chose the year's sacred chief through the dangerous race. His name means "to see" or "to know," and both meanings resonate with a god who observes the competition, knows the outcome, and bestows fertility on the community through his chosen representative.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Makemake
- **ASCII form:** makemake
- **Meaning:** "To see, to know"
- **Domain of influence:** Creator, Fertility, Bird-Man
- **Pantheon:** Polynesian (Rapa Nui)
- **Classification:** Tier 2

## Overview

Makemake is the principal creator god of Rapa Nui, an island that lies more than 2,300 miles off the coast of Chile. In the beginning, according to Rapa Nui tradition, the world emerged from darkness, and Makemake shaped the island and its people. He is associated with the *tangata manu*, the bird-man, a human being who became the sacred leader for the year by bringing the first egg from the islet of Motu Nui. This cult replaced or supplemented the earlier moai-centered religion after the island's ecological crisis, and it remained central to Rapa Nui identity until the arrival of Christian missionaries in the nineteenth century.

In the PUNICODEX lexicon, Makemake is catalogued under "Creator, Fertility, Bird-Man." The three domains are tightly linked. Creation is the original act of making land and life. Fertility is the ongoing power that sustains crops, fish, and human reproduction. The bird-man is the ritual mechanism through which that fertility is channeled into political authority. Makemake is not a distant creator who withdraws after making the world; he continues to act through the annual competition and the figure of the bird-man.

## Etymology and Meaning

The name **Makemake** comes from the Rapa Nui verb *make*, which can mean "to see," "to know," "to want," or "to desire." The reduplicated form intensifies the sense, suggesting a god who sees deeply, knows thoroughly, or desires strongly. In some interpretations, Makemake is "the one who sees everything," an apt name for a deity who oversees the bird-man competition from his ceremonial village at Orongo.

The name's polysemy is itself theologically significant. To see is to know; to know is to desire; to desire is to create. Makemake embodies the continuity between perception, knowledge, and generative will. Unlike a god whose name simply denotes a function, Makemake's name describes a mode of consciousness, the alert, desiring awareness that brings the world into being and keeps it fertile.

Some scholars have also connected the name to words for abundance and growth, fitting a god whose primary concern is the fertility of the island. Whether the emphasis falls on seeing, knowing, or desiring, the name describes a deity who is actively engaged with the world rather than passively distant.

## Mythology and Domain

The creation myth of Rapa Nui tells that in the beginning there was nothing but the sea and the sky. Makemake appeared, and from his creative power the island emerged. He made the first humans, gave them the arts of life, and established the rituals through which they could maintain contact with the divine. Some traditions say that Makemake created the first man from a gourd or from a mixture of earth and divine breath, echoing creation stories from elsewhere in Polynesia while remaining distinctively Rapa Nui.

The bird-man cult is the most spectacular expression of Makemake's power. Each year, representatives of the island's clans descended the cliffs at Orongo and swam or paddled to the islet of Motu Nui, where the sooty tern nested. The first to find an intact egg and bring it back to Orongo intact won the competition. The winner, or sometimes his sponsor, became the *tangata manu*, the bird-man, and held sacred authority for the following year. The cult thus transformed a physical contest into a divinely sanctioned election: Makemake chose the victor, and through him the island's food supply was blessed.

The transition from the moai religion to the bird-man cult has been interpreted in many ways. Some scholars see it as a response to deforestation and social crisis, a shift from ancestor veneration to a more portable and competitive form of sacred authority. Others emphasize the continuity between the two systems, noting that both involve the negotiation of power through ritual and landscape. What is clear is that Makemake remained at the center of Rapa Nui religion throughout these changes, adapting his cult to new circumstances while retaining his role as creator and fertility-giver.

The cult also had political dimensions. The *tangata manu* was not merely a religious figure but a power broker who could redistribute resources, settle disputes, and command prestige. The competition was therefore a way of managing conflict without warfare, channeling rivalry into a ritual arena where Makemake's choice, revealed through the egg, was final.

## Pronunciation, Orthography, and the Restored Form

The name **Makemake** is pronounced with four syllables in Rapa Nui: ma-ke-ma-ke. The vowels are pure, and the stress pattern gives the name a rhythmic, almost chant-like quality. The reduplication is not merely decorative; it intensifies the meaning of the root *make*. In the PUNICODEX restoration, the name appears as **Makemake**, with capitalization restored and the doubled syllables preserved. There are no diacritics in this form, so the restoration does not introduce characters blocked by the .com IDN table. ## Cultural Legacy

Makemake's legacy is visible in the archaeology of Rapa Nui, particularly at Orongo, where stone houses, petroglyphs of bird-men, and the remains of the egg ceremony can still be seen. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage area and a focus of Rapa Nui cultural tourism and identity. For contemporary Rapa Nui people, Makemake is not merely a subject of archaeological interest but an ancestor and a source of spiritual connection to the land.

The name has also traveled into the solar system. In 2005, astronomers discovered a large Kuiper Belt object and named it Makemake in honor of the Rapa Nui creator god. A moon discovered orbiting Makemake was named *Hiiaka*, linking the Rapa Nui and Hawaiian pantheons in the outer reaches of the solar system. These namings reflect a growing practice of recognizing indigenous cultures in scientific nomenclature, though they have also raised questions about who has the authority to give such names and what responsibilities come with them.

In global popular culture, Makemake appears in games, comics, and speculative fiction, often as a creator deity associated with fertility and transformation. These representations vary widely in accuracy, and they underscore the importance of restoring the name in contexts that respect its Rapa Nui origins.

The story of **Makemake** does not end with mythology or ethnography. It continues every time someone types the name into a search engine, a chat message, or a browser's address bar. The Domain Name System was designed in an era when network engineers assumed that all meaningful identifiers could be written with the letters A to Z, the digits zero to nine, and a handful of punctuation marks. That assumption encoded a particular linguistic hierarchy into the infrastructure of the internet. English and a few closely related languages fit naturally; Hawaiian, Māori, Samoan, Tahitian, Rapa Nui, and hundreds of other languages did not. ## Scholarly Notes and the Fluid Geography of the Sacred

One of the most interesting features of Mamaqucha is the slipperiness of her domain. The same name can refer to the Pacific Ocean, to Lake Titicaca, or to any large body of water that functions as a maternal source. This fluidity challenges modern distinctions between sea, lake, river, and groundwater. In the Andean view, water is a continuous sacred substance that moves between these forms, and Mamaqucha names its personified power regardless of container.

This has made Mamaqucha a useful figure for scholars of environmental humanities. She offers a way of thinking about water that is not reducible to property, infrastructure, or commodity. Coastal fishing communities, highland lake communities, and urban migrants all relate to water through concepts that echo the old sea goddess, even when they no longer use her name. The restoration of Mamaqucha is therefore not only a philological act but an ecological one: it brings a water-centered theology back into public language.

The PuniCodex restoration underscores this by giving the name a stable, searchable presence. In a world of climate crisis and water conflict, the figure who personifies the sea as mother deserves to be spelled correctly. Mamaqucha is not a footnote to the Incan pantheon; she is a reminder that the most important resources are also relatives.

The restored name Mamaqucha invites us to think of water as kin, and of the sea not as a boundary but as a mother whose memory survives in language. The tides that once carried fishermen now carry data, and Mamaqucha sails both waters under her restored name.

## Scholarly Notes and the Gender of Time

Mama Quilla has attracted significant attention from feminist scholars of the Andes. As a lunar deity, she governs cycles: the month, the agricultural season, menstruation, pregnancy, and the rhythms of women's work. In a cosmology often dominated by solar, masculine, imperial imagery, the moon offers an alternative principle of organization. This does not mean that Mama Quilla was simply a goddess for women; men also participated in her cult and depended on the lunar calendar. But her cult provided a sacred framework for experiences that the solar cult could not fully address.

The syncretism between Mama Quilla and the Virgin Mary has been especially studied. The crescent moon, the association with fertility and marriage, and the timing of festivals all created opportunities for hidden continuity. Women could pray to the Virgin in church while still addressing the moon goddess in their hearts. This double voicing was a survival strategy under colonialism, but it also produced a rich religious aesthetics that persists in Andean Catholicism today.

The PuniCodex restoration of Mama Quilla preserves the two-word structure that colonial orthography often collapsed. In doing so, it honors the grammatical and theological partnership encoded in the name: Mama Quilla is not a single compressed word but a title, a relationship, a cosmology. The moon's address is a reminder that sacred time is not uniform; it has phases.

The restored name Mama Quilla keeps lunar time alive in a world that too often forgets that darkness and light follow one another in phases. Her monthly return is a promise that no eclipse is permanent and that cyclical time remains a viable alternative to the rush of modernity.

# How Mamaragan got its name back

The ASCII form *mamaragan* is missing something. **Mamaragan** restores the capitalization that turns a string of letters into a proper name — and that capital letter changes how the name is read, cited, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly record behind it, what the restoration preserves: the Aboriginal Australian context, the reconstructed sound, the mythology of the Lightning Ancestor, and the classification logic that places this name in Tier 2.

## At a Glance

- **ASCII form:** mamaragan
- **Meaning:** "The lightning"
- **Domain of influence:** Lightning Man, storm and wet-season renewal
- **Pantheon:** Aboriginal
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** None pre-contact; the name is a scholarly transliteration of an orally transmitted Kunwinjku/Kuninjku name

## Overview

**Mamaragan** (*mamaragan*) — Lightning Man, Aboriginal — belongs to the Kunwinjku/Kuninjku tradition of western Arnhem Land. The name means "the lightning" and refers to a powerful sky ancestor whose presence is manifest in the thunderstorms of the wet season.

Mamaragan is one of the lightning beings of the stone country. In rock art he appears as a human-like figure with zigzag lines of lightning radiating from his body; in oral tradition he travels with the wet-season storms, bringing rain, renewal, and the danger of the strike. His mythology encodes practical ecological knowledge: when to travel, when to shelter, and how to read the approach of the monsoon.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Mamaragan**. The plain ASCII form *mamaragan* is a technological compromise imposed by the early domain-name system, which could not carry capitalized proper names or Aboriginal script. The restoration capitalizes the conventional scholarly romanization. Because the source languages of western Arnhem Land were oral and the Latin transcription adds no distinctive diacritic or special letter beyond capitalization, the name is placed in Tier 2. The Unicode form remains the philologically complete reference; the ASCII spelling is a practical convenience for DNS.

## The Name

The name is attested in the language complex of western Arnhem Land as **Mamaragan**. Etymologically it is a proper noun referring to the Lightning Ancestor; it does not break down into smaller everyday lexical items in English.

The name is recorded with several romanizations — Mamarkan, Mamaregan, Mamaragen — reflecting different transcription conventions and dialectal variation. The form **Mamaragan** is the most widely attested in art books and ethnographic literature. In English the figure is often called the "Lightning Man" or "Lightning Ancestor," but these are descriptive glosses, not translations of the name itself.

The ASCII form *mamaragan* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry capitalized proper names or Aboriginal script. The Unicode restoration **Mamaragan** gives the conventional scholarly romanization with initial capitalization, the standard way to cite a proper name in English transcription. The name is Tier 2 because the restoration does not add a distinctive diacritic or special letter absent from the ASCII form; it simply restores the capitalization appropriate to a proper noun.

## Pronunciation

The conventional reading of the name is **/ˈma.ma.ɹa.ɡan/** — a Kunwinjku/Kuninjku approximation.

For the English speaker, the closest approximation is: 'MA-ma-ra-gan' — pronounce each vowel as a clear 'ah', keep the rhythm even, and avoid English diphthongs. The medial consonant may be a tap or an approximant depending on dialect and transcription convention.

Mamaragan is Tier 2 because the ASCII form *mamaragan* already represents the same phonemic sequence; no stress mark, length mark, or distinctive letter is required to recover the spoken name.

## Lightning, Thunder, and the Wet Season

Mamaragan's domain is the storm. In the build-up to the wet season, the humidity gathers and the first storms roll in from the sea. He is said to travel with these storms, his presence announced by thunder and the flash of lightning across the escarpment. The rains he brings transform the stone country: dry creek beds become running water, billabongs fill, and the country wakes from the long dry.

His symbols are those of the storm itself: the zigzag lightning that strikes from the clouds, the stone axe whose clash makes thunder, the dilly bag that carries his lightning weapons, and the rain cloud that is both his vehicle and his body. In rock art across western Arnhem Land, human-like figures with radiating lightning motifs preserve the visual language of this ancestor.

## Mythology and Meaning

The central myths of Mamaragan are seasonal and pedagogical. They teach that the lightning is not random but follows the paths of the ancestors; that the storm brings life as well as danger; and that human beings must read the signs of the country with respect. To be out in the open during a severe storm, or to ignore the warnings of the season, is to risk the ancestor's anger.

These stories are preserved in rock art, song cycles, dance, and the accumulated weather knowledge of senior custodians. They are part of a living tradition that continues to shape Aboriginal land management, art, and identity in northern Australia.

## Why This Restoration Matters

For a name like Mamaragan, the difference between *mamaragan* and **Mamaragan** can seem small. But capitalization is not cosmetic: it marks a proper name. The lowercase form is a string; the capitalized form is a person, an ancestor, a figure with a homeland and a people.

Because the Aboriginal languages of western Arnhem Land were transmitted orally until the twentieth century, there is no pre-contact written form to restore. What PuniCodex can do is preserve the scholarly convention: the capitalized romanization by which the figure is cited in art books, ethnographies, and respectful popular accounts. That convention is the closest thing to a canonical written form that the record allows.

# The hidden history behind Manannán

Behind the modern ASCII form *manannan* hides a much longer story. **Manannán** reaches back through manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral tradition long before it ever touched a keyboard, and every mark in the restored spelling is a receipt from that journey. In what follows we trace the name from its Medieval Irish (Latin script) attestations through its mythology, its cult, its symbols, and its afterlife in other cultures — and we show how the PuniCodex project turned that philological record into a Unicode domain that resolves today. The history was never lost. It was only waiting for the infrastructure to catch up.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Manannán
- **ASCII form:** manannan
- **Meaning:** "Son of the sea (from Old Irish Manannán)"
- **Domain of influence:** Sea, Otherworld, Mist
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Manannán mac Lir (Medieval Irish (Latin script))
- **Live domain:** manannán.com

## Overview

**Manannán mac Lir** (Old Irish *Manannán*; *mac Lir*, 'son of Lir', the personified sea) is the principal sea deity of medieval Irish tradition and the ruler of the Otherworld islands — Emain Ablach ('Region of Apple-trees'), Mag Mell ('Plain of Delights'), and Tír Tairngire ('Land of Promise') — that lie beyond the western wave. In the tale-complex of the Túatha Dé Danann he is numbered among that divine race, and after their defeat by the sons of Míl he becomes their over-king and apportions the sídhe (Otherworld mounds) among them. His earliest major appearance is in *Immram Brain maic Febail* ('The Voyage of Bran', seventh or eighth century), where he drives his chariot across a sea that to him is a flowering plain and prophesies the birth of his son Mongán and the coming of Christ. The early glossary *Sanas Cormaic* euhemerizes him as a master merchant-pilot of the Isle of Man, the best pilot in the west of Europe, from whom the island took its name.

Manannán is patron of voyagers, shape-shifter, and keeper of treasures — the horse Aonbharr, the boat Sguaba Tuinne, the sword Fragarach, and the concealing mist called féth fíada — and he figures as fosterer and provider of heroes, above all Lugh and Cormac mac Airt. PuniCodex restores the name as **Manannán**, preserving the long final vowel of the Old Irish form; the temple stands at [manannán.com](https://xn--manannn-mwa.com), with the plain ASCII *manannan* retained only as the domain-name system's technical fallback.

## The Name

The theonym is attested in Old and Middle Irish as **Manannán**, conventionally with the patronymic *mac Lir*, 'son of Lir'. *Lir* is the genitive of *ler*, 'sea, ocean', itself a personification of the sea, so medieval and modern interpreters alike gloss the full name 'Manannán, son of the sea'. The first element is generally derived from *Manann*/*Manau*, the Old Irish name of the Isle of Man, with the suffix *-án*; whether the god was named after the island or the island after the god was debated already in the medieval glossaries and remains unresolved. The Welsh cognate *Manawydan fab Llŷr* displays the same stem (*Manaw-*) and the same patronymic, though the precise historical relationship between the two figures — common inheritance or literary borrowing — is disputed.

The ASCII form *manannan* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an attested spelling. The Unicode restoration **Manannán** recovers the long final vowel, written with the Irish acute (*síneadh fada*), directly in the address bar; in the modern pronunciation of the name that long á also carries the stress. Because the restored form preserves the long final vowel — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the name is classed Tier 1 in the PuniCodex system.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Medieval Irish (Latin script) as **Manannán mac Lir** — Old Irish / Middle Irish in Insular script, attested Old Irish, c. 7th–10th c. CE, in Ireland, Isle of Man, Scotland. The script is written left-to-right.

The scholarly transliteration is *Manannán mac Lir* (Standard scholarly Old Irish orthography), giving the normalized reading /maˈnanˠaːn makʲ lʲeɾʲ/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Old Irish was written in the Latin alphabet using Insular minuscule from the early medieval period.
- The name appears in the Ulster Cycle and Mythological Cycle as Manannán mac Lir, 'son of Lir (the sea)'.
- The acute accent on the final á marks a long vowel in modern scholarly convention.
- The Unicode restoration Manannán preserves the long vowel; the ASCII form flattens the name.

Two cautions attach to the record: the etymology of the first element *Manann-* is debated — whether it derives from the Isle of Man or the island from the god is unresolved — and Insular script spelling varies across manuscripts.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/maˈnanˠən/** — Old Irish Reconstruction. For the complete name with patronymic, the normalized scholarly reading is /maˈnanˠaːn makʲ lʲeɾʲ/, with the long á of the final syllable and the slender (palatalized) consonants of *mac Lir*.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **M-** — Voiced bilabial nasal [m], as in English 'man'.
- **-a-** — Short open front [a], the first unstressed syllable.
- **-nan-** — Alveolar nasal [n], short open front [a], and another [n]; the second syllable carries stress.
- **-án** — Long open front [aː] marked by acute, ending in alveolar nasal [n].

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'muh-NAH-nawn' — stress the middle syllable, keep the first 'a' short, and lengthen the stressed 'ah' before the final 'n'. The double n hints at a slender or velarized quality in medieval Irish.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Irish** — Manannán mac Lir, 'Manannán son of Lir (the Sea)'
- **Manx** — Mannan beg mac y Leir, the folk figure behind the Isle of Man's name
- **Welsh** — Manawydan fab Llŷr, his Brythonic counterpart in the Mabinogi

Manannán is Tier 1: the acute on á marks the long vowel of the final syllable — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The double n reflects the Old Irish spelling; the name is traditionally explained as 'son of the sea' (mac Lir).

## Mythology

Manannán moves through Irish myth like the tide: now distant, now suddenly present, always connected to the boundary between worlds. He is not a creator or a warrior king but a guardian of passages — between islands, between life and death, between the known and the hidden.

### The Voyage of Bran (Immram Brain)

In *Immram Brain maic Febail*, Manannán meets Bran's ship driving a chariot across the open sea. From the god's perspective the ocean is a plain of flowers — Mag Mell, the Plain of Delights — and the ships upon it are chariots. In the poem he sings he foretells that he himself will go to Ireland and beget a son, Mongán mac Fiachnai, and he prophesies the coming of Christ: the text makes him the poet of the threshold, the one who explains what mortals cannot yet see.

### The Shrouded Island (Lebor Gabála)

The *Lebor Gabála Érenn* ('Book of Invasions') places Manannán among the Túatha Dé Danann as master of the féth fíada, the druidic mist with which the Otherworld island of Tír Tairngire is concealed from mortal eyes. Here he is less a sea god in the maritime sense than a deity of the invisible boundary between Ireland and the Otherworld.

### Over-King of the Túatha Dé Danann (Altram Tige Dá Medar)

In the late tale *Altram Tige Dá Medar*, set after the Milesian conquest, Bodb Derg is chosen king of the defeated Túatha Dé Danann and Manannán is made their over-king. He apportions the sídhe mounds among the divine race and grants them three protecting gifts: the Feast of Goibniu, which preserves them from age and decay; his swine, which return to life after being eaten; and the féth fíada that keeps their dwellings unseen.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Manannán concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the figure:

- **Boat Sguaba Tuinne** — The Wave-sweeper, a self-propelling currach that obeys its master's thought and needs neither sail nor oar; Manannán lends it to Lugh for the muster against the Fomorians in *Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann*.
- **Horse Aonbharr** — 'Enbarr of the Flowing Mane' in popular retelling, the steed that travels over land and sea alike; lent to Lugh with the boat.
- **Sword Fragarach** — 'The Answerer,' a blade that pierces every armour and, laid at a man's throat, compels the truth; it passed from Manannán to Lugh and on into later heroic tradition.
- **Cloak of mist** — The féth fíada, the veil that hides the Otherworld from mortal eyes; in *Altram Tige Dá Medar* Manannán grants it to the Túatha Dé Danann as one of their three protecting gifts.
- **Crane bag** — His treasure-bag, made from the skin of Aoife after she was transformed into a crane, from which the treasures of the divine race are produced.

## Archaeology & Evidence
Continue.

No archaeological record of a dedicated cult of Manannán is attested: no temple, votive assemblage, or inscription can be assigned to his worship. The evidence for his antiquity is onomastic and literary rather than monumental. The Isle of Man, recorded as *Monapia* by Pliny (Natural History 4.103) and as *Monaoida* by Ptolemy (Geography 2.2), preserves the Celtic *Manau* bound up with his name from the earliest tradition. The surviving ogham corpus, some four hundred stones of roughly the fourth to seventh centuries, records personal names in funerary and boundary formulae and yields no theonym — an epigraphic silence characteristic of Irish paganism, whose cult landscape is known through place-names and texts rather than altars. Votive deposition in Irish bogs, rivers, and lakes belongs to the broader ritual world in which a sea god's cult would have operated, but none of it names him.

## Realm & Domain

Manannán mac Lir is the **great sea god of Ireland and guardian of the Otherworld**. He rules the waves, the weather, and the mist that separates the mortal island from the Land of Promise. A shape-shifter, navigator, and bestower of marvelous weapons, he appears in myth as helper, host, and boundary-keeper between this world and the next.

### Sea Lord

He commands the waters around Ireland: in *Immram Brain* he drives his chariot across the open sea as though it were a level plain, and the glossary tradition euhemerizes him as the finest pilot in the west of Europe, skilled in the prognostication of weather.

### Otherworld Guardian

The mist that hides Tír Tairngire and the Isles of the Blessed is his cloak — the féth fíada, the druidic veil of concealment he later grants to the defeated Túatha Dé Danann together with their allotted sídhe.

### Treasure-Giver

He bestows weapons, cloaks, and horses on heroes who cross his path: the steed Aonbharr and the self-steering boat Sguaba Tuinne are lent to [Lugh](/lugh/) for the war against the Fomorians.

### Shape-Shifter

He moves between forms — rider on the wave, warrior at Cormac's Tara, stranger at the door — to test or aid mortals.

## Across Cultures

Manannán's closest counterpart is the Welsh [Manawydan](/manawydan/) fab Llŷr, who appears in the Second and Third Branches of the *Mabinogi* as a patient, just, and sea-associated figure married to the goddess Rhiannon. Both names show the Common Celtic stem *Manaw-* and the same patronymic, 'son of Lir/Llŷr'; whether the two figures descend from a shared Celtic deity or the name travelled between the two literatures is still debated. No continental equivalent is attested epigraphically: no Romano-Celtic altar can be securely read as addressed to him, so the comparison rests on the insular onomastic pair alone.

Within the Gaelic world the figure was absorbed rather than replaced. *Sanas Cormaic* euhemerizes him as a master merchant of the Isle of Man and the best pilot in the west of Europe, while Manx tradition makes Mannan beg mac y Leir the island's first king and namesake, a necromancer who kept his realm hidden under mists until Saint Patrick banished him.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [Ašeratu](/aseratu/), [Ọbalúayé](/babaluaye/), [Ēa](/ea/), [Njǫrðr](/njordr/), [Póntos](/pontos/), and [Poseidôn](/poseidon/), each linked through the sea — analogies of function across traditions rather than historical identifications.

## Cultural Legacy

Manannán's deepest legacy is onomastic. The Isle of Man preserves the Celtic *Manau*/*Manann* from which medieval scholars derived his name — or which derived from him; the direction was debated already in the glossaries. In Ireland, Lough Corrib was Loch Oirbsen, 'the lake of Oirbsen', an alias of Manannán in the Dindsenchas tradition, where the lake is said to be named for him. Manx folklore kept him as Mannan beg mac y Leir, first king and namesake of the island, to whom an annual rent of rushes was paid on the summit of South Barrule at Midsummer; the early sixteenth-century Traditionary Ballad records his rule, his mist-magic, and his expulsion by Saint Patrick.

The Celtic Revival restored him to literature through Lady Gregory's *Gods and Fighting Men* (1904), and modern imagination has made him a public figure again: a statue of Manannán mac Lir by sculptor John Darren Sutton stood at Gortmore on Binevenagh from 2013, was famously stolen in January 2015, and was replaced in 2016. Since 2009 the Isle of Man Steam Packet's fast ferry HSC *Manannan* has carried his name between Douglas and the Irish Sea ports — a working vessel named, in the company's own words, after the Celtic god of the sea.

## A Meditation

Manannán is the god of the horizon. He does not rule the land; he rules the mist that hides the land beyond the land. His gifts — the boat that needs no oars, the horse that runs on water, the sword that cannot be refused — are all instruments of passage.

To meet Manannán is to discover that what looked like an end is a door. The sea that separates Ireland from Tír na nÓg is the same sea that brings the fog, the fish, and the stranger. In the *Immram Brain* he crosses that sea in a chariot, because to him the ocean is a flowery plain; the image carries the whole discipline his figure embodies — trust the invisible road, accept the cloak of mist, and remember that every shore is someone else's threshold.

# The name Manawydan and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Manawydan** opens onto an entire world: the domain of sea, craftsmanship, a Celtic tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain that makes the whole structure addressable. *manawydan* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Manawydan
- **ASCII form:** manawydan
- **Meaning:** "Manannán (Welsh form)"
- **Domain of influence:** Sea, Craftsmanship
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Classification:** Tier 2

## Overview

**Manawydan** (*manawydan*) — Sea, Craftsmanship · Manannán (Welsh form) — is the counselor and craftsman of the Mabinogi: Manawydan fab Llŷr, brother of Brân the Blessed and Branwen, one of the seven survivors who brought Brân's wondrous head home from Ireland, and the hero of the Third Branch that bears his name — the man who, when Dyfed was emptied by enchantment, kept his patience, practiced three trades in exile, and unmade the spell by hanging a mouse and refusing three ransoms.

The Welsh figure is the Brythonic form of the being Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], the great sea god: the names are cognates, derived by Ifor Williams from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, and the fathers match exactly — Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each a personification of the sea. Where Manannán strides through Irish myth as a wonder-working god of mist and ships, the Mabinogi keeps the sea-kinship and the uncanny craft but files its Manawydan down to a mortal of patience and wisdom — a euhemerized sea god turned counselor.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Manawydan** — identical to the ASCII input, because Middle Welsh writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the figure. No domain is claimed: the plain-ASCII **manawydan.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

## The Name

The name is attested in Middle Welsh as **Manawydan**, normally with the patronymic — *Manawydan fab Llŷr*, 'Manawydan son of Llŷr' — in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. The derivation the scholarship prints is Ifor Williams's: the personal name is formed from **Manaw**, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man (and of Manaw Gododdin in the old North), so that Manawydan means, in effect, 'the Manxman' — and the Old Irish **Manannán** mac Lir is the exact cognate, the two names descending from a common Celtic inheritance rather than one borrowing the other. The lexicon gloss follows that line: 'Manannán (Welsh form)'. The derivation occasionally offered from a root *man- 'mind, thought' is not the one the handbooks carry, and this edition does not use it.

The patronymic does the theological work the given name no longer does. Llŷr is the Welsh form of Irish Lir, the sea personified — so that 'Manawydan son of Llŷr' and 'Manannán mac Lir' say the same sentence in two Celtic languages: the Manxman, son of the Sea.

The ASCII form *manawydan* loses nothing, because the Middle Welsh spelling is already plain Latin letters; the restoration is therefore a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as **Manawydan** — attested Middle Welsh, c. 11th–14th c. CE, in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5) and the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi, with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters; there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet in Insular-influenced scripts; the spelling Manawydan requires no diacritic.
- The stressed penult is -wy-, the glide [w] plus the high-central vowel [ɨ] — a sound the orthography writes with the plain letter y, which Welsh uses for [ɨ] and English lacks entirely.
- The name's kin are cross-language rather than orthographic: Old Irish Manannán mac Lir is the cognate, and the patronymic fab Llŷr matches mac Lir — the Manxman, son of the Sea.
- The Unicode restoration Manawydan is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

One caution attaches to the record: because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way decades ago — **manawydan.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release**. No form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/manaˈwɨdan/** — Middle Welsh.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ma-** — Bilabial nasal [m] and short open [a], unstressed
- **-na-** — Alveolar nasal [n] and a second short [a], unstressed
- **-wy-** — The stressed penult: the glide [w] into the Welsh high-central vowel [ɨ], the sound English has no letter for
- **-dan** — [d], short [a], [n], the unstressed final syllable

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'man-ah-WIH-dan' — stress the third syllable (the Welsh penult); the w is a quick glide, and the y is the Welsh central vowel [ɨ], closest to a tight, short 'ih'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Middle Welsh** — Manawydan fab Llŷr, in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest
- **Old Irish cognate** — Manannán mac Lir, the sea god of Ireland
- **Place-name** — Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man (and of Manaw Gododdin in the old North)
- **Manx** — Mannan beg mac y Leir, the folk survival of the same figure

Manawydan is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII loses: the letters of the manuscript form are the letters of the keyboard. The capital alone marks the temple form.

## Mythology

Manawydan's mythology is the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi — *Branwen ferch Llŷr*, where he is one of the seven who bring the head home, and *Manawydan fab Llŷr*, the branch that bears his name, which critics since Ifor Williams have called the most perfectly constructed of the Four.

### The Seven Who Brought the Head Home (Second Branch)

Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses festers into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host comes home as seven men: [[pryderi|Pryderi]], Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life. They feast seven years with it at Harlech, the three birds of [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] singing to them, then pass eighty years at Gwales in Penfro in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head — two doors open, one shut toward Cornwall — until Heilyn opens the third door and all their losses return like a tide. They bury the head in the White Mount in London, facing France, and the triads count the burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain.

### The Counsel and the Marriage (Third Branch)

While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi would have fought; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the Mabinogi — the best claim to vengeance declined out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan his mother Rhiannon's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed; the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship.

### The Thunder and the Mist (Third Branch)

They go up Gorsedd Arberth, and wonder comes: a peal of thunder, and a mist so thick they cannot see one another. When it lifts, Dyfed is gone — no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman, only the four and the empty land. For two years they live by hunting; in the third they grow weary of it, and the tale turns from endurance to answer.

### The White Boar and the Golden Bowl (Third Branch)

A boar shining white leads their dogs to a fortress neither man has ever seen. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in, finds a marble slab with a chained golden bowl, reaches for it — and his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon follows and is taken the same way, and with thunder and mist the fortress vanishes with them both. Manawydan is left with Cigfa, and the branch's second act belongs to them alone.

### The Three Crafts and the Trial of the Mouse (Third Branch)
Continue.

Manawydan will not beg in an emptied kingdom: at Hereford he becomes a saddler, then a shield-maker, then a shoemaker gilding shoes — each trade mastered at first attempt, each surrendered rather than repaid in blood when the guildsmen conspire. Back in Dyfed he sows three crofts of wheat; two are stripped overnight, and on the third night he keeps watch, sees a host of mice stripping the ears, and catches the fattest — slow, and heavy with young. He sets a miniature gallows on the gorsedd and condemns her as a thief. A scholar, then a priest, then a bishop offer ransom; he refuses each until the bishop hears the terms whole: Pryderi and Rhiannon freed, the enchantment lifted, no vengeance on the mice, and no spell on the seven cantrefs ever again. The bishop is Llwyd fab Cil Coed, enchanter and friend of Gwawl fab Clud — Rhiannon's jilted suitor of the First Branch — and the mice were his own household under shape, the fat one his wife. Pryderi comes back with the gate-hammers he had been made to carry, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about her neck, the mist lifts from Dyfed — and not one mouse is harmed.

## Symbols & Iconography

Manawydan's attributes are the props of the Third Branch — a set of objects that trace, in order, the snare and its undoing:

- **The golden bowl** — The enchanted vessel on the marble slab in the sudden fortress, wrought with a craftsmanship [[pryderi|Pryderi]] could not fathom: the snare that took him and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] by their own reaching
- **The white boar** — The shining lure that led the hunters out of the world: Otherworld white, like [[arawn|Arawn]]'s hounds and the marvels of [[annwn|Annwn]]
- **Gorsedd Arberth** — The mound above Arberth where the thunder fell and Dyfed vanished — and where Manawydan later tried his thief
- **The mouse on the gallows** — The fattest wheat-thief, caught and condemned as a felon: the smallest catch that bought back a kingdom, and the branch's emblem of patience armed with procedure
- **The shoemaker's last** — The three crafts of Hereford in one tool: saddler, shield-maker, golden shoemaker — craft as survival, finer than the guilds'

## Archaeology & Evidence

Manawydan is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120.

The geography of the Third Branch is real and visitable: Dyfed is the historic kingdom of southwest Wales; Arberth is Narberth in Pembrokeshire, and the gorsedd is traditionally located on the hill above it; the seven cantrefs of Dyfed were still an administrative reality when the tales were written. The nearest linguistic trace of the sea-kinship is onomastic rather than archaeological: Manaw survives in the Welsh name of the Isle of Man and in Manaw Gododdin, the district of the old North remembered in place-names such as Clackmannan and Slamannan.

## Realm & Domain

**Manawydan** is catalogued under the domain 'Sea, Craftsmanship' — the two words that carry, between them, his whole dossier: where he comes from, and how he survives.

### Sea

He is the son of Llŷr — the sea personified, the Welsh Lir — and brother of Brân and Branwen; the Welsh form of [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], lord of the waves and the mist between worlds. The Mabinogi never puts him on the water, but the kinship is the name itself: the Manxman, son of the Sea, in two Celtic languages at once.

### Craftsmanship

When Dyfed is emptied and he must live, Manawydan takes up craft after craft in exile at Hereford — saddler, then shield-maker, then shoemaker gilding shoes — and at each trade his work is so fine the local guildsmen conspire against him. The Welsh triads never forgot: they rank him among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain.

### The Counselor's Domain the Catalogue Cannot Hold

Between the two catalogued domains lies the quality the branch actually celebrates: patience as a method. He declines war with his cousin Caswallawn, endures the emptying of Dyfed, and wins everything back by watch-keeping and exact terms — the Mabinogi's one complete victory won without a drawn sword.

## Across Cultures

Manawydan's one great comparison is also the deepest fact about him: he is the Welsh form of the figure Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], sea god and guardian of the Otherworld. The names are cognates — Ifor Williams derived both from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man — and the fathers match exactly, Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each the sea personified. What the Welsh tradition did with the inheritance is the interesting part: where Manannán strides through Irish myth as a god of mist, ships, and wonder-working treasure, the Mabinogi keeps the sea-kinship and the uncanny craft but makes its Manawydan mortal, patient, and wise — a euhemerized sea god filed down to a counselor. Whether the Welsh figure descends from the Irish or both from a lost common sea god is debated; the handbooks register the kinship and leave the direction open.

Within the Welsh corpus his closest kin are the figures of his own branches: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], the queen he marries and rescues; [[pryderi|Pryderi]], the foster-son whose case he pleads; and [[arawn|Arawn]], whose First Branch exchange-of-kings sets the pattern of tested honor the Third Branch replays as tested patience. In Manx folklore the same figure survived as Mannan beg mac y Leir and gave the Isle of Man its name. No Gaulish counterpart has ever been convincingly proposed; the comparison is an insular affair, Irish Sea water on both sides of it.

## Cultural Legacy

Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Manawydan out of the White and Red Books and into English, and the Third Branch has held a special place ever since: critics from Ifor Williams onward have called it the most perfectly constructed of the Four Branches, and the trial of the mouse — the courtly ransomers, the miniature gallows, the terms exacted one by one — is the anthology piece of Welsh prose, comedy and wisdom in one tale. Scholarship gave the name its modern standing: Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text and the Manaw etymology, and Mac Cana's The Mabinogi made the branch's architecture a set text of Celtic studies.

Modern Druid and pagan practice honors Manawydan as a patron of craft, patience, and the sea-kinship; in Wales the name survives as a rare literary given name, carried less by folk memory than by the sheer durability of the Third Branch, which has never gone out of print since Guest.

## A Meditation

Manawydan is the Mabinogi's argument that wisdom is a kind of patience. Every test the tale sets him, he passes by declining the heroic option: when Caswallawn usurps the crown, he counts the cost of war and stays his hand; when Dyfed is emptied, he hunts, endures, and waits; when his companions are taken, he does not storm the fortress — he learns three trades and practices them beautifully in exile. Even his victory is procedural: a watch kept, a mouse caught, a gallows built, three ransoms refused, and terms — release, restoration, amnesty, guarantee — exacted one by one before the noose is loosened. He is the only hero in the Four Branches who wins everything he wants and kills nothing to get it.

The sea-named son of Llŷr spends his great story on land, but the sea is in the method: he outlasts what he cannot fight, and the tide turns. The question the branch leaves is uncomfortable and exact — how much of what we call courage is only impatience wearing armor?

# From Runes to Unicode: the journey of Máni

Long before it was a domain, this name traveled through scripts. **Máni** begins in Runes, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that journey preserves some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its spelling.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Máni
- **ASCII form:** mani
- **Meaning:** "Moon (the personified moon, brother of Sól)"
- **Domain of influence:** Moon, Night, Time
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Live domain:** máni.com

## Overview

**Máni** (*mani*) — Moon, Night, Time · Moon (the personified moon, brother of Sól) — belongs to the Norse tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Moon, Night, Time". The name means "Moon (the personified moon, brother of Sól)".

In the norse tradition, **Máni** is the moon itself made personal — the shining body that crosses the night sky, imagined as a god who steers it. Where Sól, his sister, drives the sun, Máni governs the gentler light: Snorri says he 'steers the course of the moon and rules the new and the waning moons,' the phases by which men first learned to count their days.

His is a charged quietness. The gods themselves assigned him his course, a wolf runs forever at his heels, and two earth-born children ride with him, their pail still visible on his face. Every month that turns is his signature: *mánaðr*, 'month', is his own word, and Monday is his day.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Máni** and serves its temple at [máni.com](https://xn--mni-ela.com). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *mani* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Máni** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Moon (the personified moon, brother of Sól)".

The ASCII form *mani* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Máni** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **á** — Acute on a
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same

The project holds the domain **máni.com** (xn--mni-ela.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

The original script for this norse name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.

The form **Máni** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

The Old Norse form is **máni**, the ordinary common noun 'moon' borne as a theonym, attested throughout the manuscript tradition of both Eddas. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the **Younger Futhark**, the name would be rendered approximately ᛘᛅᚾᛁ — the long á written with the ᛅ (óss) rune, the Younger Futhark's sign for the a-family vowels, nasalized and long alike; no runic inscription preserves the theonym itself. In the normalized Old Norse spelling the acute on *á* marks vowel length, [ɑː], the same long vowel heard in 'father'. The PUNICODEX registrable form *Máni* preserves that acute as a Tier-1 restoration — the single distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses — carrying the long vowel that links the god directly to *mánaðr*, the month he measures.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈmɑːni/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **M-** — Bilabial nasal [m], unchanged from Proto-Germanic *m to Old Norse; the name opens with the same consonant as English 'moon'
- **-á-** — Long open back [ɑː] with the acute marking length; Old Norse stress falls on the first syllable by default
- **-ni** — Short alveolar nasal [n] and close front [i]; the light second syllable of the nominative singular

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'MAH-nee' — hold the first vowel long and open, as in 'father', with the weight squarely on the first syllable and a quick, light '-nee' to close.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old English** — Mōna, the masculine moon of the Anglo-Saxons, whose name survives in Monday (Mōnandæg)
- **Old High German** — Māno, the continental Germanic moon, likewise masculine
- **Proto-Germanic** — *Mēnô, 'moon', a masculine noun — an inheritance the Germanic languages kept where most Indo-European tongues made the moon feminine
- **Modern Icelandic** — Máni, the living reflex, unchanged in form and gender

Máni is Tier 1: the acute on á marks the long vowel [ɑː], a distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses; Old Norse initial stress is the default and needs no further mark. The name is simply the common noun máni, 'moon', raised to a person — the same word that gives mánaðr, 'month'. Attestation and reconstruction follow Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. máni; and Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. máni.

## Mythology

Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him three scenes — a father's fatal boast, a wolf's patient pursuit, and two children lifted from a well — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face. Around those scenes gathers the quieter charge the *Vafþrúðnismál* records: the gods shaped the new and waning moons so that men could reckon their years.

### Mundilfari's Boast (Vafþrúðnismál / Gylfaginning)

In the *Vafþrúðnismál*, the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike. Snorri, in *Gylfaginning*, gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr. The gods were angered by this *ofdramb* — this overweening pride — and took the siblings and set them in the heavens.

The punishment is an appointment. Sól is made to drive the horses of the sun, Árvakr and Alsviðr, while Máni is charged with steering the course of the moon and ruling its waxing and waning. What a father claimed in arrogance, the gods confirmed in office: the names became the duties, and the children became the sky.

### The Wolf at the Moon's Heels (Grímnismál / Gylfaginning)

The moon does not drift; it flees. Snorri explains its speed by its hunter: two wolves run with the lights of heaven, and Hati Hróðvitnisson is the one who runs before the moon and means to take it — 'and so it will come to pass.' The *Grímnismál* knows the same pursuit, naming Hati as the son of Hróðvitnir who waits upon the bright bride of the sky.

The chase has an ending, and the Eddas do not flinch from it. From the Iron-Wood brood, Snorri says, will come the mightiest wolf of all, called Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound: he fills himself with the lives of all who die, swallows the moon, and spatters heaven and air with blood, so that the sun loses its shining. The *Vǫluspá* names him the moon's devourer in a troll's skin. At Ragnarǫk the long pursuit is finished, and the calendar itself goes dark.

### Bil and Hjúki at the Well (Gylfaginning)

Snorri records that Máni took two children up from the earth, Bil and Hjúki, as they walked from the well called Byrgir, carrying on their shoulders the pail Sægr — often read as a mead-tub — slung from the pole Simul. Their father is named Viðfinnr. 'These children follow Máni,' Snorri adds, 'as can be seen from earth': look at the moon and you will find them there.

This is the Norse answer to the man in the moon — not a face but two small figures under a burden, fixed forever in mid-errand. The detail of the well, the pail, and the pole is too homely to be invented ornament; it reads as the residue of nursery-lore older than the manuscript, the kind of story told to children who had already been shown the markings in the moon. Scholars have sometimes linked the pair to the Jack and Jill of English rhyme, but that connection is modern speculation, not attestation.

The iconography associated with Máni concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

## Archaeology & Evidence

Máni has no secure iconography: no picture stone, runestone, or amulet has been convincingly identified as his image, and his attestation is essentially textual. The Poetic Edda poems that name him — Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, and Vǫluspá — survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), with Vǫluspá also in the Hauksbók; Snorri's account in Gylfaginning is transmitted by the main Snorra Edda manuscripts (GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis, Codex Wormianus). The older strata of Scandinavian sky-religion are, however, material: the Bronze Age Trundholm sun chariot (c. 1400 BC) proves a native tradition of a heavenly body drawn by horse across the sky, and wheel- and disc-marked Gotland picture stones show the sun and moon as enduring cultic signs. The runic record knows the common noun máni and the month-names descended from it, but no runic inscription names the god directly.

## Realm & Domain

In the norse tradition, **Máni** is the moon itself made personal — the shining body that crosses the night sky, imagined as a god who steers it. Where Sól, his sister, drives the sun, Máni governs the gentler light: Snorri says he 'steers the course of the moon and rules the new and the waning moons,' the phases by which men first learned to count their days.

His is a charged quietness. The gods themselves assigned him his course, a wolf runs forever at his heels, and two earth-born children ride with him, their pail still visible on his face. Every month that turns is his signature: *mánaðr*, 'month', is his own word, and Monday is his day.

### Mundilfari's Boast

A father's pride named his children Moon and Sun; the gods answered the boast by setting the pair to drive the lights of heaven.

### Hati's Pursuit

The wolf Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon and will one day take it; at Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound swallows the light and spatters the sky with blood.

### Bil and Hjúki

Two children with a pail on a pole, taken up from the well Byrgir; they follow Máni, Snorri says, 'as can be seen from earth' — the man in the moon.

### Measurer of Months

He rules the new and waning moons, the counting of time itself; mánaðr, 'month', is his word, and the calendar was his first temple.

## Across Cultures

Máni belongs to the common Germanic inheritance in which the moon is grammatically and mythologically **masculine** — Old English *Mōna*, Old High German *Māno*, Gothic *mēna* — a striking counterweight to the feminine moons of the classical world, Greek *Selēnē* and Latin *Luna*. The word itself runs deeper: Proto-Indo-European **mḗh₁nōt-* / **mḗh₁n̥s* meant both 'moon' and 'month', the double sense Máni still carries in *mánaðr*, so that his personification is the personification of time-reckoning itself. The pairing of a moon-god with a sun-goddess, brother and sister, is the Germanic reversal of the Greek Selene and Helios pattern, though the daily celestial chase — light pursued by devourer — has echoes from the wolves of Ragnarǫk back to the eclipse-monsters of other traditions. The liveliest survival is folkloric: the Norse reading of the moon's markings as two children with a pail stands at the head of the whole northern 'man in the moon' tradition that later fills English ballads and nursery rhymes, and the tempting equation of Hjúki and Bil with Jack and Jill has been argued since the nineteenth century — as speculation, never as proof.

Within the Norse tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], [[bifrost|Bifrǫst]], [[buri|Búri]], [[eggther|Eggþér]], [[fafnir|Fáfnir]], and [[helheimr|Helheimr]].

## Cultural Legacy

Máni's deepest legacy is calendrical: every **month** and every **Monday** in the Germanic-speaking world is his, for Mōnandæg and its Norse kin are simply the moon's day, and the words descend from his name. In literature his clearest heir is Tolkien's Tilion, the Maia who steers the vessel of the moon across the sky — the personified moon-driver of the Eddas translated into a new mythology. Notably, Wagner left him out: the *Ring* runs on gold, fire, and Wotan's will, and the moon-driver never steps onto that stage, a measure of how thin Máni's high-cultural afterlife is beside Þórr's or Óðinn's. The chase around him fares better: the pursuing wolves Skǫll and Hati stalk recent retellings, including *God of War Ragnarök* (2022), where the stolen moon and its hunters drive a whole arc of the story. And the oldest survival is still the most democratic — the face and figures people point out to children in the full moon, which Snorri already explained by Bil and Hjúki eight centuries ago. In modern heathenry Máni is honored quietly, at the turning of the months he still measures.

## A Meditation

Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. **Máni** compresses the oldest technology there is: the counting of time by a light that reliably changes. Before calendars were written they were watched, and the watcher-god is the moon — not its conqueror, like Þórr riding out, but its keeper, driving a course he did not choose, with a wolf behind him and two lost children for company. His myth is the honest one about time: it moves because it is pursued, it is beautiful because it is borrowed, and it will one day be swallowed. # How Mañjuśrī got its accent back

The ASCII form *manjushri* is missing something. **Mañjuśrī** restores the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Devanagari evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the classification logic that separates Tier 1 restorations from Tier 2. By the end, the marks in Mañjuśrī will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Mañjuśrī
- **ASCII form:** manjushri
- **Meaning:** "Gentle glory"
- **Domain of influence:** Wisdom, Intellect
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** मञ्जुश्री (Devanagari)
- **Live domain:** mañjuśrī.com

## Overview

**Mañjuśrī** (*manjushri*) — Wisdom, Intellect · The Gentle Glory, Sword of Wisdom — is the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom (prajñā): the ever-youthful prince of the Mahāyāna who wields the flaming sword that cuts through ignorance and carries the book of the Perfection of Wisdom on his lotus.

His name joins *mañju*, ‘gentle, beautiful, charming’, with *śrī*, ‘glory, splendour, majesty’ — ‘Gentle Glory’. The tradition hears the softness as the point: true wisdom is not harsh, and the sword that ends confusion is wielded by a boy. He is the bodhisattva who dares what others will not — in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa he alone accepts the call to visit the sick layman — and the patron of every student, scholar, and debater in the Buddhist world, from the academies of Nālandā to the examination halls of Tibet.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Mañjuśrī** and serves its temple at [mañjuśrī.com](https://xn--majur-pta32bwm.com). The restoration keeps the palatal ñ, the palatal ś, and the long final ī of the Sanskrit; the plain ASCII *manjushri* is a modern convenience of the early domain-name system, not an attested ancient spelling.

## The Name

The name is attested in Sanskrit as **मञ्जुश्री** (IAST *mañjuśrī*): a compound of *mañju*, ‘gentle, sweet, lovely’, and *śrī*, ‘glory, splendour’ — ‘Gentle Glory’ or ‘Sweet Majesty’. His epithets extend the music: **Mañjughoṣa**, ‘Gentle Voice’ (or ‘Beautiful Sound’); **Kumārabhūta**, ‘the Ever-Youthful’, for he is always figured as a prince of sixteen; and **Vāgīśvara**, ‘Lord of Speech’, the orators' bodhisattva.

The ASCII form *manjushri* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling, and it flattens three distinctive letters — the palatal nasal ñ, the palatal sibilant ś, and the long ī — into approximations. The Unicode restoration **Mañjuśrī** recovers all three directly in the address bar. Because the restoration preserves distinctive letters and vowel length the ASCII form loses, the name is classified Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
